fleet/cargo-spacecraft/atv.json.name: ATV (Automated Transfer Vehicle)
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/atv.json.tagline: ESA's flagship ISS cargo carrier; 5 flights
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/atv.json.dispatch: The Automated Transfer Vehicle was Europe's ISS freighter and the most sophisticated cargo craft of its time — a twenty-tonne spacecraft that navigated itself to a fully automatic docking with the Station, delivered cargo, water, air and propellant, and used its own engines to reboost the entire ISS in orbit. Five flew between 2008 and 2015, each named for a European thinker from Jules Verne to Georges Lemaître. More than a supply truck, the ATV was how Europe earned its place as a full ISS partner — and the technology it proved lives on as the European Service Module that now powers NASA's Orion on its way to the Moon.
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/atv.json.description: ATV (Automated Transfer Vehicle) is a robotic cargo spacecraft built by Astrium / Airbus in Europe. ESA's flagship ISS cargo carrier that flew five missions to the ISS from 2008 to 2015, delivering cargo, water, air and propellant while using its engines to reboost the Station.
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/atv.json.best_known_for: ESA's flagship ISS cargo carrier; 5 flights

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cargo-dragon-2.js.name: Cargo Dragon 2
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cargo-dragon-2.js.tagline: Successor to Cargo Dragon v1; trunk-mounted PV
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cargo-dragon-2.js.description: The crewless variant of Crew Dragon, with the same body-mounted solar cells on the trunk. Differs visibly from Cygnus (round arrays) and Soyuz/Progress (rectangular wings). Returns intact with downmass — unique among ISS cargo carriers.
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cargo-dragon-2.js.best_known_for: Successor to Cargo Dragon v1; trunk-mounted PV

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cargo-dragon-v1.j.name: Cargo Dragon v1
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cargo-dragon-v1.j.description: The first commercial spacecraft to berth with the ISS (COTS-2, May 2012); first contracted ISS resupply (CRS-1, October 2012). Twenty-one CRS missions plus two COTS demonstrations flew between 2010 and 2020 before the upgraded Dragon 2 took over.

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cygnus-enhanced.j.name: Cygnus Enhanced
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cygnus-enhanced.j.description: Northrop Grumman’s pressurised-cargo carrier, recognisable by its round UltraFlex solar arrays — a fan-fold accordion pattern shared with no other ISS visitor. Burns up on reentry; no downmass.

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cygnus-standard.j.name: Cygnus Standard
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/cygnus-standard.j.description: Cygnus Standard is a robotic cargo spacecraft built by Orbital Sciences in USA. Pressurised-only ISS cargo carrier. Flew 2013–2014; succeeded by the Enhanced Cygnus.

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/htv-x.json.name: HTV-X
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/htv-x.json.description: HTV-X (Kounotori-X) is JAXA's second-generation cargo spacecraft, successor to the original HTV. The first vehicle (HTV-X1) launched October 26, 2025, berthed with the ISS on October 29, and re-entered May 27, 2026. HTV-X2 is planned.

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/htv.json.name: HTV (Kounotori)
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/htv.json.tagline: Japan's H-II Transfer Vehicle to ISS
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/htv.json.description: HTV (Kounotori) is a robotic cargo spacecraft built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries in Japan. Japan's H-II Transfer Vehicle flew nine missions to the ISS from 2009 to 2020, with HTV-9 (the final flight) departing in May 2020.
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/htv.json.best_known_for: Japan's H-II Transfer Vehicle to ISS

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/progress-7k-tg.js.name: Progress 7K-TG
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/progress-7k-tg.js.description: The first robotic cargo spacecraft, derived from Soyuz. Forty-three Progress flights to Salyut and early Mir between 1978 and 1990 established the architecture every subsequent ISS resupply has followed.

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/progress-m.json.name: Progress M
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/progress-m.json.description: Progress M is a robotic cargo spacecraft built by RKK Energia in Russia. The modernised Progress-M served Mir and the ISS across 97 missions from 1989 to 2021, before being superseded by Progress-MS.

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/progress-ms.json.name: Progress MS
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/progress-ms.json.description: Progress MS is a robotic cargo spacecraft built by RKK Energia in Russia. Current Progress generation; ISS resupply. In service since 2015.

fleet/cargo-spacecraft/tianzhou.json.name: Tianzhou
fleet/cargo-spacecraft/tianzhou.json.description: China’s cargo spacecraft for the Tiangong space station, sharing spacecraft bus heritage with Tiangong-1. Refuels Tiangong’s propellant tanks and delivers experiment racks; first flight in 2017.

fleet/constellation/beidou.json.name: BeiDou (北斗)
fleet/constellation/beidou.json.tagline: China's GNSS — global ops since 2020; unique MEO + IGSO + GEO hybrid
fleet/constellation/beidou.json.description: China's GNSS, formally BeiDou-3 in current form. Unique hybrid architecture mixing MEO (24 satellites at 21,500 km, 55°), inclined geosynchronous (IGSO, 3 satellites), and GEO (3 satellites). Full global coverage declared July 2020. The only GNSS with short-message satellite communication capability built into the signal — users can send short text messages directly through the constellation, useful in remote-area emergency comms.
fleet/constellation/beidou.json.best_known_for: China's GNSS — global ops since 2020; unique MEO + IGSO + GEO hybrid

fleet/constellation/galileo-gnss.json.name: Galileo (GNSS)
fleet/constellation/galileo-gnss.json.tagline: Europe's civilian GNSS — ~30 sats, sub-metre positioning
fleet/constellation/galileo-gnss.json.description: Europe's civilian GNSS — 34 satellites have been launched (4 IOV + 30 FOC); 27 operational + 1 commissioning as of May 2026; constellation target is 30 at 23,222 km MEO in 3 orbital planes inclined 56°. First operational service 2016; full operational capability declaration pending ESA/EUSPA official announcement. Unlike GPS (military operator) and GLONASS (military operator), Galileo is managed by EUSPA, an EU civilian agency. Designed for sub-metre positioning with open + commercial + Public Regulated Service tiers. Search and Rescue payload integrated for emergency-beacon detection.
fleet/constellation/galileo-gnss.json.best_known_for: Europe's civilian GNSS — ~30 sats, sub-metre positioning

fleet/constellation/glonass.json.name: GLONASS
fleet/constellation/glonass.json.tagline: Russia's GNSS — 24 sats, restored to full coverage in 2011
fleet/constellation/glonass.json.description: Russia's GNSS — 24 active satellites at 19,130 km MEO in 3 planes inclined 64.8° (the high inclination is deliberate for better high-latitude coverage relative to GPS). First launched 1982; reached full constellation in 1995, then collapsed in the late 1990s / early 2000s after Soviet funding ended; restored to full 24-satellite operational status around 2010-2011 with funding revival. Continues operational in 2026. Operated by Roscosmos in coordination with the Russian Ministry of Defence.
fleet/constellation/glonass.json.best_known_for: Russia's GNSS — 24 sats, restored to full coverage in 2011

fleet/constellation/goes-noaa.json.name: GOES (NOAA Weather)
fleet/constellation/goes-noaa.json.tagline: NOAA geostationary weather pair — Americas continuous coverage
fleet/constellation/goes-noaa.json.description: Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite — NOAA's geostationary weather pair. GOES-19 (GOES-East at 75.2° W) and GOES-18 (GOES-West at 137.0° W) are the operational pair as of April 2025, providing continuous coverage of the Americas. GOES-16 is stored as backup; GOES-17 was decommissioned in January 2023. The GOES-R series carries the Advanced Baseline Imager capable of 30-second mesoscale scans for hurricane cores and severe-storm tracking. Built by Lockheed Martin; data products freely available.
fleet/constellation/goes-noaa.json.best_known_for: NOAA geostationary weather pair — Americas continuous coverage

fleet/constellation/gps-gnss.json.name: GPS (Global Positioning System)
fleet/constellation/gps-gnss.json.tagline: The original GNSS — 31 satellites, free public service since 2000
fleet/constellation/gps-gnss.json.description: Global Positioning System — the original GNSS and still the most widely used. 31 active satellites at 20,180 km in 6 orbital planes inclined 55°. Operated by US Space Force; originally Department of Defense. President Reagan's 1983 directive promised future civilian GPS access after the Korean Air Lines 007 shootdown, but civilian unencrypted L1 C/A signal access was not available until Selective Availability was turned off in May 2000, dramatically improving civilian accuracy. Modernised L1C, L2C, L5 signals on Block IIF and III satellites.
fleet/constellation/gps-gnss.json.best_known_for: The original GNSS — 31 satellites, free public service since 2000

fleet/constellation/inmarsat.json.name: Inmarsat
fleet/constellation/inmarsat.json.tagline: GEO mobile comms — maritime, aviation, GMDSS backbone
fleet/constellation/inmarsat.json.description: Geostationary mobile-satellite communications — 14+ satellites in GEO providing maritime, aviation, and remote-area voice + data services. Originally founded 1979 as the International Maritime Satellite Organization, an intergovernmental treaty body for ship-to-shore comms (the predecessor of GMDSS). Privatised 1999. Acquired by Viasat in 2023 to combine with Viasat's Ka-band fleet.
fleet/constellation/inmarsat.json.best_known_for: GEO mobile comms — maritime, aviation, GMDSS backbone

fleet/constellation/iridium-next.json.name: Iridium NEXT
fleet/constellation/iridium-next.json.tagline: Polar LEO comms — 66 operational sats +9 spares, GMDSS partner, global voice/data
fleet/constellation/iridium-next.json.description: Second-generation Iridium constellation — 66 operational satellites at 780 km in 6 polar planes (11 per plane), with 9 on-orbit spares, deployed 2017-2019 to replace the original 1998 Iridium fleet. Total of 75 satellites were launched; 5 additional ground spares were launched in May 2023. Carries voice + data + machine-to-machine + sat-phone services. One of two GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) satellite providers (alongside Inmarsat) — ocean-going vessels can fulfill GMDSS requirements via Iridium OR Inmarsat. The collision of the original Iridium 33 with derelict Cosmos 2251 in 2009 was the first known satellite-to-satellite collision in history.
fleet/constellation/iridium-next.json.best_known_for: Polar LEO comms — 66 operational sats +9 spares, GMDSS partner, global voice/data

fleet/constellation/kuiper.json.name: Amazon Leo (formerly Project Kuiper)
fleet/constellation/kuiper.json.tagline: Amazon LEO broadband — 3,236 sats planned, commercial beta 2026
fleet/constellation/kuiper.json.description: Amazon's answer to Starlink — 3,236 satellites at 590-630 km in 98 orbital planes. First prototype launch in October 2023 (KuiperSat-1 and -2 test launch); first 27 production satellites launched April 2025 atop Atlas V. As of mid-2026, ~230+ production satellites are operational. FCC license requires 50% deployment (1,618 sats) by July 2026 and 100% by July 2029; Amazon has requested a two-year extension due to the current shortfall. The constellation is expected to roughly double the LEO active-satellite population if fully deployed.
fleet/constellation/kuiper.json.best_known_for: Amazon Leo broadband — 3,236 sats planned, commercial beta 2026

fleet/constellation/landsat.json.name: Landsat
fleet/constellation/landsat.json.tagline: 50+ years of continuous Earth imaging — Landsat 1 to 9
fleet/constellation/landsat.json.description: The longest continuous record of Earth imaging in history — Landsat 1 launched 1972 (originally as ERTS-1), continuing through Landsat 9 (2021). Currently operational pair Landsat 8 (2013) + Landsat 9 (2021) at 705 km sun-synchronous orbit, 98.2° inclination. 30 m multispectral resolution. NASA builds + launches; USGS operates and distributes data. Free public access since 2008 turned Landsat into the global reference dataset for climate change, deforestation, and urban growth.
fleet/constellation/landsat.json.best_known_for: 50+ years of continuous Earth imaging — Landsat 1 to 9

fleet/constellation/molniya.json.name: Molniya
fleet/constellation/molniya.json.tagline: Russian 12-hour HEO comms — 63.4° critical inclination locks apogee over the north
fleet/constellation/molniya.json.description: Russian highly-eccentric orbit constellation. The 12-hour Molniya orbit (~600 × 40,000 km) at the 63.4° critical inclination exploits Earth's J2 perturbation to lock the line of apsides — apogee stays parked over the Northern Hemisphere, giving high-latitude users elevation angles a geostationary satellite can never deliver. Molniya-1 launched in 1965; the line continued through Molniya-1/2/3, the Oko early-warning satellites, and the Meridian comms successor in service today.
fleet/constellation/molniya.json.best_known_for: 12-hour HEO at 63.4° critical inclination — apogee parked over Russia

fleet/constellation/o3b-mpower.json.name: O3b / O3b mPOWER (MEO comms)
fleet/constellation/o3b-mpower.json.tagline: Only operational MEO commercial broadband — 20+ sats
fleet/constellation/o3b-mpower.json.description: The only operational commercial MEO broadband constellation — original O3b deployed 2013-2019, second-generation O3b mPOWER from 2022 onwards. 20+ satellites at 8,063 km equatorial orbit. Latency between GEO and LEO, customer base focused on telecom backhaul, maritime, and remote enterprise. Operated by SES (Luxembourg). Named for the 'other 3 billion' — the original mission was bringing connectivity to areas not served by terrestrial broadband.
fleet/constellation/o3b-mpower.json.best_known_for: Only operational MEO commercial broadband — 20+ sats

fleet/constellation/oneweb.json.name: OneWeb
fleet/constellation/oneweb.json.tagline: First-gen LEO broadband — 648 sats in 12 polar planes
fleet/constellation/oneweb.json.description: First-generation LEO broadband constellation, 648 satellites at 1,200 km in 12 polar planes. Polar orbits give full pole-to-pole coverage that mid-inclination Starlink shells cannot reach. Acquired by Eutelsat in 2023 to form Eutelsat OneWeb; commercial service now bundled with Eutelsat GEO assets. Higher altitude than Starlink means slightly higher latency but fewer satellites needed.
fleet/constellation/oneweb.json.best_known_for: First-gen LEO broadband — 648 sats in 12 polar planes

fleet/constellation/planet-labs.json.name: Planet Labs (PlanetScope + SkySat)
fleet/constellation/planet-labs.json.description: Daily-revisit Earth imaging from two fleets — ~150 PlanetScope 3U CubeSats (3-5 m resolution global daily imagery) and ~21 SkySats (50 cm tasked high-resolution). All at ~475 km sun-synchronous orbit. The 'Doves' philosophy was 'launch hundreds of cheap small satellites, accept a few failures, get every patch of land imaged every day' — and it works. Planet's image archive is consulted by NGOs, governments, and journalists.

fleet/constellation/sbirs-heo.json.name: SBIRS-HEO
fleet/constellation/sbirs-heo.json.tagline: US early-warning IR sensors hosted on classified Tundra-orbit platforms
fleet/constellation/sbirs-heo.json.description: The HEO segment of the US Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) — infrared missile-warning sensors hosted on classified host satellites in the 24-hour Tundra orbit at the 63.4° critical inclination. By dwelling at apogee over high latitudes, SBIRS-HEO covers the polar regions where geostationary DSP / SBIRS-GEO sensors look at too low an angle. SBIRS HEO-1 launched in 2006 as a hosted payload on USA-184.
fleet/constellation/sbirs-heo.json.best_known_for: HEO-segment IR early warning — covers polar latitudes the GEO sensors can't

fleet/constellation/sentinel-copernicus..name: Sentinel (Copernicus)
fleet/constellation/sentinel-copernicus..description: Europe's flagship Earth-observation programme, operated by ESA on behalf of the European Commission's Copernicus environmental-monitoring service. Sentinel-1 (C-band SAR radar imaging), Sentinel-2 (multispectral optical at 10-60 m), Sentinel-3 (ocean + land), Sentinel-5P (atmospheric chemistry), Sentinel-6 (altimetry). All in sun-synchronous LEO. Free + open data policy — every Sentinel image is downloadable without licensing fees.

fleet/constellation/starlink.json.name: Starlink
fleet/constellation/starlink.json.tagline: Largest LEO broadband constellation — over 11,000 active satellites (as of October 2026)
fleet/constellation/starlink.json.description: SpaceX's broadband LEO constellation — over 11,000 active satellites (as of October 2026) at 550 km altitude split across multiple shells (53°, 70°, 97.6° inclinations). First operational service 2019; achieved global coverage 2023. Each Gen-2 satellite carries laser inter-satellite links, allowing the constellation to route packets between satellites without ground station hops. Autonomous collision-avoidance system performed over 355,000 manoeuvres from June 2025 to May 2026.
fleet/constellation/starlink.json.best_known_for: Largest LEO broadband constellation — over 11,000 active satellites (as of October 2026)

fleet/constellation/tundra-sirius.json.name: Sirius Satellite Radio (Tundra) — Historical (2000-2016)
fleet/constellation/tundra-sirius.json.description: Historic satellite-radio constellation in the 24-hour Tundra orbit (~25,000 × 35,786 km) at the 63.4° critical inclination. The three original Sirius FM satellites (FM-1, FM-2, FM-3) each dwelt over CONUS for roughly two-thirds of every orbit, giving urban-canyon receivers elevation angles a geostationary signal couldn't match. Sirius FM-1 launched from Baikonur in 2000 on a Proton-K; FM-2 and FM-3 followed. The company merged with XM Radio in 2008 to form Sirius XM. The Tundra-orbit constellation was decommissioned in 2016, and Sirius XM now operates a fleet of ~7 geostationary satellites.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-csm-block.tagline: Original Apollo CSM design — never flew crewed; killed Apollo 1 crew on the pad 1967-01-27. Redesign produced the Block II flown 1968-1975
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-csm-block.dispatch: Block I is the Apollo hardware that never flew a crew, and part of the reason the rest of the program survived. It was the first cut at the Command Module — meant only for uncrewed and early Earth-orbit tests — and it carried a set of assumptions that looked reasonable in 1966: a cabin of pure oxygen held above sea-level pressure, a hatch that opened inward, and interior materials chosen without much thought to fire. On 27 January 1967 a spark on the launch pad turned those assumptions lethal in seconds, and the Apollo 1 crew died in a test everyone had treated as routine. Block I was retired into that lesson; the Block II that reached the Moon was, in large part, the list of everything Block I got wrong.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-csm-block.description: Block I was the first design iteration of the Apollo Command and Service Module — intended as a pure Earth-orbit shakedown vehicle before the lunar-capable Block II. Pure-O₂ pressurised cabin at 16.7 psi pre-launch (5 psi in flight); inward-opening hatch sealed by atmospheric differential. CSM-009 + CSM-011 flew uncrewed suborbital tests (AS-201 1966-02-26 + AS-202 1966-08-25). CSM-017 and CSM-020 flew uncrewed on Apollo 4 (1967-11-09) and Apollo 6 (1968-04-04) respectively — Block I command modules on the first two Saturn V flights. CSM-012 — the Apollo 1 ship — was sealed for a Plugs-Out test 1967-01-27 when a flash fire ignited in the lower-equipment bay, killing the crew in seconds; the cabin couldn't be vented because the hatch opened inward against the spike to 29 psi. The Apollo 204 Accident Review Board led to the Block II redesign: outward-opening unified hatch, non-flammable cabin materials, pre-launch nitrogen-rich atmosphere, redesigned wire bundles. No Block I CSM ever flew crewed; Block II flew Apollo 7 (1968) through ASTP (1975).
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-csm-block.best_known_for: Original Apollo CSM design — never flew crewed; killed Apollo 1 crew on the pad 1967-01-27. Redesign produced the Block II flown 1968-1975

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-csm-block.name: Apollo CSM Block II
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-csm-block.dispatch: The Command Module was the only piece of Apollo that came home — everything else was spent and thrown away along the route. That made it the part that could not fail on reentry, and reentry from the Moon was the hardest version of the problem: the capsule met the atmosphere at nearly eleven kilometres a second, half again as fast as anything returning from Earth orbit, wrapped in a fireball hot enough to boil steel. Its answer was an ablative heat shield engineered to char and peel away in a controlled way, carrying the heat off with it. Block II was the version that flew crews — the ground-up redesign forced by the Apollo 1 fire — and it brought every astronaut who set out for the Moon back alive.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-csm-block.description: The lunar-capable Command and Service Module that carried Apollo astronauts to lunar orbit between 1968 and 1972. Fifteen crewed flights in total: Apollo 7–17 (eleven Moon-targeted missions), three Skylab crew rotations (1973–1974), and the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz Test Project — including Apollo 13’s improvised lifeboat configuration.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-lm.json.name: Apollo Lunar Module
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-lm.json.tagline: First crewed lunar lander; Eagle, Antares, Falcon...
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-lm.json.dispatch: The Lunar Module was the first true spacecraft — the first crewed vehicle built to fly only in vacuum, never through an atmosphere, so it could throw away streamlining and heat shielding and become exactly what it was: a machine for one job. Grumman split it in two — a descent stage that carried the crew down and then served as the launch pad for a separate ascent stage that carried them back up — because that staging was the only way to close the mass budget for a Moon landing. It flew on spidery legs, its skin in places as thin as a few sheets of foil. Nothing before it had set people on another world, and its ungainly, purpose-built shape is simply what a spacecraft looks like when it never has to survive coming home.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-lm.json.description: The only crewed lunar lander ever built. Six successful landings between 1969 and 1972 — Eagle, Intrepid, Antares, Falcon, Orion, Challenger — plus Aquarius, which served as Apollo 13’s lifeboat. Descent stage stays on the Moon; ascent stage rejoined the CSM in lunar orbit.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/apollo-lm.json.best_known_for: First crewed lunar lander; Eagle, Antares, Falcon...

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/atlantis.json.tagline: OV-104 — fourth Shuttle. Flew final mission STS-135 (2011), final Hubble servicing STS-125 (2009), deployed Galileo + Magellan
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/atlantis.json.dispatch: Atlantis, OV-104, flew the bookends of the Shuttle's greatest partnerships. It made the most dockings with the Russian station Mir, opening the era of US-Russian cooperation, and it flew STS-125, the final, daring servicing mission that left the Hubble Space Telescope good for another decade. In July 2011 Atlantis flew STS-135, the 135th and last Shuttle mission — the flight that closed thirty years of reusable American spaceflight and left the Space Station it had helped build in orbit above.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/atlantis.json.description: Fourth operational orbiter; first flight STS-51-J (1985-10-03) was a classified DoD mission. Highlights: deployed Magellan (STS-30, 1989) and Galileo (STS-34, 1989) — the two planetary probes that opened Venus and Jupiter to long-duration observation; flew 7 of the 9 Shuttle-Mir docking missions between 1995-1997; flew the final Hubble servicing mission STS-125 (2009-05) — the only post-Columbia non-ISS-rendezvous mission approved; flew STS-135 (2011-07) — the final Shuttle flight ever. On display at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex since 2013.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/atlantis.json.best_known_for: Flew final Shuttle mission STS-135 (2011); deployed Galileo + Magellan; final Hubble servicing STS-125

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/buran-ok-gli.jso.tagline: Buran's atmospheric analog — equivalent of NASA's Enterprise. Four jet engines, 24 atmospheric tests 1985-88, never to orbit
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/buran-ok-gli.jso.dispatch: OK-GLI was Buran's atmospheric test orbiter — the equivalent of NASA's Enterprise, built to prove the spaceplane could glide and land before anything flew to orbit. Fitted with four jet engines, it made its own runway approaches and landings in the atmosphere, validating Buran's aerodynamics and its automated landing systems. It never went to space and was never meant to, and it outlived the orbiter that did: while the flown Buran was destroyed in 2002, OK-GLI survives as a museum exhibit in Germany, one of the few tangible remains of the largest space program the Soviet Union ever attempted.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/buran-ok-gli.jso.description: Officially BTS-002, nicknamed OK-GLI. Full-scale atmospheric test article for the Buran orbital programme — same outer mold-line as the flight vehicle Buran 1.01 but fitted with four AL-31 turbojet engines so it could take off under its own power from a conventional runway. 24 atmospheric flights between 1985-11-10 and 1988-04-15 at the Zhukovsky Flight Research Institute airfield validated Buran's automated landing system + flight-control software for the 1988-11-15 orbital flight. After the Buran programme cancellation OK-GLI sat at LII for years; sold to an Australian museum in 1999, then Bahrain, finally to the Technik Museum Speyer / Sinsheim in Germany where it is on display today — Buran's equivalent of NASA's Enterprise.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/buran-ok-gli.jso.best_known_for: Buran's atmospheric analog; 24 jet-powered flights 1985-88 at Zhukovsky; never to orbit

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/buran.json.name: Buran
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/buran.json.tagline: Soviet shuttle; one unmanned flight, never crewed
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/buran.json.dispatch: Buran was the Soviet Union's answer to the Space Shuttle — outwardly almost identical, but with two decisions that arguably bettered the original: it carried no main engines (all the lift came from the separate Energia rocket), and it could fly with no one aboard. On 15 November 1988 it proved the second, flying a complete uncrewed orbital mission and landing itself on a runway in a crosswind, something no winged spacecraft had ever done. It was a flawless flight and its only one. The Soviet Union collapsed, the money and the mission vanished, and Buran was cancelled — the flown orbiter later crushed when its hangar roof fell in 2002. One of the most impressive and most pointless achievements in spaceflight.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/buran.json.description: The Soviet shuttle, externally similar to the American orbiter but with no main engines (Energia carried it). Flew exactly once, in 1988, fully autonomous and unmanned — the only Soviet shuttle to ever reach orbit before the program ended.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/buran.json.best_known_for: Soviet shuttle; one unmanned flight, never crewed

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/challenger.json.tagline: OV-099 — second operational Shuttle. Lost 73s after launch on STS-51-L (1986-01-28) with all seven crew including teacher Christa McAuliffe
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/challenger.json.dispatch: Challenger, OV-099, was the fleet's early workhorse and the site of its first catastrophe. It flew the program's first spacewalk and carried the first American woman, Sally Ride, to orbit. On 28 January 1986, launching in unusually cold weather, a rubber seal in one of its solid boosters — stiffened by the cold, a failure mode engineers had warned of — gave way, and the vehicle broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff. All seven aboard died. The disaster grounded the fleet for nearly three years and exposed a management culture that had flown past a known, flagged risk.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/challenger.json.description: Built from a structural test article (STA-099) converted to flight after Enterprise was deemed too expensive to upgrade. First flew STS-6 (1983-04-04) carrying out the first Shuttle EVA. Flew 10 missions in total: STS-6, STS-7, STS-8, STS-41-B, STS-41-C, STS-41-G, STS-51-B, STS-51-F, STS-61-A, and final flight STS-51-L. On 1986-01-28, STS-51-L launched at unprecedented cold (−1 °C) — the right SRB's O-rings failed to seal, hot gas burned through the strut attaching the SRB to the external tank, and the orbiter broke apart at Max-Q (T+73s) at 14 km altitude. All seven crew perished, including teacher Christa McAuliffe. The Rogers Commission grounded the Shuttle for 32 months and rewrote NASA's safety culture.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/challenger.json.best_known_for: Second Shuttle; lost 73s after launch on STS-51-L 1986-01-28 with 7 crew

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/columbia.json.tagline: OV-102 — the first Shuttle orbiter to fly to space (STS-1, 1981-04-12); lost on re-entry STS-107 2003-02-01
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/columbia.json.dispatch: Columbia was the first — OV-102, the orbiter that opened the Shuttle era. On STS-1 in April 1981 it did something no crewed spacecraft had done before or has since: flew to orbit on its maiden launch, with two astronauts aboard an untested reusable vehicle, and glided home on a runway. It was the heaviest of the fleet and flew much of the program's science, including the Spacelab laboratories. In 2003, on STS-107, a hole punched in its wing by launch debris let the heat of reentry into the structure, and Columbia broke apart over Texas minutes from home — the loss that ended the program's complacency about debris strikes.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/columbia.json.description: The first operational Space Shuttle orbiter. Flew 28 missions over 22 years including STS-1 (the first and only US crewed spacecraft to fly its maiden voyage with crew aboard), the 1990 Astro-1 UV-astronomy mission, the 1993 SLS-2 life-sciences flight, and Senator John Glenn's STS-95 return-to-space in 1998. Lost on re-entry during STS-107 (2003-02-01) — a foam strike during launch breached the left wing's RCC leading edge and the vehicle disintegrated over Texas at Mach 18 with the loss of all seven crew. The accident grounded the Shuttle fleet for 29 months and triggered the Vision for Space Exploration.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/columbia.json.best_known_for: First Shuttle orbiter to fly to space (STS-1, 1981); lost on STS-107 re-entry 2003

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/crew-dragon.json.name: Crew Dragon
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/crew-dragon.json.description: SpaceX’s human-rated spacecraft, the first privately developed and operated spacecraft to carry humans to orbit (Demo-2, 2020-05-30). The trunk features two solar array panels that deploy after fairing separation for power during orbital operations.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/discovery.json.tagline: OV-103 — third Shuttle. Deployed Hubble (STS-31, 1990); flew both return-to-flight missions. 39 missions — most of any orbiter
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/discovery.json.dispatch: Discovery, OV-103, was the fleet's most-flown and most-trusted orbiter, logging 39 missions across 27 years. It was NASA's choice to return the Shuttle to flight after both disasters — the vehicle sent up first when the program most needed to prove itself safe again. Among its flights was the one that may matter most: STS-31, which carried the Hubble Space Telescope to orbit and released it, beginning the most productive chapter in the history of astronomy.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/discovery.json.description: Third operational orbiter; first flight STS-41-D (1984-08-30). The most-flown Shuttle — 39 missions over 27 years. Career highlights: STS-31 (1990-04-24) deployed the Hubble Space Telescope; STS-26 (1988-09-29) was the post-Challenger return-to-flight; STS-114 (2005-07-26) was the post-Columbia return-to-flight; STS-95 (1998) returned John Glenn to orbit at age 77; multiple ISS-assembly flights (STS-92, 120, 124, 128, 131, 133). Final flight STS-133 (2011-02-24) delivered the Leonardo Permanent Multipurpose Module. On display at Udvar-Hazy since 2012.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/discovery.json.best_known_for: Most-flown Shuttle (39 missions); deployed Hubble + flew both return-to-flight missions

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/endeavour.json.tagline: OV-105 — fifth Shuttle, built from spares to replace Challenger. First Hubble servicing STS-61 (1993); delivered Unity + Canadarm2
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/endeavour.json.dispatch: Endeavour, OV-105, was the last orbiter built — assembled from structural spares to replace Challenger, so that even the fleet's newest member carried the memory of its worst day. It flew the first Hubble servicing mission, STS-61, the flight that corrected the telescope's flawed mirror and rescued the observatory's reputation, and it did heavy lifting in the assembly of the International Space Station. It was the youngest of the fleet and among the busiest, flying until the program's final years.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/endeavour.json.description: Fifth and last operational orbiter, built from structural spares after Challenger left NASA with only three flight-rated orbiters. Named via a national schools competition after Captain Cook's HMS Endeavour. First flight STS-49 (1992-05-07) included the first three-person EVA (to capture the stranded Intelsat VI satellite). Highlights: STS-61 (1993-12) first Hubble servicing restored Hubble's optics; STS-88 (1998-12-04) first ISS assembly flight delivering Node 1 Unity; STS-100 (2001-04) installed Canadarm2; STS-130 (2010-02) installed Tranquility + Cupola; STS-134 (2011-05) installed the AMS-02 cosmic-ray detector — final EVA crew of the Shuttle programme. On display at the California Science Center, Los Angeles.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/endeavour.json.best_known_for: Youngest Shuttle; first Hubble servicing (STS-61); delivered Unity + Canadarm2 + Tranquility / Cupola

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/enterprise.json.tagline: OV-101 — prototype Shuttle. Renamed from Constitution after Star Trek fan campaign. Flew 1977 atmospheric tests; never reached orbit
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/enterprise.json.description: Originally called Constitution, renamed Enterprise after a fan-letter campaign organized by Star Trek fans in 1976 when the shuttle was being named. Built as a prototype for the Approach and Landing Tests (ALT) — eight captive flights and five free flights from the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft over Edwards Air Force Base in 1977. First free flight 1977-08-12 piloted by Fred Haise + Gordon Fullerton proved the orbiter could glide and land. Did NOT contain propulsion or active TPS tiles; converting Enterprise to flight-rated was estimated heavier than building a new orbiter from structural spares, so Challenger was built instead. Now on display at the Intrepid Sea, Air & Space Museum in NYC.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/enterprise.json.best_known_for: Prototype Shuttle; 1977 atmospheric drop tests; never flew to orbit

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/gaganyaan.json.name: Gaganyaan
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/gaganyaan.json.description: India’s first crewed spacecraft, targeting a 2027 crewed flight on the LVM3 (formerly GSLV Mk III). Three astronauts on a roughly seven-day low-Earth-orbit mission — the start of an Indian human-spaceflight programme. ISRO has completed crew module qualification tests and trained astronaut candidates.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/gemini.json.name: Gemini
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/gemini.json.tagline: Two-person crew; rendezvous and EVA practice
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/gemini.json.dispatch: The Gemini spacecraft was the first one Americans could actually fly. Mercury's astronaut mostly rode a capsule the ground controlled; Gemini's two-person crew got thrusters, a flight computer, and the ability to change their own orbit — to chase down another craft and dock with it. That was its entire reason to exist: not to go anywhere new, but to be a machine for practicing the maneuvers Apollo would need. Roomier than Mercury but still cramped, split into a crew module and an equipment section like Apollo after it, across ten flights it turned rendezvous, docking, and two-week endurance from open questions into things a crew could simply do.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/gemini.json.description: The two-person spacecraft that taught NASA how to rendezvous, dock, and walk in space — the techniques that made Apollo possible. Two uncrewed test flights (Gemini 1 and 2) in 1964–1965 preceded ten crewed missions (Gemini 3–12) in 1965–1966, every one a step toward the Moon.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/gemini.json.best_known_for: Two-person crew; rendezvous and EVA practice

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/mercury-capsule..name: Mercury capsule
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/mercury-capsule..dispatch: The Mercury capsule was designed to be the smallest thing that could keep a person alive in space — and it shows. There was no room to do much but sit; the astronaut wore the spacecraft as much as rode it. But its shape solved the era's hardest unsolved problem — how to come back. The blunt end, coated in a shield built to char and carry the heat away, turned reentry from a fatal certainty into something survivable, and its cone was the first American answer to the question of what a crewed spacecraft even looks like. Every capsule since — Gemini, Apollo, Dragon — is a descendant of this cramped little cone.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/mercury-capsule..description: The cone-shaped capsule that carried six American astronauts on Project Mercury between 1961 and 1963. Tiny enough that John Glenn famously described being "spam in a can" — but it proved orbital flight was achievable for the United States.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/new-shepard.json.name: New Shepard
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/new-shepard.json.description: Blue Origin’s suborbital crewed spacecraft, named for Alan Shepard. Reusable booster + capsule architecture, with the capsule landing under parachutes. Crewed since 2021; carried Jeff Bezos, William Shatner, and others on brief suborbital flights.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/orion.json.name: Orion
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/orion.json.tagline: Crew vehicle for the Artemis lunar program
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/orion.json.description: The crew vehicle for NASA’s Artemis program, built jointly with ESA (the European Service Module is provided by Airbus). Designed to support up to four astronauts on multi-week missions to lunar orbit. Flew uncrewed on Artemis I in 2022. Flew its first crewed mission (Artemis II) in April 2026 with a four-person crew on a lunar flyby trajectory.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/orion.json.best_known_for: Crew vehicle for the Artemis lunar program

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/shenzhou.json.name: Shenzhou
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/shenzhou.json.description: China’s crewed spacecraft, externally Soyuz-derived but enlarged. First crewed flight in 2003 (Shenzhou 5, Yang Liwei); now the standard ferry to Tiangong, with crew rotations every six months.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-7k-ok.json.name: Soyuz 7K-OK
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-7k-ok.json.tagline: First Soyuz generation; Komarov's fatal flight
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-7k-ok.json.dispatch: The Soyuz 7K-OK was the first of the line — the original version of the spacecraft that would outlive them all. It introduced the three-module layout every Soyuz since has kept: a spherical orbital module to live and work in, a compact descent module to ride home in, and a service module for power and propulsion. It was also the version that killed Vladimir Komarov on its first crewed flight and, in an improved form, the three cosmonauts of Soyuz 11 — the hard early schooling that turned a rushed design into a reliable one. Crude and dangerous at the start, its basic architecture proved so sound that, refined over decades, it is still carrying crews to orbit today.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-7k-ok.json.description: The first generation of Soyuz, with all the architectural choices that have endured for sixty years: orbital module sphere, descent module, service module with deployable solar arrays. Tragically introduced by Soyuz 1 (Komarov’s fatal flight, 1967).
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-7k-ok.json.best_known_for: First Soyuz generation; Komarov's fatal flight

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-ms.json.name: Soyuz MS
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-ms.json.description: The current Soyuz generation, in service since 2016. New software and GLONASS/GPS-aided rendezvous makes ISS docking possible in as little as 3 hours. Part of the Soyuz family — the most-flown crewed spacecraft lineage in history.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-t.json.name: Soyuz T
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-t.json.description: The 1979–1986 Salyut-era Soyuz with three-cosmonaut capacity restored after the Soyuz 11 fatal decompression. Modernised avionics and hypergolic propulsion; the bridge between the original 7K-OK and the long-running TM/TMA/MS lineage.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-tm.json.name: Soyuz TM
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-tm.json.description: The Mir-era Soyuz (1986–2002), with redesigned avionics and the new Kurs automated docking system. Flew Soviet, Russian, and partner-country cosmonauts to Mir for 15 years.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-tma.json.name: Soyuz TMA
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-tma.json.tagline: ISS-era Soyuz; expanded crew height envelope
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-tma.json.description: The ISS-era Soyuz (2002–2012), with a digital flight computer and a wider crew-height envelope to accommodate the international partner astronaut corps. Carried the first space tourists alongside professional crews.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/soyuz-tma.json.best_known_for: ISS-era Soyuz; expanded crew height envelope

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/space-shuttle-or.name: Space Shuttle Orbiter
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/space-shuttle-or.description: The reusable winged spacecraft that flew 135 missions between 1981 and 2011 — the only crewed vehicle ever to land like a glider. Five flight orbiters were built (Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis, Endeavour); Columbia and Challenger were lost with their crews.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/starliner.json.name: Starliner (CST-100)
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/starliner.json.description: Boeing’s Commercial Crew vehicle, with a pusher launch-abort system using its own service-module thrusters. Crew Flight Test (June 2024) suffered thruster failures and helium leaks; NASA returned the capsule uncrewed (September 2024). Wilmore and Williams returned via SpaceX Crew-9 (February 2025). Crewed flights suspended pending recertification.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/voskhod.json.name: Voskhod
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/voskhod.json.dispatch: The Voskhod spacecraft was a Vostok pushed past its design, and it shows exactly what improvisation under deadline looks like. To make the one-seat capsule carry more, engineers pulled out the ejection seat — the crew's only escape — and for the first flight left out the pressure suits too; for the second they bolted on an inflatable airlock so a cosmonaut could go outside. It scored the first multi-person crew and the first spacewalk, the last two firsts the Soviet program would claim. But it had no margin left, and after the near-disaster of its second flight it was retired — a stopgap that did its narrow job and was wisely not asked to do more.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/voskhod.json.description: A modified Vostok refitted to carry up to three cosmonauts. Two crewed flights — Voskhod 1 (first multi-crew) and Voskhod 2 (Alexei Leonov’s first spacewalk in 1965). Pushed beyond the design margin and was retired in favour of Soyuz.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/vostok.json.name: Vostok
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/vostok.json.dispatch: The Vostok spacecraft was the first machine to carry a human into space and bring one back, and its design is a study in doing the minimum that works. Reentry is the hardest part of coming home, so Vostok used the one shape that survives it from any angle — a sphere — which meant the automatic systems never had to point the craft precisely; it would tumble in and still come down heat-shield-heavy. The catch was that the sphere landed too hard for a person, so the cosmonaut ejected near the ground and parachuted separately, a fact hidden for years to protect the records. Crude, secretive, and completely effective, it flew six people to orbit and lost none — and its capsule-plus-service-module layout became the pattern for Soyuz, still flying today.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/vostok.json.description: The spherical descent module that returned Yuri Gagarin from orbit on 1961-04-12 — the first human spaceflight. Six crewed flights between 1961 and 1963, including Valentina Tereshkova’s solo orbital mission as the first woman in space.

fleet/crewed-spacecraft/x37b.json.tagline: USSF reusable robotic spaceplane — multi-year classified orbital missions, the only US spaceplane operational after the Shuttle's retirement
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/x37b.json.description: Robotic mini-spaceplane (8.9 m long, ~5 t) built by Boeing Phantom Works for the USAF, transferred to the USSF in 2019. Launches vertically (Atlas V 501 originally; SpaceX Falcon 9 from OTV-5; Falcon Heavy from OTV-7) and lands horizontally on Kennedy's former Shuttle runway. Most payloads and orbital parameters are classified — known mission durations stretch from 224 days (OTV-1, 2010) to a record 908 days (OTV-6, 2020-2022). Declassified experiments include Hall-effect thruster tech demo, an AFRL radio-frequency communication test, and a 1 W solar-power-to-microwave-beaming experiment (PRAM, OTV-6). As of 2026 has flown seven missions.
fleet/crewed-spacecraft/x37b.json.best_known_for: USSF reusable robotic spaceplane — classified multi-year orbital missions, post-Shuttle US spaceplane

fleet/engine/ce-20.json.name: CE-20
fleet/engine/ce-20.json.tagline: India's first home-grown cryogenic engine, born from necessity
fleet/engine/ce-20.json.description: When technology-transfer restrictions blocked India from acquiring cryogenic engine technology in the early 1990s, ISRO's Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre developed one from the ground up. The CE-20 is the result: a gas-generator cycle burning LOX and LH2 that powers the upper stage of LVM3, India's heaviest operational rocket. It first flew on 5 June 2017 on the GSLV Mk III D1 developmental flight, capping a two-decade development program that turned a geopolitical barrier into independent capability. The CE-20 is the engine that will carry Gaganyaan — India's first crewed mission — to orbit.
fleet/engine/ce-20.json.best_known_for: India's first home-grown cryogenic engine — the LVM3 upper stage

fleet/engine/f-1.json.name: F-1
fleet/engine/f-1.json.tagline: The most powerful single-chamber engine ever flown
fleet/engine/f-1.json.description: Five F-1s on Saturn V's first stage produced combined thrust that no single rocket before or since has matched at sea level. Rocketdyne's gas-generator cycle burned LOX and RP-1 at a rate that demanded turbopumps the size of car engines and a combustion chamber that engineers had to solve combustion instability in by trial, explosion, and redesign. It first flew on 9 November 1967 and put Apollo on its way to the Moon six times before the program ended.
fleet/engine/f-1.json.best_known_for: Most powerful single-chamber liquid engine ever flown — five lifted Saturn V

fleet/engine/h-1.json.name: H-1
fleet/engine/h-1.json.tagline: Eight engines, eight missions — the Saturn I workhorse
fleet/engine/h-1.json.description: The H-1 was the engine Rocketdyne built to bridge the gap between early ballistic-missile powerplants and the F-1 that would follow. Running a gas-generator cycle on LOX and RP-1, eight H-1s clustered together formed Saturn I's first stage — and later Saturn IB's — flying every unmanned Apollo hardware test and crewed Apollo 7. Its first flight was 27 October 1961; it ran continuously through the end of the Saturn IB program in 1975.
fleet/engine/h-1.json.best_known_for: Eight-cluster Saturn I/IB booster engine — the F-1 rehearsal

fleet/engine/hm7b.json.name: HM7B
fleet/engine/hm7b.json.tagline: Ariane's cryogenic upper stage, three decades of service
fleet/engine/hm7b.json.description: The HM7B is the hydrogen-fuelled upper-stage engine that gave Ariane rockets a high-energy kick after the core stage shut down. Running a gas-generator cycle on LOX and LH2, it first flew on Ariane 2 in May 1986 and continued through the end of Ariane 5's operational life in July 2023. Its small size belies a high specific impulse that made it the workhorse for geostationary transfer injections, carrying commercial satellites and scientific payloads — including Rosetta, Mars Express, and Venus Express — to their departure trajectories over more than three decades.
fleet/engine/hm7b.json.best_known_for: Europe's cryogenic upper-stage engine — Ariane's translunar workhorse

fleet/engine/j-2.json.name: J-2
fleet/engine/j-2.json.tagline: The engine that sent Apollo to the Moon — twice
fleet/engine/j-2.json.description: The J-2 burned hydrogen and oxygen, and it could restart in the vacuum of space — a capability that made Saturn V's trans-lunar injection burn possible. Rocketdyne's gas-generator design flew on Saturn V's second and third stages and on Saturn IB, combining performance with the in-space restarts that turned a launch vehicle into a true departure stage. It first flew in February 1966 and last flew on the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project in July 1975.
fleet/engine/j-2.json.best_known_for: Restartable hydrogen upper-stage engine that sent Apollo translunar

fleet/engine/le-5b.json.name: LE-5B
fleet/engine/le-5b.json.tagline: Japan's restartable upper stage, flying from H-IIA through H3
fleet/engine/le-5b.json.description: The LE-5B is the cryogenic upper-stage engine that has bridged two generations of Japanese launch vehicles. Running an expander-bleed cycle on LOX and LH2, it can be restarted in flight — a requirement for placing payloads in precise orbits after a coast phase. It first flew on H-IIA in August 2001 and has since been uprated as the LE-5B-3 for continued service on H3, giving Japan unbroken upper-stage continuity from the ISS assembly era into the present. Its combination of restartability and the clean simplicity of the expander-bleed cycle made it the natural upper-stage complement to both the LE-7A and the LE-9.
fleet/engine/le-5b.json.best_known_for: Japan's restartable cryogenic upper stage — H-IIA through H3

fleet/engine/le-7a.json.name: LE-7A
fleet/engine/le-7a.json.tagline: Japan's staged-combustion hydrogen core, two decades of H-II service
fleet/engine/le-7a.json.description: The LE-7A is the engine that gave Japan a fully indigenous heavy-lift capability. Developed by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries for JAXA, it runs a staged-combustion cycle on LOX and LH2 — the thermodynamic approach that extracts maximum efficiency from hydrogen propellant — and first flew on H-IIA in August 2001 as a refined successor to the original LE-7. The redesign addressed turbopump issues that had caused early H-II failures, and the LE-7A went on to anchor H-IIA and H-IIB's operational careers through 2024, launching Japan's HTV cargo ships to the International Space Station and JAXA's ALOS Earth-observation satellites.
fleet/engine/le-7a.json.best_known_for: Japan's staged-combustion hydrogen core — powered H-IIA/H-IIB

fleet/engine/le-9.json.name: LE-9
fleet/engine/le-9.json.tagline: The largest expander-bleed engine ever built — powering H3
fleet/engine/le-9.json.description: The LE-9 is a deliberate choice of elegance over complexity. Rather than the turbopump-preburner arrangement of staged combustion, it uses an expander-bleed cycle: hydrogen is heated by the chamber and nozzle walls, and a portion of that gas is bled off to drive the turbopumps before being dumped overboard. The cycle has inherently lower chamber pressures and a simpler hot-section design, trading some performance for a reduction in the mechanical failure modes that plagued earlier Japanese engines. Developed by Mitsubishi for JAXA's H3 rocket, the LE-9 first flew in March 2023 and is the largest engine of its type to reach operational service.
fleet/engine/le-9.json.best_known_for: The largest expander-bleed engine ever flown — the H3 core

fleet/engine/lr87.json.name: LR87
fleet/engine/lr87.json.tagline: Twin-chamber hypergolic first stage that flew every Gemini crew
fleet/engine/lr87.json.description: The LR87 is the engine that launched all ten crewed Gemini missions on Titan II. Aerojet's design places two combustion chambers on a single turbopump assembly, burning Aerozine-50 and nitrogen tetroxide in a gas-generator cycle — a hypergolic combination that was standard equipment in American ICBMs of the era. The propellant choice had a direct consequence for crew safety: unlike RP-1 or hydrogen, Aerozine-50 and N2O4 ignite on contact, giving a hypergolic reliability that let Gemini fly with ejection seats rather than a launch-escape tower across all ten crewed missions. The LR87 was later developed into larger variants that flew on Titan III and Titan IV commercial and military missions through October 2005.
fleet/engine/lr87.json.best_known_for: The twin-chamber first stage that launched Gemini crews on Titan II

fleet/engine/merlin-1d.json.name: Merlin 1D
fleet/engine/merlin-1d.json.tagline: Nine engines, one booster, flown and re-flown dozens of times
fleet/engine/merlin-1d.json.description: SpaceX's Merlin 1D is the engine that made the reusable Falcon 9 possible. Nine of them cluster on Falcon 9's first stage, running a gas-generator cycle on LOX and RP-1, with the center engine also used for entry and landing burns. First flown in September 2013, the Merlin 1D matured into a high-cadence workhorse: individual engines have accumulated more than twenty flights apiece, a reuse record that changed what the industry believed was economically achievable. The vacuum variant, Merlin 1D Vacuum, powers Falcon 9's upper stage with a larger nozzle optimised for the near-vacuum environment.
fleet/engine/merlin-1d.json.best_known_for: The reusable workhorse — nine lift Falcon 9, flown and re-flown dozens of times

fleet/engine/raptor.json.name: Raptor
fleet/engine/raptor.json.tagline: Full-flow staged combustion — the hardest cycle, finally flying
fleet/engine/raptor.json.description: The Raptor is the first full-flow staged-combustion engine to reach operational flight. In this thermodynamic cycle, both propellants — LOX and liquid methane — pass through preburners before entering the main combustion chamber, extracting maximum energy and leaving virtually no unburned propellant. Engineers had studied the concept for decades and concluded it was prohibitively complex; SpaceX built it anyway. Thirty-three Raptors ignite simultaneously on Super Heavy's first stage, and a vacuum-optimised variant powers Starship's upper stage. The first integrated Starship flight carrying Raptors lifted off on 20 April 2023.
fleet/engine/raptor.json.best_known_for: First full-flow staged-combustion engine to fly — 33 lift Super Heavy

fleet/engine/rd-107-108.json.name: RD-107 / RD-108
fleet/engine/rd-107-108.json.tagline: Sputnik's engine — still flying humans 65 years later
fleet/engine/rd-107-108.json.description: The RD-107 and RD-108 are the engines of the R-7, the world's first intercontinental ballistic missile, which Sergei Korolev's team repurposed as a launch vehicle. The RD-107 powers the R-7's four strap-on boosters; the RD-108 drives the sustainer core. Both run a gas-generator cycle on LOX and kerosene, and both first flew on 21 August 1957 — months before Sputnik. Upgraded as the RD-107A and RD-108A, they continue to power Soyuz rockets carrying crews to the International Space Station, making them the longest-operating human-rated propulsion system in history.
fleet/engine/rd-107-108.json.best_known_for: The R-7 engines — still flying humans on Soyuz after 65+ years

fleet/engine/rd-180.json.name: RD-180
fleet/engine/rd-180.json.tagline: Russian ox-rich staged combustion the US could not replicate
fleet/engine/rd-180.json.description: The RD-180 represents a branch of propulsion technology the United States effectively ceded to the Soviet Union during the Cold War. Oxygen-rich staged combustion — burning excess oxidiser through the preburner to drive the turbopump — demands materials and manufacturing tolerances that American industry had not mastered. NPO Energomash's two-chamber, single-turbopump design flew on Atlas V from May 2000, providing the first stage with a combination of thrust and efficiency that no American-made kerolox engine of the era could match. It was retired with Atlas V in 2023.
fleet/engine/rd-180.json.best_known_for: Oxygen-rich staged combustion the US could not match — flew on Atlas V

fleet/engine/rd-253.json.name: RD-253
fleet/engine/rd-253.json.tagline: Six hypergolic engines powered every Proton first stage
fleet/engine/rd-253.json.description: The RD-253 is the engine that made Proton one of the most capable heavy lifters of the Soviet era. Six of them ring Proton's first stage, each running oxygen-rich staged combustion on nitrogen tetroxide and unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine — a hypergolic pair that ignites on contact and requires no ignition system. The propellant choice is toxic and corrosive, but it stores at room temperature and delivers reliability that Proton sustained across decades of commercial and planetary missions. The RD-253 first flew on 16 July 1965 and powered every Proton first stage through the rocket's retirement.
fleet/engine/rd-253.json.best_known_for: Proton's hypergolic workhorse — six lifted every Proton first stage

fleet/engine/rl10.json.name: RL10
fleet/engine/rl10.json.tagline: Hydrogen upper stage, six decades and counting
fleet/engine/rl10.json.description: The RL10 introduced the expander cycle to spaceflight: propellant flows through the nozzle and chamber walls, picks up heat, and drives the turbopump before it ever reaches the combustion chamber — no separate gas generator required. First flown in November 1963 on the Centaur upper stage, the RL10 family has since powered upper stages for Atlas, Delta, and Vulcan missions. Its longevity is the record; no other rocket engine family has remained in continuous production and flight for as long, evolving through block upgrades while the core thermodynamic concept stays intact.
fleet/engine/rl10.json.best_known_for: Longest-serving engine in spaceflight — the first hydrogen upper stage

fleet/engine/rocketdyne-a7.json.name: Rocketdyne A-7
fleet/engine/rocketdyne-a7.json.tagline: The engine that launched the first American into space
fleet/engine/rocketdyne-a7.json.description: On 5 May 1961, Alan Shepard rode a Mercury-Redstone rocket to an altitude of 187 kilometres and back — making him the first American in space — and the engine that lifted him was the Rocketdyne A-7. Derived from the A-6 that powered the Redstone ballistic missile, the A-7 ran a gas-generator cycle on LOX and ethyl alcohol: the same propellant pairing that traced back through Redstone to the German V-2. Shepard's Freedom 7 flight lasted fifteen minutes and changed the political calculus of the Space Race. The A-7 flew only on Mercury-Redstone missions, retiring in May 1963.
fleet/engine/rocketdyne-a7.json.best_known_for: The engine that launched the first American — Freedom 7

fleet/engine/rs-25.json.name: RS-25 (SSME)
fleet/engine/rs-25.json.tagline: Reusable, hydrogen-fuelled, and still flying on SLS
fleet/engine/rs-25.json.description: The RS-25 was the engine the Space Shuttle Main Engine program spent a decade perfecting: a staged-combustion cycle on LOX and LH2 that could throttle, restart, and be refurbished for the next flight. Over 135 Shuttle missions from April 1981 it accumulated a near-perfect operational record. The engines were recovered, inspected, and reflown — an ambition that no earlier rocket engine had achieved at this power level. After the Shuttle retired, the inventory was requalified and repurposed for NASA's Space Launch System, where RS-25s now power SLS's core stage.
fleet/engine/rs-25.json.best_known_for: Reusable staged-combustion engine — 135 Shuttle flights, now flies on SLS

fleet/engine/vikas.json.name: Vikas
fleet/engine/vikas.json.tagline: India's licensed Viking — three decades powering PSLV and GSLV
fleet/engine/vikas.json.description: The Vikas traces directly to the French Viking engine: ISRO licensed the design in the 1970s and indigenised it at the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre, adapting it for Indian manufacturing and progressively increasing performance through successive marks. Running a gas-generator cycle on nitrogen tetroxide and UDMH, Vikas first flew in September 1993 on PSLV and has since become the core liquid stage for PSLV, GSLV, and LVM3. It is the engine that powered Chandrayaan-1 to lunar orbit, Mangalyaan to Mars, and the Chandrayaan-3 mission that put Vikram on the Moon's south polar region.
fleet/engine/vikas.json.best_known_for: India's workhorse — powers PSLV, GSLV and LVM3 to this day

fleet/engine/viking.json.name: Viking
fleet/engine/viking.json.tagline: The French engine that became India's workhorse
fleet/engine/viking.json.description: The Viking engine, developed by SEP in France for CNES and ESA, powered the first through fourth generations of the Ariane family from Ariane 1's inaugural launch on 24 December 1979. It burns nitrogen tetroxide and UH25 — a nitrogen-hydrazine blend — in a gas-generator cycle, a hypergolic propellant combination that trades efficiency for room-temperature storability and ignition simplicity. The Viking's most consequential second act came when ISRO licensed the design from France in the 1970s and developed it into the Vikas engine, which still flies on Indian launch vehicles today. One French engine design seeded two nations' access to space.
fleet/engine/viking.json.best_known_for: The French engine later licensed to India as Vikas — powered Ariane 1–4

fleet/engine/vulcain-2.json.name: Vulcain 2
fleet/engine/vulcain-2.json.tagline: Europe's hydrogen core engine — every Ariane 5 depended on it
fleet/engine/vulcain-2.json.description: Vulcain 2 was the engine Europe built to achieve independent access to geostationary orbit. Developed by Snecma under ESA's Ariane 5 program, it runs a gas-generator cycle on LOX and LH2, powering the cryogenic main stage from liftoff through main-engine cutoff while the solid boosters do the heavy lifting of the first minutes. Its December 2002 debut was lost to a nozzle-cooling failure that destroyed the vehicle; after redesign it flew successfully from 2005 and became the reliable heart of Ariane 5 through the rocket's final flight in July 2023, placing satellites and interplanetary probes — including JWST — on their trajectories.
fleet/engine/vulcain-2.json.best_known_for: Europe's hydrogen core engine — powered every Ariane 5

fleet/engine/yf-100.json.name: YF-100
fleet/engine/yf-100.json.tagline: China's staged-combustion kerolox engine, powering the new generation
fleet/engine/yf-100.json.description: The YF-100 is the engine that moved China's launch capability into the performance tier that Russia and the United States had occupied for decades. Developed by AALPT in Xi'an, it applies oxygen-rich staged combustion to LOX and RP-1 — the thermodynamic cycle that extracts the most energy from kerosene propellants — and first flew on 20 September 2015. Two YF-100s power the core stage of Long March 5, China's heaviest operational rocket, and clustered variants fly on Long March 6 and Long March 7. The YF-100 underpins China's lunar program, its space station resupply, and its growing commercial launch cadence.
fleet/engine/yf-100.json.best_known_for: China's modern staged-combustion kerolox engine — Long March 5/6/7

fleet/engine/yf-77.json.name: YF-77
fleet/engine/yf-77.json.tagline: China's first large hydrogen engine — Long March 5's foundation
fleet/engine/yf-77.json.description: The YF-77 is China's first large-scale cryogenic engine burning LOX and LH2, ending a multi-decade dependence on storable hypergolic propellants for core stages. Developed by AALPT and running a gas-generator cycle, two YF-77s power Long March 5's central core, providing the efficiency boost that made lunar-return and space-station-module missions achievable without a prohibitively large rocket. It first flew on 3 November 2016, and the early flights were not without difficulty — a YF-77 anomaly grounded Long March 5 for nearly three years before engineers identified and resolved the failure mode.
fleet/engine/yf-77.json.best_known_for: China's first large hydrogen engine — the Long March 5 core

fleet/lander/beagle2.json.tagline: UK/ESA Mars lander from Mars Express (2003). Silent on arrival; HiRISE found it intact in 2015 — a solar panel had failed to deploy
fleet/lander/beagle2.json.description: A 33-kg UK-led Mars lander released from ESA's Mars Express on 2003-12-19, six days before its planned 2003-12-25 landing at Isidis Planitia. Beagle 2 (named after HMS Beagle which carried Darwin) carried a clamshell payload of a Gas Analysis Package mass spectrometer for atmospheric + sub-surface volatiles, a stereo camera, a microscope, a Mössbauer + APX spectrometer pair, and a mole drill. It went silent at separation and was presumed crashed for 12 years — until 2015-01, when high-resolution HiRISE imagery from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter clearly showed Beagle 2 sitting on the Martian surface (~5 km from its target), with one of four solar panels (petals) failing to fully deploy, preventing the antenna from clearing the housing and collecting enough power. So: a successful landing, an unsuccessful deployment, and a 12-year mystery solved by the same kind of imagery that LRO uses for the Moon.
fleet/lander/beagle2.json.best_known_for: UK/ESA Mars lander — landed 2003, silent for 12 years, found by HiRISE 2015

fleet/lander/beresheet.json.name: Beresheet
fleet/lander/beresheet.json.description: The first private lunar landing attempt, by Israel’s SpaceIL nonprofit. Crashed in April 2019 when an IMU gyroscope failure triggered repeated computer reboots, each shutting the engine down; by the time control was recovered, the lander was too low and fast to survive. Demonstrated that landing on the Moon is much harder than reaching it.

fleet/lander/blue-moon-mk1.json.tagline: Blue Origin's first-generation lunar cargo lander — single-stage hydrogen / oxygen vehicle, ~3 t to the surface
fleet/lander/blue-moon-mk1.json.description: Single-stage cryogenic lander built around the LH₂ / LOX BE-7 engine. Mk1 is the cargo-only precursor to the much larger Mk2 crewed Artemis HLS variant; both share the BE-7 propulsion and hydrogen-based reusability architecture. The first crewed lunar flight to carry Blue Moon Mk1 has not yet launched, with first landing currently planned no earlier than 2026. Cargo Mk1 will deliver up to ~3000 kg to the lunar surface; the crewed Mk2 derivative anchored Blue Origin's HLS contract awarded by NASA in 2023 as the second Artemis-era human lander alongside SpaceX Starship HLS.
fleet/lander/blue-moon-mk1.json.best_known_for: Blue Origin cargo lunar lander — BE-7 hydrogen propulsion, ~3 t to the surface, NASA CLPS

fleet/lander/change-3.json.name: Chang'e 3
fleet/lander/change-3.json.description: China’s first lunar lander (December 2013), carrying the Yutu rover. Mare Imbrium touchdown — the first soft landing on the Moon since Luna 24 in 1976.

fleet/lander/change-4.json.name: Chang'e 4
fleet/lander/change-4.json.tagline: First soft landing on lunar far side
fleet/lander/change-4.json.description: The first soft landing on the lunar far side (January 2019). Required a relay satellite (Queqiao) at Earth-Moon L2 to maintain communications. Yutu-2 has since roamed the Von Kármán crater terrain for years.
fleet/lander/change-4.json.best_known_for: First soft landing on lunar far side

fleet/lander/change-5.json.name: Chang'e 5
fleet/lander/change-5.json.description: The first lunar sample return since Luna 24 in 1976. Returned 1.731 kg of basalt from a region 1.2 billion years younger than the Apollo and Luna samples — extending the timeline of recent lunar volcanism.

fleet/lander/change6.json.tagline: First-ever lunar far-side sample return. Apollo basin landing 2024-06-01 (UTC); 1935 g returned to Inner Mongolia 2024-06-25
fleet/lander/change6.json.description: The first-ever sample-return mission from the lunar far side — a 53-year-after-Apollo landmark that no other space agency has yet attempted. Launched 2024-05-03 on a Long March 5 from Wenchang, Chang'e 6 used the Queqiao-2 relay satellite (positioned in a halo orbit around Earth-Moon L2 since March 2024) to communicate with Earth across the lunar limb. The lander touched down in the Apollo basin within the giant South Pole-Aitken impact basin (-153.99° W, -41.64° S) on 2024-06-01 (UTC, 2024-06-02 Beijing time). Its drill + scoop collected ~1935 g of regolith from a region that has remained largely undisturbed since the basin-forming impact ~4.3 billion years ago — material from the lunar mantle excavated by SPA. The ascender lifted off 2024-06-03, rendezvoused with the orbiter in lunar orbit, and the return capsule landed in Siziwang Banner, Inner Mongolia, on 2024-06-25 14:07 local time. France, Italy, Sweden, and Pakistan contributed instruments — the first international science payloads on a Chinese sample-return mission.
fleet/lander/change6.json.best_known_for: First-ever lunar far-side sample return. Apollo basin landing 2024-06-02; 1935 g returned to Inner Mongolia 2024-06-25

fleet/lander/hakuto-r.json.name: Hakuto-R program
fleet/lander/hakuto-r.json.tagline: Japan's first private Moon landing attempts; Mission 1 (2023) and Mission 2 (2025) both crashed
fleet/lander/hakuto-r.json.description: Hakuto-R is a lunar lander program of the Japanese company ispace. Its Mission 1 lander, launched in December 2022, was Japan's first private attempt at a Moon landing and crashed in April 2023. The Mission 2 lander, Resilience, crashed in June 2025.
fleet/lander/hakuto-r.json.best_known_for: Japan's first private Moon landing attempts; Mission 1 (2023) and Mission 2 (2025) both crashed

fleet/lander/im-1-odysseus.json.name: IM-1 Odysseus
fleet/lander/im-1-odysseus.json.tagline: First U.S. lunar landing since Apollo; sideways
fleet/lander/im-1-odysseus.json.description: The first US lunar landing since Apollo 17 in 1972. Touched down sideways near the lunar south pole on 2024-02-22 (the primary laser rangefinder had been left inactive — safety switch not armed pre-launch); operated briefly before sunset.
fleet/lander/im-1-odysseus.json.best_known_for: First U.S. lunar landing since Apollo; sideways

fleet/lander/insight.json.name: InSight
fleet/lander/insight.json.description: NASA’s 2018–2022 Mars seismometer mission. Detected over 1,300 marsquakes, mapped the planet’s internal structure for the first time, and confirmed the existence of a large molten core. Ended when dust accumulation on its solar panels finally starved its power.

fleet/lander/luna-16.json.name: Luna 16
fleet/lander/luna-16.json.description: Built by NPO Lavochkin, Luna 16 achieved the first fully robotic lunar sample return, bringing 101 g of soil back to Earth in September 1970.

fleet/lander/luna-9.json.name: Luna 9
fleet/lander/luna-9.json.tagline: First soft landing on another world
fleet/lander/luna-9.json.description: The first soft landing on another world. Touched down on Oceanus Procellarum in February 1966, returning the first photographs from the lunar surface — a panorama of the cratered landscape just centimeters from the lander’s eye.
fleet/lander/luna-9.json.best_known_for: First soft landing on another world

fleet/lander/luna24.json.tagline: Last successful Soviet Moon mission — returned 170 g of Mare Crisium regolith 1976-08-22; last lunar sample return until Chang'e 5
fleet/lander/luna24.json.description: The last successful Soviet Moon mission and the last sample-return lunar lander until Chang'e 5 in 2020 — a 44-year gap. Launched 1976-08-09 from Baikonur on a Proton-K, Luna 24 soft-landed in Mare Crisium (12.7° N, 62.2° E) on 1976-08-18, drilled to a depth of 2.25 m using its rotary-percussive drill, retrieved a 1.6 m core sample, and lifted off the ascent stage which returned 170.1 g of lunar regolith to western Siberia (~200 km southeast of Surgut) on 1976-08-22. Soviet scientists at the Vernadsky Institute confirmed the presence of water (~0.1 % by mass) in the samples in a 1978 paper that was largely ignored in the West until LCROSS and Chandrayaan-1 (2008-09) re-confirmed lunar water.
fleet/lander/luna24.json.best_known_for: Last successful Soviet Moon mission — returned 170 g of Mare Crisium regolith 1976-08-22; last lunar sample return until Chang'e 5

fleet/lander/mars-2.json.name: Mars 2
fleet/lander/mars-2.json.tagline: First human-made object to reach Mars surface; lander crashed (1971)
fleet/lander/mars-2.json.description: The first human-made object to reach the Martian surface — by hard impact. The descent module crashed during the 1971 dust storm that obscured every other Mars probe in orbit at the time. Companion Mars 3 made the first soft landing two days later.
fleet/lander/mars-2.json.best_known_for: First human-made object to reach the Martian surface; lander crashed on impact (1971)

fleet/lander/mars-3.json.name: Mars 3
fleet/lander/mars-3.json.tagline: First soft landing on Mars; ~20 s of surface transmission
fleet/lander/mars-3.json.description: The first soft landing on Mars (December 1971). Began transmitting what would have been a surface image, but contact was lost after ~20 seconds leaving only a featureless grey frame. The global dust storm raging across the planet may have contributed to the early transmission loss.
fleet/lander/mars-3.json.best_known_for: First soft landing on Mars; ~20 s of surface transmission

fleet/lander/mars-polar-lander.json.name: Mars Polar Lander
fleet/lander/mars-polar-lander.json.tagline: Lost during landing in 1999; the failure led NASA to review its “faster, better, cheaper” approach
fleet/lander/mars-polar-lander.json.description: Mars Polar Lander was a NASA lander built by Lockheed Martin. Contact was lost during its descent to the Martian south polar region in December 1999. Coming months after the loss of Mars Climate Orbiter, the failure led NASA to review its “faster, better, cheaper” approach.
fleet/lander/mars-polar-lander.json.best_known_for: Lost during landing in 1999; the failure led NASA to review its “faster, better, cheaper” approach

fleet/lander/mars6.json.tagline: Soviet 1973 Mars lander — first descent telemetry from Mars atmosphere (224 s, mostly corrupted)
fleet/lander/mars6.json.description: Part of the Soviet four-spacecraft Mars wave of 1973 (Mars 4, 5, 6, 7) — and the only one to return useful science from a descent through Mars' atmosphere. Launched 1973-08-05 from Baikonur on a Proton-K, arrived 1974-03-12. The descent module separated from the flyby bus, entered the Martian atmosphere over Margaritifer Terra (23.90° S, 19.42° W), and returned 224 seconds of direct atmospheric telemetry — the first in-situ measurements of Mars' atmospheric temperature, pressure, and composition profile. However, due to a design flaw in the mass spectrometer's data system, a large amount of the data was corrupted and only partially recoverable. Signal was lost just before landing, during retrorocket firing; whether the lander crashed or survived to the surface is unknown. The flyby bus continued past Mars and acted as a relay station.
fleet/lander/mars6.json.best_known_for: Soviet 1973 Mars lander — first descent telemetry from Mars atmosphere (224 s, mostly corrupted)

fleet/lander/phoenix.json.name: Phoenix
fleet/lander/phoenix.json.tagline: Confirmed water ice in Martian soil
fleet/lander/phoenix.json.description: Phoenix is a planetary lander built by Lockheed Martin in USA. Confirmed water ice in Martian soil. Mission ended in 2008.
fleet/lander/phoenix.json.best_known_for: Confirmed water ice in Martian soil

fleet/lander/schiaparelli.json.name: Schiaparelli
fleet/lander/schiaparelli.json.tagline: ExoMars precursor; lessons fed Rosalind Franklin
fleet/lander/schiaparelli.json.description: ESA’s 2016 ExoMars demonstrator that crashed during landing — the IMU saturated during parachute descent, causing the flight computer to believe it was below ground level; it released the parachute and fired the retrorockets for only 3 seconds instead of 30, then went silent and impacted at ~300 km/h from 3.7 km altitude. Lessons fed directly into the Rosalind Franklin lander design.
fleet/lander/schiaparelli.json.best_known_for: ExoMars precursor; lessons fed Rosalind Franklin

fleet/lander/slim.json.name: SLIM
fleet/lander/slim.json.tagline: Pinpoint lunar landing; toppled but operational
fleet/lander/slim.json.description: JAXA’s 2024 lunar lander. Touched down within 100 m of its target — pinpoint accuracy unprecedented for a lunar lander — but landed on its nose at roughly 90 degrees, with solar panels facing away from the Sun. Still operated and survived four lunar nights without radioisotope heating — a record for passively-heated lunar surface missions.
fleet/lander/slim.json.best_known_for: Pinpoint lunar landing; toppled but operational

fleet/lander/surveyor-3.json.name: Surveyor 3
fleet/lander/surveyor-3.json.description: Surveyor 3 is a planetary lander built by Hughes Aircraft in USA. Apollo 12 visited it 2.5 years later. Mission ended in 1967.

fleet/lander/venera-13.json.tagline: First colour images of the Venusian surface — survived 127 minutes in 457 °C / 89-atm conditions
fleet/lander/venera-13.json.description: Soviet Venus lander pair (with Venera 14). Launched 1981-10-30 on a Proton-K / D-1. Venus arrival 1982-03-01: the 1645 kg titanium descent capsule entered the atmosphere at 11.2 km/s, deployed a parachute through the upper haze, then jettisoned it at 47 km and free-fell through the lower atmosphere with a disc-brake for terminal descent. Surface touchdown at 7.5°S, 303°E (Phoebe Regio volcanic flank). First panoramic colour images of the Venusian surface; first X-ray fluorescence soil-composition analysis (basaltic, like terrestrial ocean floor); first acoustic recordings from another planet. Operated 127 minutes — far beyond the 32-minute design life — before silicon-electronic failure in the 457 °C / 89-atmosphere CO₂ environment.
fleet/lander/venera-13.json.best_known_for: First colour images of Venus surface — 127-minute survival in 457 °C / 89-atm conditions

fleet/lander/venera-7.json.name: Venera 7-class
fleet/lander/venera-7.json.tagline: First soft landing on another planet and first to transmit data from another planet's surface (Venus, 1970)
fleet/lander/venera-7.json.description: Venera 7-class is a planetary lander built by NPO Lavochkin in USSR. First soft landing on another planet and first to transmit data from another planet's surface (Venus, 1970). Mission ended in 1970.
fleet/lander/venera-7.json.best_known_for: First soft landing on another planet and first to transmit data from another planet's surface (Venus, 1970)

fleet/lander/viking-1.json.name: Viking 1
fleet/lander/viking-1.json.tagline: First successful Mars lander; biology experiments
