fleet/lander/viking-1.json.dispatch: Viking 1 solved the problem nothing had solved: how to land on Mars and live. The Soviet landers before it had died within about twenty seconds of touchdown, returning only a featureless grey frame; Viking had to descend through an atmosphere too thin to rely on and too thick to ignore, and it did it with a first-of-its-kind sequence — an aeroshell to survive entry, a parachute for the middle of the fall, and throttled rocket engines to set its three legs down softly at the end. It was two machines in one, an orbiter to survey and relay and a lander to work the ground, and it carried the first laboratory ever sent to test another planet’s soil for life. Every Mars landing since has flown some version of the descent Viking proved.
fleet/lander/viking-1.json.description: The first successful Mars lander mission, on the surface from July 1976 through November 1982. Carried four biology experiments and returned high-resolution images of the Chryse Planitia plains. The Viking 1 / Viking 2 pair set the template for every Mars lander that followed.
fleet/lander/viking-1.json.best_known_for: First successful Mars lander; biology experiments

fleet/lander/viking2-lander.json.tagline: Second US Mars surface lander (Utopia Planitia 1976-09-03). Twin of Viking 1 lander; ran biology, soil chemistry + meteorology until 1980
fleet/lander/viking2-lander.json.description: The surface half of NASA's Viking 2 mission and the second successful US Mars lander, 47 days after Viking 1. Launched 1975-09-09 on a Titan IIIE-Centaur, touched down at Utopia Planitia (47.97° N, 134.04° E) on 1976-09-03 — much further north than Viking 1, in a different plains type to broaden the science return. Ran the same instrument suite as Viking 1: a biology package (Pyrolytic Release / Labeled Release / Gas Exchange experiments looking for microbial metabolism — the famously ambiguous Labeled Release positive that remains debated), GC-MS for soil organics (none detected), facsimile cameras returning > 1,400 images, X-ray fluorescence soil chemistry, meteorology, and seismometer (one of two ever flown on Mars — unable to detect quakes through cabin noise). Operated until 1980-04-11 when batteries failed.
fleet/lander/viking2-lander.json.best_known_for: Second US Mars surface lander (Utopia Planitia 1976-09-03). Twin of Viking 1 lander; ran biology, soil chemistry + meteorology until 1980

fleet/lander/vikram-cy2.json.name: Vikram (Chandrayaan-2)
fleet/lander/vikram-cy2.json.tagline: Lander of India's Chandrayaan-2; it crashed in 2019, but the orbiter kept working
fleet/lander/vikram-cy2.json.description: Vikram was the lander of India's Chandrayaan-2 mission, built by ISRO. It crashed during its landing attempt in September 2019, but the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter kept working in lunar orbit.
fleet/lander/vikram-cy2.json.best_known_for: Lander of India's Chandrayaan-2; it crashed in 2019, but the orbiter kept working

fleet/lander/vikram-cy3.json.name: Vikram (Chandrayaan-3)
fleet/lander/vikram-cy3.json.tagline: First landing near the lunar south pole
fleet/lander/vikram-cy3.json.description: India’s first successful lunar lander (August 2023), the first spacecraft to land near the lunar south pole. Four years after Vikram CY-2 crashed in the same region — the redemption arc India and ISRO needed.
fleet/lander/vikram-cy3.json.best_known_for: First landing near the lunar south pole

fleet/launch-site/alcantara.json.name: Alcântara Space Center
fleet/launch-site/alcantara.json.tagline: Brazil's equatorial launch centre: VLS-1 failures, the 2003 pad explosion, sounding rockets
fleet/launch-site/alcantara.json.description: Alcântara, on Brazil's northern coast in Maranhão at 2.3 degrees south, is among the launch sites closest to the equator. Construction began in 1982, and the Brazilian Air Force runs it for the Brazilian Space Agency. The first launch was a Sonda 2 sounding rocket on 21 February 1990. Brazil's VLS-1 satellite launcher failed on both flights, on 2 November 1997 and 11 December 1999. On 22 August 2003 the third VLS-1 exploded on its pad two days before launch and killed 21 people. No orbital launch from Alcântara has yet succeeded: Innospace's Hanbit-Nano failed in December 2025. Sounding rockets and test vehicles keep flying, a 2019 agreement with the United States covers foreign launches, and the site was built on land from which over 300 families were moved in 1980.
fleet/launch-site/alcantara.json.best_known_for: Brazil's equatorial launch centre: VLS-1 failures, the 2003 pad explosion, sounding rockets

fleet/launch-site/baikonur-1-5.json.name: Baikonur Site 1/5 (Gagarin's Start)
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-1-5.json.tagline: Sputnik 1 (1957). Vostok 1 — Gagarin (1961). Five hundred and forty Soyuz launches from a single pad.
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-1-5.json.description: The single most historically significant orbital launch pad in the world. R-7 ICBM test stand from 1957; immediately repurposed for Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957 — the start of the Space Age. Yuri Gagarin lifted from here on April 12, 1961. Every Vostok crew, every Voskhod, the bulk of all Soyuz manifests through to MS-15 in September 2019. Five hundred and forty launches from one pad over sixty-two years. Preserved as a museum monument; the 2019-era refurbishment plan was abandoned when the site was transferred to Kazakhstan in 2025.
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-1-5.json.best_known_for: Sputnik 1 (1957). Vostok 1 — Gagarin (1961). Five hundred and forty Soyuz launches from a single pad.

fleet/launch-site/baikonur-200.json.name: Baikonur Site 200
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-200.json.tagline: Proton pad — the Mir core, Salyut 7, Nauka, and probes from Venera to ExoMars
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-200.json.description: Baikonur Site 200 has two Proton pads, 200/39 and 200/40. Pad 39 launched the core of the Mir space station in 1986 and its Kvant-1, Kvant-2 and Kristall modules, and in 2021 the Nauka module for the ISS; pad 40 launched Salyut 7. Planetary probes left from both pads: Venera 13 to 16, the Vega 1 and 2 missions to Venus and Halley's Comet, Fobos 1 and 2, the failed Mars-96, and the 2016 ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter. Pad 40 has stood idle since it was set aside for an Angara rebuild that moved to another site; pad 39 still flies Proton-M, including commercial launches for International Launch Services.
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-200.json.best_known_for: Proton pad — the Mir core, Salyut 7, Nauka, and probes from Venera to ExoMars

fleet/launch-site/baikonur-31-6.json.name: Baikonur Site 31/6
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-31-6.json.tagline: Active Soyuz crewed pad — every ISS Soyuz crew rotation since 2020 has lifted from Site 31
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-31-6.json.description: The other half of the Baikonur Soyuz operation. Originally an R-7 ICBM pad from 1961; modernised for Soyuz-2.1a in 2014. When Site 1/5 went down for refurbishment in 2019, Site 31 picked up the entire Soyuz crew programme — every Soyuz MS rotation to the ISS since MS-16 in April 2020 has lifted from here. Continuous human spaceflight cadence: roughly two crews per year, with no interruption.
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-31-6.json.best_known_for: Active Soyuz crewed pad — every ISS Soyuz crew rotation since 2020 has lifted from Site 31

fleet/launch-site/baikonur-81.json.name: Baikonur Site 81
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-81.json.tagline: Baikonur's Proton complex: Proton 1, Salyut 1, Mir and ISS modules, Mars and Luna probes
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-81.json.description: Site 81 is the Proton complex at Baikonur Cosmodrome, with two pads, 81/23 and 81/24, used alongside Site 200. Pad 23 saw the first Proton launch, Proton 1, on 16 July 1965. It also launched Mars 3, Luna 16, 17, 21 and 24, the Spektr and Priroda modules of Mir, and the Zarya (20 November 1998) and Zvezda (12 July 2000) modules of the International Space Station. Pad 24 launched Mars 2, 5 and 7, Venera 9, 10 and 12, and the Salyut stations 1, 4 and 6; Salyut 2, 3 and 5 went from pad 23. In 2013 a Proton-M crashed beside pad 24 just after lift-off. Pad 23 is inactive; pad 24 flew Elektro-L No. 5 on 12 February 2026, the final Proton-M in the DM-03 configuration.
fleet/launch-site/baikonur-81.json.best_known_for: Baikonur's Proton complex: Proton 1, Salyut 1, Mir and ISS modules, Mars and Luna probes

fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-lc-17.j.name: Cape Canaveral Launch Complex 17 (LC-17)
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-lc-17.j.tagline: Thor and Delta pad pair: Spirit, Opportunity, Pathfinder, MESSENGER, Dawn; demolished in 2018
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-lc-17.j.description: Two Thor-lineage pads, 17A and 17B, near the beach at Cape Canaveral. The Air Force built them in 1956 for the Thor missile, then upgraded them in the early 1960s for Thor-derived rockets, which became the Delta family. Pioneer 0, an attempted lunar orbiter, was lost here on 17 August 1958 when its Thor-Able exploded 73.6 seconds after liftoff. In the Delta II years the pads sent NASA probes to Mars and beyond: NEAR Shoemaker and Mars Pathfinder in 1996, Spirit and Opportunity in 2003, MESSENGER in 2004, Phoenix and Dawn in 2007. The Delta III flew three times from 17B between 1998 and 2000 before the programme was abandoned. The last launch was GRAIL on 10 September 2011, and both towers were demolished on 12 July 2018.
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-lc-17.j.best_known_for: Thor and Delta pad pair: Spirit, Opportunity, Pathfinder, MESSENGER, Dawn; demolished in 2018

fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-lc-36b..tagline: USAF Atlas-Centaur pad — Mariner 10, Pioneer 11 (1973), Pioneer Venus (1978); now Blue Origin New Glenn (leased 2015, flew 2025)
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-lc-36b..description: Cape Canaveral Launch Complex 36B was the second of two Atlas-Centaur pads at Cape Canaveral (alongside LC-36A, built first). LC-36B first flew 1965-08-11 with Atlas-Centaur AC-6 and became the workhorse pad for the high-energy Atlas-Centaur stack — flying Mariner 10 (1973-11-03, first Mercury flyby), Pioneer 11 (1973-04-06, first Saturn flyby), Pioneer Venus 1 + 2 (1978), and many Intelsat / Inmarsat / Hot Bird commercial GEO comsats through the 1990s and early 2000s. Final flight 2005-02-03 — Atlas IIIB AC-208 — the last Atlas IIIB launch and last LC-36B flight under USAF auspices. The complex was leased to Blue Origin in 2015 and demolished + rebuilt as the Blue Origin New Glenn pad (LC-36 unified), with first New Glenn flight 2025-01-16. The original LC-36B mobile service tower was felled 2007-06-16.
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-lc-36b..best_known_for: USAF Atlas-Centaur pad — Mariner 10 + Pioneer 11 (1973), Pioneer Venus (1978), Intelsat — now Blue Origin New Glenn (since 2015)

fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-slc-40..name: Cape Canaveral SLC-40
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-slc-40..tagline: Highest-cadence Falcon 9 pad on the planet — workhorse for ISS resupply + Starlink + national-security
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-slc-40..description: Originally a Titan III / Titan IV pad from 1965 through 2005, refit by SpaceX in 2008 for Falcon 9. Today SLC-40 is the highest-cadence orbital pad ever operated, flying Starlink batches, commercial sats, ISS resupply via Cargo Dragon, and US national-security payloads. Rebuilt after the AMOS-6 explosion in September 2016 with an upgraded propellant system; the pad still does most of the SpaceX manifest the world sees.
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-slc-40..best_known_for: Highest-cadence Falcon 9 pad on the planet — workhorse for ISS resupply + Starlink + national-security

fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-slc-41..name: Cape Canaveral SLC-41
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-slc-41..tagline: Atlas V's main pad — flew every Atlas V mission including Mars Perseverance + Lucy + Starliner CFT
fleet/launch-site/cape-canaveral-slc-41..description: United Launch Alliance's primary Atlas V pad at Cape Canaveral, originally built for Titan III in the 1960s, entirely demolished in 1999 and rebuilt as the Atlas V pad; first Atlas V flight 2002-08-21. Every Atlas V flight has launched from here — Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Curiosity, Perseverance, Lucy, Juno, the Boeing Starliner Crew Flight Test, and dozens of NSSL national-security missions. Also hosts Vulcan Centaur, which began flying from SLC-41 in January 2024.

fleet/launch-site/hammaguir.json.name: Hammaguir Brigitte
fleet/launch-site/hammaguir.json.tagline: France's first satellite, Astérix, launched on a Diamant A in 1965
fleet/launch-site/hammaguir.json.description: Hammaguir was a French rocket range in the Algerian Sahara, about 120 km south-west of Béchar. The French Army's CIEES developed it from the late 1940s for sounding rockets and missiles. Its Brigitte complex tested the 'precious stones' rockets (Agate, Topaze, Émeraude, Saphir, Rubis), which led to the Diamant launcher. On 26 November 1965 a Diamant A put Astérix, France's first satellite, into orbit: France became the third country to orbit a satellite on its own rocket, after the Soviet Union and the United States. Three more French satellites followed in 1966 and 1967. Under the Évian accords France kept the base until July 1967, and Diamant launches then moved to Kourou in French Guiana. More than 270 rockets were fired from Hammaguir.
fleet/launch-site/hammaguir.json.best_known_for: France's first satellite, Astérix, launched on a Diamant A in 1965

fleet/launch-site/jiuquan-slc-43.json.name: Jiuquan SLC-43
fleet/launch-site/jiuquan-slc-43.json.tagline: China's crewed-spaceflight pad — every Shenzhou crew
fleet/launch-site/jiuquan-slc-43.json.description: The first Chinese space launch site (1958), operational orbital launches since 1970, and from 1999 onward the dedicated home of human spaceflight: every Shenzhou crew (1 through 19 as of 2025) has lifted from SLC-43 Pad 91 on Long March 2F rockets. Jiuquan is inland in the Gobi desert at 40.96°N — too far north for the equatorial geometry that Wenchang handles. Tianzhou cargo missions to Tiangong fly from Wenchang Space Launch Site instead.
fleet/launch-site/jiuquan-slc-43.json.best_known_for: China's crewed-spaceflight pad — every Shenzhou crew

fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-2.json.name: Kourou ELA-2
fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-2.json.tagline: Early Ariane pad — 1 Ariane 2, 2 Ariane 3, 116 Ariane 4 (1986-2003)
fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-2.json.description: ELA-2 (Ensemble de Lancement Ariane 2) at Kourou's Centre Spatial Guyanais hosted 119 Ariane launches: one Ariane 2 (1986-03-28), two Ariane 3, and all 116 launches of the Ariane 4 rocket (1988-2003). Its near-equatorial position gave Ariane 4 a substantial GTO performance advantage over launch sites at higher latitudes, anchoring Arianespace's commercial dominance in the 1990s. Decommissioned after Ariane 4 retired; ELA-3 (Ariane 5) and ELA-4 (Ariane 6) are its successors.

fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-3.json.name: Kourou ELA-3
fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-3.json.tagline: Ariane 5's home pad — JWST + Galileo + a quarter of geostationary commercial sats over a decade
fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-3.json.description: Europe chose French Guiana in the 1960s because 5.2°N is just five degrees off the equator — the geometry adds about 460 m/s of free eastward velocity for geostationary launches, and the Atlantic to the east is empty. ELA-3 hosted Ariane 5 from its maiden flight in June 1996 — which failed 37 seconds after launch due to a software error — through the successful final mission in July 2023: James Webb, the Galileo navigation system, BepiColombo, Rosetta, Herschel + Planck, JUICE, and the bulk of Western commercial GEO traffic for two decades. ELA-4 next door is now active with Ariane 6.
fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-3.json.best_known_for: Ariane 5's home pad — JWST + Galileo + a quarter of geostationary commercial sats over a decade

fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-4.json.name: Kourou ELA-4
fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-4.json.tagline: Ariane 6's home pad — Europe's geostationary access after Ariane 5
fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-4.json.description: The sister pad to ELA-3 at the Centre Spatial Guyanais. Construction started in 2015; Ariane 6's maiden flight VA262 lifted from here on July 9, 2024. ELA-4 inherits the same 5.2°N equatorial advantage that made Ariane 5 the most successful Western geostationary launcher of its era, with a redesigned ground-segment for higher cadence: horizontal-integration assembly building, sliding mobile gantry, full integration of the new ESC-B upper stage. Europe's strategic-autonomy launcher for institutional payloads (Galileo upgrade, Copernicus, ESA science missions) plus commercial GEO traffic.
fleet/launch-site/kourou-ela-4.json.best_known_for: Ariane 6's home pad — Europe's geostationary access after Ariane 5

fleet/launch-site/kourou-els.json.name: Kourou ELS (Soyuz launch complex)
fleet/launch-site/kourou-els.json.tagline: Europe's Soyuz pad: first Soyuz outside Baikonur or Plesetsk (2011), 27 launches, eight for Galileo
fleet/launch-site/kourou-els.json.description: ELS was the Soyuz pad at Europe's Spaceport, about 13 km north-west of the Ariane pads near Sinnamary. Soyuz-ST flew from it 27 times between 21 October 2011 and 10 February 2022, the first Soyuz launches outside Baikonur and Plesetsk. At 5.3 degrees north the rocket could lift up to 3 tonnes to geostationary transfer orbit, against 1.7 tonnes from Baikonur. Payloads included eight Galileo launches, Pleiades 1A and 1B, Gaia (2013), Sentinel-1A and 1B, MetOp-C and CHEOPS. Twenty-six of the 27 flights succeeded; on 22 August 2014 a Fregat upper-stage fault left two Galileo satellites in the wrong orbit. Russia suspended operations in February 2022, and Wikipedia reports that the pad was demolished on 24 April 2026 to make room for MaiaSpace's Maia rocket.
fleet/launch-site/kourou-els.json.best_known_for: Europe's Soyuz pad: first Soyuz outside Baikonur or Plesetsk (2011), 27 launches, eight for Galileo

fleet/launch-site/kourou-zlv.json.name: Kourou ZLV (Vega launch complex)
fleet/launch-site/kourou-zlv.json.tagline: Kourou's first launch site: Europa II, Ariane 1 and Giotto on this ground, rebuilt in 2001 for Vega and Vega-C
fleet/launch-site/kourou-zlv.json.description: Three launch bases have stood on this spot at Kourou. Europe built the first for the Europa II, whose only flight on 5 November 1971 failed. Rebuilt as ELA-1, it flew Ariane 1 from 24 December 1979, then Ariane 2 and 3 until 11 July 1989. Giotto left from here on an Ariane 1 on 2 July 1985 to meet Halley's Comet. From November 2001 the pad was rebuilt for Vega, keeping the Ariane 1 flame trench and adding a 50 m retractable assembly building. Vega first flew on 13 February 2012, Vega-C on 13 July 2022. Payloads include LISA Pathfinder, Sentinel-2A and 2B, ADM-Aeolus and BIOMASS. Wikipedia counts 56 launches from the site by September 2026, 22 of them Vega and 8 Vega-C. The tower sits close to the equator at 5.2 degrees north.
fleet/launch-site/kourou-zlv.json.best_known_for: Kourou's first launch site: Europa II, Ariane 1 and Giotto on this ground, rebuilt in 2001 for Vega and Vega-C

fleet/launch-site/lc-14.json.tagline: Cape Canaveral Mercury-Atlas pad — launched all 4 orbital Mercury flights (Glenn / Carpenter / Schirra / Cooper, 1962-1963)
fleet/launch-site/lc-14.json.dispatch: If Complex 5 is where Americans first touched space, Complex 14 is where they first stayed. This was the Atlas pad, and all four orbital Mercury flights left from it — Glenn, Carpenter, Schirra, Cooper — the flights that put an American in orbit rather than on an arc. It later launched the Gemini-Atlas target vehicles that taught crews to rendezvous, so the same patch of ground bridges the first orbits and the docking skills Apollo would need. Where 5 holds the starting line, 14 holds the moment the United States became a genuinely orbital nation.
fleet/launch-site/lc-14.json.description: Cape Canaveral Launch Complex 14 hosted Atlas missile tests then the four orbital Mercury-Atlas crewed missions: Friendship 7 (1962-02-20, Glenn — first American in orbit), Aurora 7 (1962-05-24, Carpenter), Sigma 7 (1962-10-03, Schirra), and Faith 7 (1963-05-15, Cooper). After Mercury, LC-14 hosted four Atlas-Agena uncrewed missions before being deactivated in 1967. A steel Mercury 7 monument was dedicated on November 10, 1964 at the pad. The launch ring + service tower base remain visible.
fleet/launch-site/lc-14.json.best_known_for: Cape Canaveral Mercury-Atlas pad — launched all 4 orbital Mercury flights (Glenn / Carpenter / Schirra / Cooper, 1962-1963)

fleet/launch-site/lc-34.json.tagline: NASA pad at Cape Canaveral (1961-68) — first Saturn I; Apollo 1 fire site 1967-01-27; Apollo 7 first crewed launch 1968-10-11
fleet/launch-site/lc-34.json.dispatch: Launch Complex 34 is where the Saturn era began — and where it almost ended. The first Saturn rocket lifted off from this single-towered pad in 1961, proving von Braun's outsized boosters could fly at all. It is also the place where, on 27 January 1967, the Apollo 1 fire killed Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee during a ground test — the program's darkest day, on the pad, before anything had left the ground. And it is where Apollo came back twenty-one months later: Apollo 7, the first crewed flight, launched from LC-34 and proved the redesigned spacecraft was sound. One small pad held the whole arc — the beginning, the catastrophe, and the recovery. A memorial stands there now.
fleet/launch-site/lc-34.json.description: Cape Canaveral Launch Complex 34 served NASA from 1961-10-27 (first Saturn I, SA-1) through 1968-10-11 (Apollo 7, the first crewed Apollo flight). LC-34's single steel umbilical tower hosted four uncrewed Saturn I flights (SA-1 through SA-4, 1961-1963), was then reconstructed for Saturn IB, and flew two uncrewed Saturn IB flights (AS-201 in 1966, AS-202 in 1966) before the Apollo 1 test. On 1967-01-27 during a Plugs-Out test of Apollo 1 — the planned first crewed Block I CSM flight — a flash fire in the pure-O₂ cabin killed Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee in seconds. The pad was rebuilt for Apollo 7 (1968-10-11) which launched the first crewed Apollo flight, then deactivated 1968-11. The pad's concrete deluge ring + main flame trench still stand; a memorial plaque on site reads "They gave their lives in service to their country in the ongoing exploration of humankind's final frontier."
fleet/launch-site/lc-34.json.best_known_for: NASA pad at Cape Canaveral (1961-68) — first Saturn I; Apollo 1 fire site 1967-01-27; Apollo 7 first crewed launch 1968-10-11

fleet/launch-site/lc-39a.json.name: Launch Complex 39A
fleet/launch-site/lc-39a.json.tagline: Launched Apollo 8, 9 and 11–17 (Apollo 9 in Earth orbit; Apollo 10 flew from 39B); today flies Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, and Crew Dragon
fleet/launch-site/lc-39a.json.dispatch: Launch Complex 39A was built around an idea nearly as radical as the rocket it served: don't build the rocket at the pad. Instead, stack the Saturn V inside the cavernous Vehicle Assembly Building, then carry the whole ~3,000-tonne stack out to the pad — standing upright — on a crawler-transporter creeping along at walking pace. That "clean pad" approach let one site turn around the largest rocket ever flown far faster than assembling it in place ever could. The design outlived Apollo by half a century: the same pad launched most of the Space Shuttle fleet and, leased to SpaceX in 2014, now flies Falcon Heavy and astronauts on Crew Dragon. Good infrastructure, it turns out, is the quietest kind of moonshot — build it once and it keeps paying off.
fleet/launch-site/lc-39a.json.description: Built for Saturn V, kept for the Shuttle, leased to SpaceX in 2014. From Pad A: Apollo 4 (the first Saturn V), Apollo 11 (the first lunar landing), Apollo 13, Apollo 17 (the last lunar landing), Skylab, eighty-two Space Shuttle flights including the first STS-1, and since 2017 every Falcon Heavy and every Crew Dragon to the ISS. The same flame trench, the same crawlerway, three eras of US human spaceflight.
fleet/launch-site/lc-39a.json.best_known_for: Launched Apollo 8, 9 and 11–17 (Apollo 9 in Earth orbit; Apollo 10 flew from 39B); today flies Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, and Crew Dragon

fleet/launch-site/lc-39b.json.name: Launch Complex 39B
fleet/launch-site/lc-39b.json.tagline: Apollo 10 + Skylab + 53 Shuttle flights; now NASA's SLS / Artemis pad
fleet/launch-site/lc-39b.json.description: Pad 39B carried Apollo 10 (the lunar dress rehearsal), Skylab 2/3/4 crew launches, and fifty-three Space Shuttle flights — the first of which was the ill-fated STS-51-L Challenger in January 1986. Rebuilt as a clean pad in the late 2000s — no permanent service tower, mobile launcher platform per mission — to host the next generation of vehicles. Artemis I lifted from 39B in November 2022; Artemis II and III will follow.
fleet/launch-site/lc-39b.json.best_known_for: Apollo 10 + Skylab + 53 Shuttle flights; now NASA's SLS / Artemis pad

fleet/launch-site/lc-5.json.tagline: Cape Canaveral Mercury-Redstone pad — launched Freedom 7 (Shepard, 1961-05-05) and Liberty Bell 7 (Grissom, 1961-07-21)
fleet/launch-site/lc-5.json.dispatch: Launch Complex 5 is a modest concrete pad with an outsized claim: it is where American human spaceflight physically began. It had been a Redstone missile test stand before NASA adapted it, and from it, on 5 May 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American to leave the planet. It launched only the two suborbital Mercury hops before the program moved to the more powerful Atlas pads down the Cape — a short career, but it holds the starting line. The first American flight of everything that followed traces back to this spot.
fleet/launch-site/lc-5.json.description: Cape Canaveral Launch Complex 5 hosted Redstone IRBM tests (1956-1961) before being modified for NASA's Mercury-Redstone programme. Freedom 7 (1961-05-05, Shepard, first American in space) and Liberty Bell 7 (1961-07-21, Grissom) both launched from LC-5. The pad's blockhouse — heavy reinforced concrete with thick blast-resistant glass — survives intact and is part of the Cape Canaveral Air Force Station Museum, used as a Mercury programme exhibit space. The blockhouse interior preserves the period instrument panels, including the consoles where launch teams worked through the Cuban missile crisis. Final launch 1961-07-21 — LC-5 was retired after Liberty Bell 7 when NASA shifted to LC-14 for the Atlas-Mercury flights.
fleet/launch-site/lc-5.json.best_known_for: Cape Canaveral Mercury-Redstone pad — launched Freedom 7 (Shepard, 1961-05-05) and Liberty Bell 7 (Grissom, 1961-07-21)

fleet/launch-site/naro-space-center.json.name: Naro Space Center
fleet/launch-site/naro-space-center.json.tagline: South Korea's spaceport: Naro-1 (2009-13) and the home-built Nuri rocket since 2021
fleet/launch-site/naro-space-center.json.description: Naro Space Center stands on the south coast of South Korea, in Goheung County about 485 km south of Seoul, and is run by KARI. It has two pads. The Naro-1 rocket, with a Russian first stage, flew from LC-1 three times: the flights of 25 August 2009 and 10 June 2010 failed to reach orbit, and on 30 January 2013 the third put the STSAT-2C satellite into low orbit. On 28 November 2018 a Nuri test vehicle flew a 10-minute suborbital hop to qualify its KRE-075 engine. Nuri, the first orbital rocket designed and built entirely in South Korea, lifted off from LC-2 on 21 October 2021 and failed in its third stage. Its second flight, on 21 June 2022, reached a 700 km orbit, and further flights followed on 25 May 2023, 26 November 2025 and 7 October 2026, all from LC-2.
fleet/launch-site/naro-space-center.json.best_known_for: South Korea's spaceport: Naro-1 (2009-13) and the home-built Nuri rocket since 2021

fleet/launch-site/palmachim.json.name: Palmachim Airbase
fleet/launch-site/palmachim.json.tagline: Israel's launch site: Shavit rockets put Ofeq satellites in retrograde orbit since 1988
fleet/launch-site/palmachim.json.description: Palmachim Airbase stands on the Mediterranean coast west of Yavne, about 12 km south of the Tel Aviv area. The Israeli Air Force and the Israel Space Agency operate it jointly as Israel's spaceport. Israel Aerospace Industries' three-stage solid-fuel Shavit rocket first flew from here on 19 September 1988, carrying Ofeq-1 into orbit and making Israel the eighth country able to launch its own satellite. Launching east would send stages over neighbouring states, so Shavit flies west over the sea into retrograde orbits, with Ofeq at 143 degrees inclination. At this latitude the Earth's rotation works against the rocket by about 1,420 km/h, which cuts payload. The Shavit is widely reported to be derived from the Jericho II missile. The base also hosts helicopter and drone squadrons and an Arrow missile battery.
fleet/launch-site/palmachim.json.best_known_for: Israel's launch site: Shavit rockets put Ofeq satellites in retrograde orbit since 1988

fleet/launch-site/plesetsk-41-1.json.name: Plesetsk Cosmodrome
fleet/launch-site/plesetsk-41-1.json.tagline: Russia's northern military cosmodrome — more launches than any other site
fleet/launch-site/plesetsk-41-1.json.description: Plesetsk Cosmodrome lies in Russia's far north, at about 62.9°N. It was founded in 1957 as an R-7 intercontinental-missile base and became a space launch site on 17 March 1966, when a Vostok-2 rocket put Kosmos 112 into orbit from Site 41/1. Run by the Russian Ministry of Defence, it launched most Soviet military satellites — reconnaissance, navigation, early-warning and Molniya communications — and by 1997 had made more than 1,500 launches, more than any other site in the world. R-7 family rockets flew from Sites 41/1, 16/2 and 43; Kosmos-3M and Rokot from Sites 132 and 133; Tsyklon-3 from Site 32; and, since 2014, Angara from Site 35. Site 43 has its own entry.
fleet/launch-site/plesetsk-41-1.json.best_known_for: Russia's northern military cosmodrome — over 1,500 launches by 1997, more than any other site

fleet/launch-site/plesetsk-43.json.name: Plesetsk Site 43
fleet/launch-site/plesetsk-43.json.tagline: Plesetsk's workhorse Soyuz pad at 62.9°N — the world's highest-latitude active orbital launch complex
fleet/launch-site/plesetsk-43.json.description: Plesetsk Cosmodrome sits at 62.9°N — the world's highest-latitude active orbital launch complex. Site 43 is one of several pads at Plesetsk and operates Soyuz-2 today for Russian polar / Molniya / GLONASS payloads. Originally an R-7 ICBM base in the late 1950s, repurposed for space launches in 1966, and for several decades Plesetsk held the record for most orbital launches from any single site on Earth. The high latitude limits how much the Earth's rotation contributes (less than at Baikonur or Wenchang), but it's perfect for high-inclination missions that Baikonur can't easily reach without dogleg manoeuvres.
fleet/launch-site/plesetsk-43.json.best_known_for: World's most northerly orbital launch site — Russia's polar / Molniya military + GLONASS pad

fleet/launch-site/rocket-lab-lc-1.json.name: Rocket Lab Launch Complex 1
fleet/launch-site/rocket-lab-lc-1.json.tagline: First private orbital launch site: Rocket Lab's Electron from Mahia, New Zealand
fleet/launch-site/rocket-lab-lc-1.json.description: On the Māhia Peninsula, on the east coast of New Zealand's North Island, Rocket Lab built the first private spaceport to host a successful orbital launch. It opened on 26 September 2016. The pads stand on a raised plateau about 104 m above the sea, with cliffs on three sides and a single access road. Electron's first flight, "It's a Test", left Pad A on 25 May 2017 and reached space but not orbit; the second, on 21 January 2018, put its satellites into orbit. Pad B flew its first mission on 28 February 2022. Rocket Lab's user guide gives a capacity of up to 120 launches a year. The company picked Māhia for its open sea to the east and sparse air traffic.
fleet/launch-site/rocket-lab-lc-1.json.best_known_for: First private orbital launch site: Rocket Lab's Electron from Mahia, New Zealand

fleet/launch-site/san-marco.json.name: San Marco Platform
fleet/launch-site/san-marco.json.tagline: Italian sea platform off Kenya that launched Uhuru, the first satellite dedicated to X-ray astronomy
fleet/launch-site/san-marco.json.description: San Marco was a launch platform in the Indian Ocean off Ras Ngomeni, near Malindi, Kenya, about 3 degrees south of the equator, where an eastward launch gets the most help from Earth's rotation. A former oil platform, it was run by the University of Rome's Aerospace Research Centre under a 1962 agreement with NASA; a second platform, Santa Rita, housed launch control, and a smaller one the radar. NASA supplied Scout rockets and trained the Italian crews. San Marco 2 flew from here on 26 April 1967, the first satellite launched from a sea platform. Uhuru, the first satellite dedicated to X-ray astronomy, followed on 12 December 1970 on a Scout B. The last satellite, San Marco D/L, flew in March 1988. ASI has managed the centre since 2004, and its ground station still tracks satellites.
fleet/launch-site/san-marco.json.best_known_for: Italian sea platform off Kenya that launched Uhuru, the first satellite dedicated to X-ray astronomy

fleet/launch-site/semnan-imam-khomeini.j.name: Semnan Space Center (Imam Khomeini Spaceport)
fleet/launch-site/semnan-imam-khomeini.j.tagline: Iran's orbital launch site: Safir put Omid, Iran's first home-built satellite, in orbit in 2009
fleet/launch-site/semnan-imam-khomeini.j.description: Semnan Space Center lies about 50 km southeast of the city of Semnan, in the northern Dasht-e Kavir desert; the Iranian Space Agency runs it. Its oldest pad is a 65 m circular platform with a service tower, used by the Safir rocket. A Safir flew from Semnan on 17 August 2008 with a dummy satellite, and on 2 February 2009 it put the 40 cm cube Omid into orbit, making Iran the ninth country to launch its own satellite. A larger complex to the east, the Imam Khomeini Space Launch Terminal, has a rail-mounted service tower for the bigger Simorgh, which first flew on 19 April 2016. Airstrikes on 24 to 26 March 2026 damaged or destroyed four structures around the Simorgh complex, according to an IISS analysis of satellite imagery; no launch from Semnan has followed.
fleet/launch-site/semnan-imam-khomeini.j.best_known_for: Iran's orbital launch site: Safir put Omid, Iran's first home-built satellite, in orbit in 2009

fleet/launch-site/sohae.json.name: Sohae Satellite Launching Station
fleet/launch-site/sohae.json.tagline: North Korea's satellite launch site: Unha rockets (2012, 2016) and Chollima-1 (2023)
fleet/launch-site/sohae.json.description: Sohae, also called Tongchang-ri, lies in hills near North Korea's border with China, in Cholsan County. Construction was visible in satellite images from the early 1990s and reported complete in 2011; the site covers over six square kilometres. The first launch was an Unha-3 rocket carrying Kwangmyongsong-3 on 13 April 2012; it failed shortly after liftoff. A second Unha-3 on 12 December 2012 placed an object in orbit, according to NORAD, and another Unha flew on 7 February 2016. A smaller, newer pad hosts Chollima-1: it failed on 30 May and 23 August 2023 (UTC), then put the Malligyong-1 reconnaissance satellite into orbit on 21 November 2023. The United States and others regard these launches as missile tests; parts of the site were dismantled in 2018 and rebuilt from 2019.
fleet/launch-site/sohae.json.best_known_for: North Korea's satellite launch site: Unha rockets (2012, 2016) and Chollima-1 (2023)

fleet/launch-site/sriharikota-slp.json.name: Sriharikota SLP
fleet/launch-site/sriharikota-slp.json.tagline: India's heavy-lift pad — GSLV Mk III / LVM3 to Chandrayaan-3 and the upcoming Gaganyaan crew programme
fleet/launch-site/sriharikota-slp.json.description: Sriharikota Island on India's east coast, 13.7°N — closer to the equator than Cape Canaveral, with the Bay of Bengal corridor empty downrange. The Second Launch Pad (SLP) handles ISRO's heavy-lift programme: PSLV manifests, LVM3 (formerly GSLV Mk III), Chandrayaan-1 (October 2008, lunar orbiter/impactor), Chandrayaan-2 (July 2019, lost on landing), Chandrayaan-3 (July 2023, successful soft landing near the south pole), and the planned Gaganyaan crewed missions. The First Launch Pad next door handles smaller PSLV / SSLV manifests and hosted the Mangalyaan Mars launch (November 2013).
fleet/launch-site/sriharikota-slp.json.best_known_for: India's heavy-lift pad — GSLV Mk III / LVM3 to Chandrayaan-3 and the upcoming Gaganyaan crew programme

fleet/launch-site/starbase-orbital-a.jso.name: Starbase Orbital Pad A
fleet/launch-site/starbase-orbital-a.jso.tagline: First Starship orbital flight test; designed for the full reusable Mars-bound stack
fleet/launch-site/starbase-orbital-a.jso.description: SpaceX's Starship pad at Boca Chica, Texas — built from scratch starting in 2019 for the fully reusable Starship + Super Heavy. First integrated flight test (IFT-1) lifted off April 20, 2023; vehicle lost ~4 minutes post-liftoff after engine failures caused loss of control, but the pad survived. Subsequent IFTs through 2024-25 demonstrated booster catch via the Mechazilla tower arms, successful sea splashdowns, and increasing payload-class capability. The water deluge system at this pad is the largest ever built for an orbital launch — the over-pressure footprint from 33 Raptor-class engines is unlike anything else flying.
fleet/launch-site/starbase-orbital-a.jso.best_known_for: First Starship orbital flight test; designed for the full reusable Mars-bound stack

fleet/launch-site/taiyuan-lc-9.json.name: Taiyuan LC-9
fleet/launch-site/taiyuan-lc-9.json.tagline: Long March 2D / 4B / 4C polar-orbit workhorse — Yaogan, Gaofen, weather sats
fleet/launch-site/taiyuan-lc-9.json.description: Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center's LC-9 (also known as Pad 9) handles most of TYSC's polar and sun-synchronous orbit launches with the Long March 2D, 4B, 4C, and 6A. Typical payloads include the Yaogan reconnaissance series, the Gaofen Earth-observation constellation, and the Fengyun meteorological satellites. Active since 2008.
fleet/launch-site/taiyuan-lc-9.json.best_known_for: Polar-orbit workhorse for Yaogan + Gaofen + Fengyun

fleet/launch-site/tanegashima-yoshinobu..name: Tanegashima Yoshinobu LP-1
fleet/launch-site/tanegashima-yoshinobu..tagline: Japan's heavy-lift gateway — H-IIA + H3, HTV / HTV-X cargo to the ISS
fleet/launch-site/tanegashima-yoshinobu..description: On Tanegashima, the southern Japanese island that's been home to JAXA's orbital programme since 1969. LP-1 hosted the H-II maiden flight in 1996; the H-IIA from 2001 (49 successes in 50 flights; retired June 2025 after its final mission); the seven HTV cargo flights to the ISS between 2009 and 2020; and from 2023 the new H3 rocket. Tanegashima's 30°N geometry is workable for geostationary launches — the south Pacific is empty downrange — and the fishing fleet stand-down windows are famously short, giving Japan some of the tightest launch-window protocols in the world.
fleet/launch-site/tanegashima-yoshinobu..best_known_for: Japan's heavy-lift gateway — H-IIA + H3, HTV / HTV-X cargo to the ISS

fleet/launch-site/uchinoura.json.name: Uchinoura Space Center
fleet/launch-site/uchinoura.json.tagline: Japan's first satellite Ohsumi (1970), the M-V rockets, Hayabusa and Epsilon
fleet/launch-site/uchinoura.json.description: Uchinoura Space Center sits on the Pacific coast of Kagoshima Prefecture, on Kyushu, in hilly ground at 31 degrees north. It opened in February 1962 as the Kagoshima Space Center and took its present name when JAXA formed in 2003. After four failed launches, a Lambda 4S-5 put Ohsumi in orbit on 11 February 1970, Japan's first satellite. Until the solid-fuel M-V rockets retired in 2006, every Japanese scientific satellite flew from here: HALCA in 1997, the Nozomi Mars probe in July 1998, Hayabusa to asteroid Itokawa on 9 May 2003, ASTRO-E2 in 2005 and Hinode on 22 September 2006. The smaller Epsilon rocket first flew from Uchinoura on 14 September 2013 with the SPRINT-A satellite. Large antennas at the site also talk to deep-space probes.
fleet/launch-site/uchinoura.json.best_known_for: Japan's first satellite Ohsumi (1970), the M-V rockets, Hayabusa and Epsilon

fleet/launch-site/vandenberg-slc-4e.json.name: Vandenberg SLC-4E
fleet/launch-site/vandenberg-slc-4e.json.tagline: Polar / sun-synchronous gateway — Falcon 9 to Starlink + national-security + earth-observation
fleet/launch-site/vandenberg-slc-4e.json.description: The US west-coast orbital gateway. Built for Atlas-Agena in 1963; Titan III/IV through to 2005; refit by SpaceX in 2011. Vandenberg's geographic advantage is the corridor due south over the Pacific — that's how US payloads reach polar and sun-synchronous orbits without overflying populated land. Today SLC-4E flies Falcon 9 to Starlink polar shells, NRO classified payloads, USSF + commercial earth-observation satellites. SLC-4W next door is the booster recovery zone.
fleet/launch-site/vandenberg-slc-4e.json.best_known_for: Polar / sun-synchronous gateway — Falcon 9 to Starlink + national-security + earth-observation

fleet/launch-site/vostochny-1s.json.name: Vostochny Site 1S
fleet/launch-site/vostochny-1s.json.tagline: Russia's Soyuz-2 pad in the Far East: first launch 2016, OneWeb batches, Luna 25 (2023)
fleet/launch-site/vostochny-1s.json.description: Site 1S is the Soyuz-2 launch pad at the Vostochny Cosmodrome in Amur Oblast, in Russia's Far East at 51.9 degrees north. Russia began building Vostochny in 2011, on the site of the former Svobodny missile base, so it could launch from its own territory instead of renting Baikonur from Kazakhstan. The first launch from 1S, a Soyuz-2.1a carrying the Mikhailo Lomonosov gamma-ray satellite, lifted off on 28 April 2016 at 02:01 UTC. The second, Meteor-M 2-1 in November 2017, was lost because the Fregat stage had been programmed for a Baikonur launch. Between December 2020 and October 2021, six Soyuz launches for Arianespace put 216 OneWeb satellites into orbit from here. On 10 August 2023 it launched Luna 25, which reached lunar orbit and then crashed on the Moon.
fleet/launch-site/vostochny-1s.json.best_known_for: Russia's Soyuz-2 pad in the Far East: first launch 2016, OneWeb batches, Luna 25 (2023)

fleet/launch-site/wallops-lc-0.json.name: Wallops Launch Pad 0 (MARS LP-0A and 0B)
fleet/launch-site/wallops-lc-0.json.tagline: Antares pad for Cygnus ISS cargo (2013-2023) and the Minotaur V launch of the LADEE Moon probe
fleet/launch-site/wallops-lc-0.json.description: Pad 0 is the launch complex at the southern tip of Wallops Island, Virginia, owned by the Virginia Spaceport Authority beside NASA's Wallops Flight Facility. Pad 0A was built for the Conestoga rocket, which flew once, on 23 October 1995, and self-destructed 46 seconds after liftoff. It was rebuilt for Antares, which launched from it 18 times between 21 April 2013 and 2 August 2023, mostly Cygnus cargo ships bound for the International Space Station: 17 successes and one failure, Orb-3 on 28 October 2014. The pad reopened with Cygnus OA-5 on 17 October 2016, and since August 2023 has been rebuilt for the Antares 330. Pad 0B, a few hundred metres to the south-west, has launched Minotaur rockets, most recently in June 2021. Its Minotaur V sent LADEE to the Moon on 7 September 2013, so far the only mission to another celestial body launched from Wallops. Launch azimuths of 38 to 60 degrees suit station orbits.
fleet/launch-site/wallops-lc-0.json.best_known_for: Antares pad for Cygnus ISS cargo (2013-2023) and the Minotaur V launch of the LADEE Moon probe

fleet/launch-site/wenchang-lc-101.json.name: Wenchang LC-101
fleet/launch-site/wenchang-lc-101.json.tagline: China's heavy-lift pad — Long March 5 to Tianhe, Chang'e 5/6, Tianwen-1, and the lunar return programme
fleet/launch-site/wenchang-lc-101.json.description: Built in 2014, operational from 2016, on Hainan Island at 19.6°N — the southernmost CNSA launch site. The low latitude adds about 460 m/s of free eastward velocity vs Jiuquan or Xichang, which is how Long March 5B can reach the 25-tonne LEO class needed to put the Tianhe core module into orbit in a single launch. Wenchang LC-101 is dedicated to Long March 5 / 5B; maiden flight November 3, 2016. It also flew Chang'e 5 (lunar sample return, 2020), Chang'e 6 (the farside sample return, 2024), and Tianwen-1 (Mars orbiter + Zhurong rover, 2020). Sister pad LC-201 next door handles Long March 7/8 manifests and achieved its first launch in June 2016.
fleet/launch-site/wenchang-lc-101.json.best_known_for: China's heavy-lift pad — Long March 5 to Tianhe, Chang'e 5/6, Tianwen-1, and the lunar return programme

fleet/launch-site/wenchang-lc-201.json.name: Wenchang LC-201
fleet/launch-site/wenchang-lc-201.json.tagline: Long March 7 pad on Hainan: all ten Tianzhou cargo ships to Tiangong, plus Long March 8 flights
fleet/launch-site/wenchang-lc-201.json.description: LC-201 is the second of Wenchang's three pads, on the north-east coast of Hainan at 19.6 degrees north. It was built for the Long March 7, which made its maiden flight from here on 25 June 2016 with the Yuanzheng-1A upper stage, which released small satellites in several orbits. That was the first launch from the whole site; the Long March 5 followed from LC-101 on 3 November 2016. Tianzhou 1, the first Chinese automated cargo ship, left LC-201 on 20 April 2017, and all ten Tianzhou ships flown through 11 May 2026 launched from this pad to the Tiangong station. The Long March 8 first flew from LC-201 on 22 December 2020 and carried the Queqiao-2 lunar relay satellite on 20 March 2024. Rockets reach Wenchang by sea, through its own seaport.
fleet/launch-site/wenchang-lc-201.json.best_known_for: Long March 7 pad on Hainan: all ten Tianzhou cargo ships to Tiangong, plus Long March 8 flights

fleet/launch-site/woomera.json.name: Woomera Range Complex
fleet/launch-site/woomera.json.tagline: Australia's first satellite, WRESAT (1967), and Britain's Black Arrow launch of Prospero (1971)
fleet/launch-site/woomera.json.description: Woomera is a rocket range in the South Australian desert, about 450 km north-west of Adelaide, set up in 1946-47 for the Anglo-Australian long-range weapons project. Two of its launch areas reached orbit. From Launch Area 8, a US Redstone with Sparta upper stages put WRESAT, a 45 kg satellite built by the Weapons Research Establishment, into a near-polar orbit on 29 November 1967: Australia's first satellite. From Launch Area 5B, a Black Arrow carried Prospero into orbit on 28 October 1971, the first British satellite launched on a British rocket; the programme was cancelled afterwards. The orbital launch areas are disused, but the range, now run by the RAAF, is still used for defence testing; its prohibited area covers 122,188 km2.
fleet/launch-site/woomera.json.best_known_for: Australia's first satellite, WRESAT (1967), and Britain's Black Arrow launch of Prospero (1971)

fleet/launch-site/xichang-lc-2.json.name: Xichang LC-2
fleet/launch-site/xichang-lc-2.json.tagline: Long March 3A/3B family — most Chinese GTO commercial launches and Beidou GNSS deployments
fleet/launch-site/xichang-lc-2.json.description: Xichang Satellite Launch Center's LC-2 has handled the majority of China's commercial geostationary launches, the Beidou/Compass navigation constellation, and the Chang'e lunar program through the Long March 3A, 3B, and 3C variants. Located in the mountainous Sichuan province, the site combines a low-latitude advantage for GTO performance with year-round operational availability.

fleet/launch-site/xichang-lc-3.json.name: Xichang LC-3
fleet/launch-site/xichang-lc-3.json.tagline: First CZ-3 operational successes — DFH-2 first GTO success, Apstar / Asiasat / Sinosat era
fleet/launch-site/xichang-lc-3.json.description: Xichang LC-3 hosted the first Long March 3 launch attempt on January 29, 1984 (DFH-2-01), which partially failed on third-stage re-ignition. The first successful Long March 3 flight occurred on April 8, 1984 (DFH-2-02), which placed the DFH-2 'Dong Fang Hong-2' communications satellite into geostationary transfer orbit — China's first GTO success. Both CZ-3 flights were from LC-3. Through the 1990s it supported many Apstar, Asiasat, and Sinosat commercial communications launches. Today it remains in active use alongside LC-2 for Long March 3B operations.
fleet/launch-site/xichang-lc-3.json.best_known_for: First Chinese GTO success (1984) + comsat workhorse

fleet/launcher/antares.json.name: Antares
fleet/launcher/antares.json.tagline: Workhorse for Cygnus ISS resupply through NG-19
fleet/launcher/antares.json.description: Northrop Grumman's medium-lift launcher, originally built around the Aerojet AJ26 and later RD-181 first stages with a Castor solid second stage. Carried Cygnus to the ISS from 2013 through NG-19 in 2023. The Antares 330 successor (jointly developed with Firefly Aerospace) replaces the Russian first stage with seven Miranda engines.
fleet/launcher/antares.json.best_known_for: Workhorse for Cygnus ISS resupply through NG-19

fleet/launcher/ariane-1.json.tagline: Europe's first independent orbital launcher — opened the commercial-comsat era for ESA, flew Giotto to Halley
fleet/launcher/ariane-1.json.dispatch: Ariane 1 was where Europe won its independence in space. Built after the United States made clear it would launch European satellites only on its own terms, Ariane 1 flew from Kourou in 1979 and gave Europe, for the first time, a launcher it fully controlled — answerable to no other power. It was a modest rocket by later standards, but the principle it established was not modest at all: that a continent's access to orbit should belong to that continent. Every Ariane since has flown that principle.
fleet/launcher/ariane-1.json.description: Three-stage rocket built by CNES at ESA's request after the cancelled Europa programme — hypergolic UH-25 / N2O4 first + second stages topped with the LH₂ / LOX HM7 third stage. 11 launches from Kourou between 1979-12-24 and 1986-02-22 carried 27 European telecom and science satellites including ECS-1, Marecs A/B, Spacenet, Telecom 1A/1B, and ESA's Giotto Halley flyby probe. Retired in favour of the bigger Ariane 2/3/4; the HM7 cryogenic upper-stage line lived on through Ariane 4 and into Ariane 5's ESC-A.
fleet/launcher/ariane-1.json.best_known_for: Europe's first independent orbital launcher — 11 flights 1979-1986, opened commercial comsats + Giotto to Halley

fleet/launcher/ariane-5.json.name: Ariane 5
fleet/launcher/ariane-5.json.dispatch: Ariane 5 was the heavy-lift workhorse that carried European spaceflight to its peak — after one of the most famous failures in the field. Its 1996 maiden flight self-destructed 37 seconds up when guidance software inherited from Ariane 4 overflowed at the new rocket's higher speed, a software-engineering cautionary tale now taught worldwide. It recovered to become one of the most reliable heavy launchers ever built, lofting Rosetta, Galileo (navigation constellation), BepiColombo, the ATV freighters to the ISS, and finally the James Webb Space Telescope — placed so precisely it saved years of the observatory's fuel.
fleet/launcher/ariane-5.json.description: ESA’s long-running heavy lifter, retired in 2023 after 117 launches. Carried Rosetta to comet 67P, JWST to L2, and dual-manifested geostationary commercial payloads for two decades.

fleet/launcher/ariane-6.json.name: Ariane 6
fleet/launcher/ariane-6.json.dispatch: Ariane 6 is Europe's answer to a market it no longer dominates. For two decades Ariane owned commercial launch; then reusable rockets undercut its prices and ended that reign. Ariane 6, flying from 2024, is the established power's response to the disruptive one — cheaper and more flexible than Ariane 5, built to keep Europe's independent access to space alive as the economics of launch are rewritten around it. Whether an expendable rocket can hold its ground against reusable rivals is the open question it now carries.
fleet/launcher/ariane-6.json.description: Ariane 6 is an orbital launcher built by ArianeGroup in Europe. Successor to Ariane 5. In service since 2024.

fleet/launcher/atlas-lv-3b.json.name: Atlas LV-3B
fleet/launcher/atlas-lv-3b.json.dispatch: If the Redstone was the cautious step, the Atlas was the leap. It was America's first intercontinental missile, and it reached orbital speed by being audaciously, almost alarmingly light: its skin was so thin that the rocket had to be kept pressurised like a balloon just to stand up without crumpling. Man-rating that — trusting a person to a missile that would collapse if you let the pressure drop — was the hard call that separated Mercury's suborbital half from its orbital one. Every American orbital flight of the program rode this thin steel balloon, and it is why Glenn, Carpenter, Schirra, and Cooper circled the Earth while Shepard and Grissom only touched the edge of it.
fleet/launcher/atlas-lv-3b.json.description: Atlas LV-3B was Convair's orbital launcher that lifted Mercury astronauts to orbit on four flights (Mercury-Atlas 6 through 9) between February 1962 and May 1963. The thin-skinned booster — so light it required pressurization to stand upright — proved that a ballistic missile could be man-rated. Retired after the Mercury program.

fleet/launcher/atlas-slv-3d.json.tagline: 1970s NASA outer-planet workhorse — Pioneer 10/11, Helios 1/2, Mariner 9/10, Pioneer Venus
fleet/launcher/atlas-slv-3d.json.description: Stretched Atlas SLV-3D first stage with the world's first hydrogen-fuelled upper stage (Centaur D-1A, LOX/LH₂) — the combination that enabled every American Jupiter, Saturn, Mariner, and Helios mission of the 1970s. A Star-37E or Star-48 solid-kick stage was added on top for the very-high-energy trajectories (Pioneer 11 past Jupiter to Saturn). Served 1973-1983; superseded by the Atlas G/H/I family that fed into the Atlas II of the 1990s.
fleet/launcher/atlas-slv-3d.json.best_known_for: 1970s NASA outer-planet workhorse — Centaur D-1A's first H₂ upper stage opened the gas giants

fleet/launcher/atlas-v.json.name: Atlas V
fleet/launcher/atlas-v.json.description: The reliable workhorse of United Launch Alliance, with over 100 successful launches since 2002. Carried Curiosity, Perseverance, MAVEN, MRO, New Horizons, and many of the most consequential US planetary missions of the 21st century.

fleet/launcher/delta-ii.json.description: Two- or three-stage Delta variant with an RS-27A LOX/RP-1 first stage, up to nine GEM strap-on solid boosters, and an optional Star-48B kick stage for high-energy escape trajectories. 155 launches over 29 years with a 98.7% success rate; carried Dawn, Messenger, MRO, Phoenix, Kepler, Spitzer, GRAIL, and the original GPS Block II constellation. The 'Delta II Heavy' (7920H + Star-48B) was the configuration that delivered enough C3 for direct-to-Ceres + Mercury orbital insertion. Retired after the medium-lift market shifted to Atlas V and Falcon 9.
fleet/launcher/delta-ii.json.best_known_for: NASA's medium-lift planetary-science workhorse 1989-2018 — Dawn, Messenger, MRO, Phoenix, Kepler

fleet/launcher/energia.json.name: Energia
fleet/launcher/energia.json.dispatch: Energia was the rocket that redeemed the N1 — the super-heavy launcher the Soviet Union finally got right. Where the N1 exploded on all four attempts, Energia worked, lifting the Polyus payload in 1987 and the Buran orbiter in 1988. Crucially, it was a launcher in its own right, not a shuttle stack: because Buran had no main engines, Energia did the whole job of reaching orbit and could just as well have lifted other heavy payloads with no orbiter at all. It was the most powerful rocket the Soviet Union ever flew successfully — and, like Buran, it was cancelled for want of anything left to launch.
fleet/launcher/energia.json.description: The only Soviet super-heavy launcher to fly successfully. Designed to carry the Buran orbiter or stand-alone payloads up to 100 t to LEO. Two flights: Polyus payload test (1987) and Buran orbiter (1988), both successful. Program shelved at the end of the Cold War.

fleet/launcher/falcon-9.json.name: Falcon 9 Block 5
fleet/launcher/falcon-9.json.description: SpaceX’s Block 5 booster, designed for ten flights without refurbishment. The first orbital-class rocket to land and re-fly itself, fundamentally reshaping the commercial-launch market and dropping the cost-to-orbit by roughly an order of magnitude.

fleet/launcher/falcon-heavy.json.name: Falcon Heavy
fleet/launcher/falcon-heavy.json.description: Three Falcon 9 first-stage cores strapped together, with the two side boosters returning to land while the center core lands downrange on a drone ship. Presently among the most-powerful operational heavy-lift rockets, with payload capacity rivalling Saturn V on a cost-per-kg basis far below it. (As of mid-2026, Starship has demonstrated increasingly operational capability.)

fleet/launcher/h-iia.json.name: H-IIA
fleet/launcher/h-iia.json.description: Japan's H-IIA launched 50 successful missions between 2001 and June 2025 for JAXA's flagship missions including Hayabusa, Hayabusa2, Himawari, and SLIM. Dependable liquid-propellant workhorse that became one of the most reliable launchers ever built.

fleet/launcher/h3.json.name: H3
fleet/launcher/h3.json.tagline: Replaces H-IIA / H-IIB at lower cost
fleet/launcher/h3.json.description: H3 is an orbital launcher built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries in Japan. Replaces H-IIA / H-IIB at lower cost. In service since 2024.
fleet/launcher/h3.json.best_known_for: Replaces H-IIA / H-IIB at lower cost

fleet/launcher/long-march-2f.json.name: Long March 2F
fleet/launcher/long-march-2f.json.description: Long March 2F is an orbital launcher built by CALT in China. Crew-rated for all Shenzhou flights. In service since 1999.

fleet/launcher/long-march-3b.json.name: Long March 3B
fleet/launcher/long-march-3b.json.tagline: China's GTO workhorse — Chang'e lunar landers + most Chinese comsats
fleet/launcher/long-march-3b.json.description: Three-stage liquid-hypergolic launcher (UDMH/N2O4 on the lower stages, LH2/LOX on the third) with four side-mounted strap-on boosters. Lifts ~11 t to LEO / ~5.1 t to GTO from Xichang Satellite Launch Centre. The maiden flight (1996-02-15, Intelsat 708) failed catastrophically due to a guidance-loop fault and killed villagers downrange; the redesigned vehicle has since flown well over 100 successful missions and is the standard launcher for Chang'e lunar exploration.
fleet/launcher/long-march-3b.json.best_known_for: China's GTO workhorse — Chang'e 3 / 4 lunar landers + most commercial comsats from Xichang

fleet/launcher/long-march-5.json.name: Long March 5 / 5B
fleet/launcher/long-march-5.json.tagline: Heavy-lift backbone of the Chinese space program
fleet/launcher/long-march-5.json.description: China’s first heavy-lift launcher, capable of putting 25 t to LEO. Lifts the Tiangong space station modules and Tianwen Mars probes; Long March 5B is the variant used for station modules.
fleet/launcher/long-march-5.json.best_known_for: Heavy-lift backbone of the Chinese space program

fleet/launcher/long-march-7.json.name: Long March 7
fleet/launcher/long-march-7.json.description: Long March 7 is an orbital launcher built by CALT in China. Tianzhou cargo launcher to Tiangong. In service since 2016.

fleet/launcher/lvm3.json.name: LVM3 (GSLV Mk III)
fleet/launcher/lvm3.json.description: LVM3 (GSLV Mk III) is an orbital launcher built by ISRO in India. Crew-rated launcher for Gaganyaan. In service since 2014.

fleet/launcher/mercury-redstone.json.tagline: First US human-rated launcher — variant of the Army's Redstone IRBM. Launched Freedom 7 (1961-05-05) and Liberty Bell 7 (1961-07-21)
fleet/launcher/mercury-redstone.json.dispatch: The Mercury-Redstone was a weapon taught to carry a passenger. Its ancestor was the German V-2, and its direct parent an Army ballistic missile built to deliver a warhead — now modified, softened, and made just reliable enough to trust with a human life. It could manage only a suborbital arc; it never had the power to reach orbit. But that was exactly its job: the cautious first step, the machine that let America prove a person could ride a rocket up and come back down alive before betting a life on the bigger, riskier booster that could actually reach orbit.
fleet/launcher/mercury-redstone.json.description: The Mercury-Redstone launch vehicle was a man-rated derivative of the U.S. Army's Redstone ballistic missile, modified at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center for the suborbital Mercury crewed missions. Single-stage liquid-propellant (LOX + alcohol), 25 metres tall with capsule and escape tower (~18 m booster alone), producing approximately 347 kN (~35 tonnes-force) of thrust. The first crewed flight was Mercury-Redstone 3 / Freedom 7 (1961-05-05, Alan Shepard) — the first American in space, 23 days after Gagarin. Mercury-Redstone 4 / Liberty Bell 7 followed (1961-07-21, Gus Grissom). After Liberty Bell 7's hatch malfunction, NASA moved the orbital Mercury flights to the more powerful Atlas LV-3B. Final flight 1961-07-21; total 6 Mercury-Redstone vehicles built, 2 crewed flights flown.
fleet/launcher/mercury-redstone.json.best_known_for: First US human-rated launcher — variant of the Army's Redstone IRBM. Launched Freedom 7 (1961-05-05) and Liberty Bell 7 (1961-07-21)

fleet/launcher/n1.json.name: N1
fleet/launcher/n1.json.tagline: Soviet Moon rocket; four launches all failed
fleet/launcher/n1.json.dispatch: The N1 was the Soviet Union's Saturn V — and the reason it never reached the Moon. Standing 105 metres tall, its first stage clustered thirty engines around its base, not by choice but by necessity: no single Soviet engine came close to the power of the American F-1, so Korolev's team ganged thirty smaller ones together and hoped they would fire in concert. They never did. With no test stand large enough to fire the assembled stage on the ground, every launch was the first full test of the propulsion system — and all four, between 1969 and 1972, failed. The second launch (N1-5L, 3 July 1969) fell back onto its pad in one of the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded. Its NK-33 engines, hidden away after the programme was cancelled, proved among the finest ever built and flew on American rockets a quarter-century later — a brilliant machine beaten by the one thing it was never allowed to do: be tested before it flew.
fleet/launcher/n1.json.description: The Soviet Union’s answer to Saturn V — a 105 m super-heavy rocket with thirty NK-15 engines on the first stage. All four launches between 1969 and 1972 failed; the program was cancelled when Apollo 17 ended any chance of a Soviet crewed lunar landing.
fleet/launcher/n1.json.best_known_for: Soviet Moon rocket; four launches all failed

fleet/launcher/new-glenn.json.name: New Glenn
fleet/launcher/new-glenn.json.tagline: Blue Origin's two-stage reusable heavy-lift orbital launcher
fleet/launcher/new-glenn.json.description: Two-stage heavy-lift vehicle built around seven BE-4 methane engines on the first stage (the same engine Vulcan uses) and two hydrogen-burning BE-3U engines on the second. Designed for first-stage recovery via a downrange ship landing. Lifts ~45 t to LEO and is certified for NSSL Phase 3 + Project Kuiper deployments. Maiden flight NG-1 launched from Cape Canaveral LC-36 on 2025-01-16 and successfully delivered the Blue Ring pathfinder to orbit — the first-stage landing attempt was lost but the orbital insertion was clean.
fleet/launcher/new-glenn.json.best_known_for: Blue Origin's two-stage reusable heavy-lift orbital launcher — BE-4 first stage + cryogenic second

fleet/launcher/proton-k.json.tagline: The Soviet / Russian heavy-lift workhorse 1967-2012 — Salyut, Mir, Venera, Vega, Luna sample-return
fleet/launcher/proton-k.json.description: Three-stage hypergolic (N2O4 / UDMH) heavy-lift vehicle with optional Blok-D / D-1 / D-2 high-energy upper stages. 311 launches between 1967-03-10 and 2012-03-30 — anchored every Salyut + Mir + ISS Russian-segment module, every Venera and Vega Venus probe, every Luna sample-return, and Soviet Mars-2/-3/-5/-7. The Blok-D upper stage was originally developed for the cancelled N1-L3 crewed lunar architecture; reusing it on Proton-K kept the heavy-energy Soviet planetary line viable into the 1980s. Replaced by Proton-M which still flies.
fleet/launcher/proton-k.json.best_known_for: Soviet / Russian heavy-lift workhorse 1967-2012 — Salyut, Mir, every Venera + Vega Venus probe, every Luna sample-return, and every Soviet outer-planet attempt

fleet/launcher/proton-m.json.name: Proton-M
fleet/launcher/proton-m.json.tagline: Successor to Proton-K; modernised heavy lift
fleet/launcher/proton-m.json.description: Proton-M is an orbital launcher built by Khrunichev in Russia. Successor to Proton-K; modernised heavy lift. In service since 2001.
fleet/launcher/proton-m.json.best_known_for: Successor to Proton-K; modernised heavy lift

fleet/launcher/pslv-xl.json.name: PSLV-XL
fleet/launcher/pslv-xl.json.tagline: ISRO's heavy strap-on PSLV variant — Chandrayaan-1 + Mars Orbiter
fleet/launcher/pslv-xl.json.description: Four-stage Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle in its extended (XL) configuration: six PS0M-XL strap-on solid boosters with ~50 % more propellant than the standard PSLV. Lifts ~3.8 t to LEO / ~1.8 t to SSO / ~1.4 t to GTO and has carried India's most significant interplanetary missions — Chandrayaan-1 (2008) and Mangalyaan / Mars Orbiter Mission (2013) — from Sriharikota's First Launch Pad. Still active for hyperspectral + radar Earth-observation deployments.
fleet/launcher/pslv-xl.json.best_known_for: ISRO's heavy-strap-on PSLV variant — launched Chandrayaan-1 + Mars Orbiter Mission

fleet/launcher/r-7-vostok.json.name: R-7 / Vostok rocket
fleet/launcher/r-7-vostok.json.tagline: Carried Sputnik and Gagarin to orbit
fleet/launcher/r-7-vostok.json.description: The launcher that put Sputnik in orbit in 1957 and Yuri Gagarin into space in 1961. A direct ancestor of every Soyuz rocket flown since — the longest production lineage in spaceflight, with thousands of flights across six decades.
fleet/launcher/r-7-vostok.json.best_known_for: Carried Sputnik and Gagarin to orbit

fleet/launcher/saturn-ib.json.name: Saturn IB
fleet/launcher/saturn-ib.json.tagline: Lifted Apollo 7, Skylab crews, and ASTP
fleet/launcher/saturn-ib.json.dispatch: Not every Apollo job needed the Moon rocket. The Saturn IB was the pragmatic option — a crew-rated lifter for the work that stayed in Earth orbit: Apollo 7's shakedown of the redesigned spacecraft, the ferry flights to Skylab, and the handshake-in-orbit of Apollo-Soyuz. Its first stage was famously a bundle of tanks borrowed from the earlier Redstone and Jupiter missiles, clustered together — proven parts doing a new job rather than a clean-sheet design. It's the least glamorous rocket in the program, and a quiet lesson in not overbuilding: match the machine to the mission.
fleet/launcher/saturn-ib.json.description: Saturn IB is an orbital launcher built by Chrysler / Douglas / IBM in USA. Lifted Apollo 7, Skylab crews, and ASTP.
fleet/launcher/saturn-ib.json.best_known_for: Lifted Apollo 7, Skylab crews, and ASTP

fleet/launcher/saturn-v.json.name: Saturn V
fleet/launcher/saturn-v.json.dispatch: The Saturn V existed to solve one brutal piece of arithmetic: putting a crew on the Moon means throwing roughly 45 tonnes onto a path out of Earth's gravity, and in 1961 nothing on Earth could throw a fraction of that. So von Braun's Marshall team built the largest machine that had ever flown — five F-1 engines at its base, each the most powerful single-chamber rocket engine ever fired at the time, together burning some thirteen tonnes of propellant every second. Everything about it was sized by the destination, not by what looked reasonable. That it flew thirteen times and never once failed to reach space is the part that still doesn't quite seem possible.
fleet/launcher/saturn-v.json.description: The 110.6 m three-stage rocket that put 24 humans on a translunar trajectory and 12 of them on the lunar surface. Thirteen launches between 1967 and 1973, zero losses on ascent. The most powerful rocket to reach orbit for over five decades until Starship's Super Heavy surpassed it in 2024.

fleet/launcher/sls-block-1.json.name: SLS Block 1
fleet/launcher/sls-block-1.json.tagline: Heavy lift for Artemis lunar program
fleet/launcher/sls-block-1.json.description: NASA’s super-heavy successor to the Space Shuttle stack, sharing its RS-25 engines and SRB heritage. Carried Orion on Artemis I in 2022 and the Artemis II crew around the Moon in 2026; planned to launch crewed missions through Artemis V. The more powerful Block 1B upgrade was cancelled in 2026.
fleet/launcher/sls-block-1.json.best_known_for: Heavy lift for Artemis lunar program

fleet/launcher/soyuz-2.json.name: Soyuz-2
fleet/launcher/soyuz-2.json.tagline: Modern Soyuz workhorse — carries Soyuz MS crew + Progress MS cargo to the ISS
fleet/launcher/soyuz-2.json.description: RKTs Progress's modernised Soyuz family, with digital flight controls replacing the analogue systems of Soyuz-FG / Soyuz-U. Variants 2.1a (RD-107A/RD-108A first stage + RD-0124 third stage), 2.1b (uprated third stage), and 2.1v (no boosters, single RD-110 stage). Carries every modern Russian crewed and cargo flight to the ISS plus Glonass, Resurs-P, and Lotos-S payloads.
fleet/launcher/soyuz-2.json.best_known_for: Modern Soyuz workhorse for ISS crew + cargo

fleet/launcher/soyuz-fg.json.name: Soyuz-FG
fleet/launcher/soyuz-fg.json.description: Soyuz-FG is an orbital launcher built by Progress Rocket Space Centre in Russia. Crewed Soyuz launches 2001-2019.

fleet/launcher/soyuz-u.json.name: Soyuz-U
fleet/launcher/soyuz-u.json.description: Soyuz-U is an orbital launcher built by Progress Rocket Space Centre in USSR. Most-launched orbital rocket in history — 786 missions from 1973 to 2017.

fleet/launcher/soyuz.json.tagline: R-7-derived launcher for the first-generation Soyuz spacecraft — flew Soyuz 1 (1967) and Soyuz 11 (1971)
fleet/launcher/soyuz.json.dispatch: The launcher that opened the Soyuz era also carried its two tragedies. The 11A511 was the next step in Korolev's R-7 lineage — the same rocket family that lofted Sputnik and Gagarin, now uprated to carry the heavier, more capable Soyuz spacecraft that would become the workhorse of Soviet and Russian human spaceflight for the next half-century. Its first crewed flight, Soyuz 1 in 1967, ended when the descent module's parachutes fouled and Vladimir Komarov was lost. Four years later, Soyuz 11 returned its crew from the world's first space station — but a valve had opened at separation, and all three men died of depressurisation before touchdown. The rocket performed; the spacecraft's early margins did not. The R-7 lineage it belonged to still flies crews today.
fleet/launcher/soyuz.json.description: The Soyuz 11A511 was the R-7 derivative built to loft the first-generation Soyuz 7K-OK spacecraft, adding a more capable upper stage to the Vostok/Voskhod launcher lineage. Three-stage liquid-propellant (LOX + kerosene), ~50 metres tall, ~308 tonnes lift-off mass. It carried the crewed Soyuz programme's earliest flights, including its two fatal missions — Soyuz 1 (1967), lost when its recovery parachutes fouled, and Soyuz 11 (1971), whose crew died of depressurisation during descent. The 11A511 was succeeded by the Soyuz-U in 1973; the same R-7 lineage still flies crews as the Soyuz-2 today.
fleet/launcher/soyuz.json.best_known_for: R-7-derived launcher for the first-generation Soyuz spacecraft — flew Soyuz 1 (1967) and Soyuz 11 (1971)

fleet/launcher/space-shuttle-stack.json.name: Space Shuttle stack
fleet/launcher/space-shuttle-stack.json.description: The reusable orbiter, external tank, and twin solid rocket boosters that flew 135 missions between 1981 and 2011. Built the ISS, deployed and serviced Hubble, and demonstrated the engineering trade-offs of a partially-reusable crewed launcher.

fleet/launcher/starship.json.name: Starship
fleet/launcher/starship.json.description: Two-stage vehicle built around the methane-burning Raptor engine — Super Heavy first stage (33 Raptors) + Starship second stage (6 Raptors). Designed for full and rapid reuse via tower-catch recovery of both stages, targeting Mars transit timelines + Artemis Human Landing System. First integrated flight test (IFT-1) cleared the pad on 2023-04-20 but lost vehicle control before stage separation; demonstrated controlled recovery of both stages beginning with IFT-4 in June 2024.
fleet/launcher/starship.json.best_known_for: Fully reusable super-heavy launch vehicle in development for Artemis HLS + Mars

fleet/launcher/titan-ii-glv.json.name: Titan II GLV
fleet/launcher/titan-ii-glv.json.dispatch: The Titan II that launched Gemini was, like Mercury's rockets, a converted weapon — America's largest intercontinental missile, man-rated to carry a crew. Its defining trait was its fuel: where cryogenic propellants have to be loaded just before launch and can force a scrub, the Titan burned storable liquids that let it sit ready and lift off close to on time. That reliability of timing mattered more than it sounds, because Gemini's whole job was rendezvous, and catching another spacecraft in orbit depends on launching at an exact moment. The workhorse of the program, it flew all ten crewed Geminis without losing a crew.
fleet/launcher/titan-ii-glv.json.description: Titan II GLV is an orbital launcher built by Martin Marietta in USA. Workhorse for Project Gemini. Flew 12 times, 1964–1966.

fleet/launcher/voskhod-11a57.json.tagline: Vostok-K successor — more thrust for the heavier Voskhod capsule. Launched Voskhod 1 (1964) + Voskhod 2 (1965 Leonov EVA)
fleet/launcher/voskhod-11a57.json.dispatch: The Voskhod 11A57 was the R-7 turned up a notch. The modified Vostok capsule was heavier than the original, so it needed more push than the Vostok-K could give — which the R-7 family, endlessly adaptable, duly provided with an uprated upper stage. It's a small chapter in a very long story: the same basic rocket that launched Sputnik and Gagarin, stretched again to loft the two Voskhod flights, and still being stretched, decades later, to fly Soyuz crews. Few designs have been asked to do so many different jobs for so long.
fleet/launcher/voskhod-11a57.json.description: Voskhod (GRAU index 11A57) was the next iteration of the R-7 family after Vostok-K, with uprated Blok-I third-stage engines for the heavier Voskhod capsule. Three-stage LOX + kerosene, 44 metres tall, 298 tonnes lift-off mass. Launched both crewed Voskhod flights (Voskhod 1 first 3-person crew in 1964; Voskhod 2 with Leonov's first EVA in 1965). After the Voskhod programme ended the 11A57 continued in service for ~300 uncrewed military / civilian satellite launches through 1976, when it was superseded by the Soyuz 11A511 line.
fleet/launcher/voskhod-11a57.json.best_known_for: Vostok-K successor — more thrust for the heavier Voskhod capsule. Launched Voskhod 1 (1964) + Voskhod 2 (1965 Leonov EVA)

fleet/launcher/vostok-k.json.tagline: Soviet R-7-derived launcher that put Gagarin in space — Vostok 1 (1961-04-12) and 5 more Vostok flights through 1963
fleet/launcher/vostok-k.json.dispatch: The rocket that launched Gagarin was a weapon that changed careers. The Vostok-K was a human-rated version of Korolev's R-7 — the world's first intercontinental ballistic missile, built to throw a warhead across the planet, now asked to lift a person into orbit. It was the same lineage that had lofted Sputnik, and it is, astonishingly, the same lineage still flying: the Soyuz rocket that carries crews to the Space Station today is a direct descendant, which makes the R-7 family by far the most-launched rocket in history. Few machines built for war have had so long or so peaceful a second life.
fleet/launcher/vostok-k.json.description: Vostok-K (GRAU index 8K72K) was the human-rated derivative of Korolev's R-7 ICBM, with a Blok-E upper stage and crew-rated parameters. Three-stage liquid-propellant (LOX + kerosene), 38 metres tall, 287 tonnes lift-off mass. Launched all six crewed Vostok flights (1-6, 1961-1963) plus a handful of uncrewed precursors. Reliability evolved from early R-7 teething problems (3 of 6 first-stage failures before Gagarin) to perfect record across the crewed series. The Vostok-K design lineage continues today as the Soyuz-2 launcher (the only crew-capable Russian launch vehicle of 2026).
fleet/launcher/vostok-k.json.best_known_for: Soviet R-7-derived launcher that put Gagarin in space — Vostok 1 (1961-04-12) and 5 more Vostok flights through 1963

fleet/launcher/vulcan.json.name: Vulcan Centaur
fleet/launcher/vulcan.json.tagline: Atlas V + Delta IV successor; certifies for NSSL Phase 3 + planned for Dream Chaser
fleet/launcher/vulcan.json.description: United Launch Alliance's two-stage successor to Atlas V and Delta IV. Powered by twin BE-4 methalox engines on the first stage and Centaur V (RL10) above. First flight 2024-01-08 carried Astrobotic Peregrine. Slated to certify for National Security Space Launch Phase 3 contracts and planned as the launch vehicle for Sierra Space's Dream Chaser cargo spaceplane.

fleet/observatory/chandra.json.name: Chandra X-ray Observatory
fleet/observatory/chandra.json.description: NASA’s flagship X-ray observatory, in service since 1999. Resolution roughly 25× better than any previous X-ray telescope, allowing direct imaging of black-hole accretion disks, supernova remnants, and the hot gas threading galaxy clusters.

fleet/observatory/compton-gro.json.name: Compton Gamma Ray Observatory
fleet/observatory/compton-gro.json.tagline: One of NASA's four Great Observatories
fleet/observatory/compton-gro.json.description: One of NASA’s four "Great Observatories" alongside Hubble, Chandra, and Spitzer. In orbit 1991–2000, mapped the gamma-ray sky and discovered that gamma-ray bursts come from cosmological distances rather than nearby sources.
fleet/observatory/compton-gro.json.best_known_for: One of NASA's four Great Observatories

fleet/observatory/euclid.json.name: Euclid
fleet/observatory/euclid.json.tagline: Dark-energy survey across one third of the sky
fleet/observatory/euclid.json.description: Euclid surveys the sky in visible and near-infrared light to map the large-scale structure of the Universe and constrain dark energy. In service since 2023.
fleet/observatory/euclid.json.best_known_for: Dark-energy survey across one third of the sky

fleet/observatory/gaia.json.name: Gaia
fleet/observatory/gaia.json.description: ESA’s star-charting satellite, mapping the position, brightness, and motion of nearly two billion stars in the Milky Way at unprecedented precision. Operated 2013–2025; the resulting catalogue will underpin galactic astronomy for decades.

fleet/observatory/hitomi.json.name: Hitomi (ASTRO-H)
fleet/observatory/hitomi.json.tagline: Spun apart in orbit; loss drove XRISM development
fleet/observatory/hitomi.json.description: JAXA’s X-ray observatory, lost 37 days after launch in February 2016. A reaction-wheel saturation triggered a sequence of attitude-control errors that spun the spacecraft so fast it broke apart. Lessons drove the development of XRISM (launched 2023).
fleet/observatory/hitomi.json.best_known_for: Spun apart in orbit; loss drove XRISM development

fleet/observatory/hubble.json.name: Hubble Space Telescope
