fleet/observatory/hubble.json.tagline: Iconic visible/UV space telescope; 5 servicing missions
fleet/observatory/hubble.json.description: NASA’s and ESA’s shared visible/UV space telescope, in low Earth orbit since 1990 and serviced five times by Space Shuttle missions through 2009. Still in operation 35+ years later, with major instruments installed by spacewalking astronauts and a primary mirror flaw corrected in 1993 by COSTAR (later replaced by instruments with built-in corrective optics).
fleet/observatory/hubble.json.best_known_for: Iconic visible/UV space telescope; 5 servicing missions

fleet/observatory/jwst.json.name: James Webb Space Telescope
fleet/observatory/jwst.json.tagline: Largest infrared space telescope; L2 orbit
fleet/observatory/jwst.json.description: The largest infrared space telescope ever built. Stationed at Sun-Earth L2 since January 2022, with a 6.5 m segmented gold-coated beryllium primary mirror behind a tennis-court-sized sunshield. Sees back to the first galaxies after the Big Bang.
fleet/observatory/jwst.json.best_known_for: Largest infrared space telescope; L2 orbit

fleet/observatory/kepler.json.name: Kepler
fleet/observatory/kepler.json.description: NASA’s exoplanet hunter (2009–2018). Stared at a single patch of sky and detected exoplanets via transit photometry — the brief dip in starlight when a planet passes in front of its star. Discovered more than 2,700 confirmed exoplanets and demonstrated that Earth-sized worlds are common.

fleet/observatory/spektr-rg.json.name: Spektr-RG
fleet/observatory/spektr-rg.json.description: Spektr-RG is a space observatory built by NPO Lavochkin in Russia. Russian-German X-ray sky-mapping observatory. In service since 2019; its German eROSITA telescope entered safe mode in February 2022, while the Russian ART-XC instrument keeps observing.

fleet/observatory/spitzer.json.name: Spitzer Space Telescope
fleet/observatory/spitzer.json.tagline: Infrared Great Observatory; 16 years of data
fleet/observatory/spitzer.json.description: NASA’s infrared Great Observatory, in service 2003–2020. Designed for a five-year cryogenic mission but operated for sixteen, including a "warm mission" phase after its liquid-helium coolant was exhausted in 2009.
fleet/observatory/spitzer.json.best_known_for: Infrared Great Observatory; 16 years of data

fleet/observatory/tess.json.name: TESS
fleet/observatory/tess.json.description: The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, in orbit since 2018. Surveys nearly the entire sky in 26 sectors per year, looking for short-period exoplanets around the brightest, closest stars to Earth — the targets that will be most amenable to follow-up atmospheric characterisation by JWST.

fleet/observatory/xmm-newton.json.name: XMM-Newton
fleet/observatory/xmm-newton.json.description: XMM-Newton is a space observatory built by Airbus Defence and Space in Europe. ESA's flagship X-ray observatory. In service since 1999.

fleet/orbiter/akatsuki.json.name: Akatsuki
fleet/orbiter/akatsuki.json.tagline: Japan's first Venus orbiter; recovered from a 2010 orbit-insertion failure to study cloud-top dynamics
fleet/orbiter/akatsuki.json.description: JAXA's Venus Climate Orbiter, Japan's first spacecraft to successfully orbit Venus. Originally failed orbit insertion in 2010 but was recovered on a backup attempt five years later (2015) using less efficient thrusters. Studied cloud-top winds, lightning, and atmospheric dynamics of Venus's super-rotating atmosphere. Mission ended September 2025 after contact was lost.
fleet/orbiter/akatsuki.json.best_known_for: Japan's first Venus orbiter; studied cloud-top winds and atmospheric dynamics. Recovered after a 2010 orbit-insertion failure

fleet/orbiter/bepicolombo.json.tagline: Twin-orbiter joint ESA + JAXA Mercury mission — splits into MPO + Mio at Mercury arrival in 2026
fleet/orbiter/bepicolombo.json.description: Joint ESA + JAXA mission. Launched 2018-10-20 on an Ariane 5 ECA. Mercury Transfer Module carries the stack on a 7-year flyby cruise (1 Earth + 2 Venus + 6 Mercury gravity assists) before Mercury orbit insertion on 2026-11-21. At arrival the two science orbiters separate: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) flies a 480 × 1500 km polar orbit with 11 instruments for surface composition, topography, gravity, and exosphere; JAXA's Mio (Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter) flies a 590 × 11 640 km polar orbit with 5 instruments for the magnetosphere and plasma. Together they are the first European + Japanese spacecraft ever in Mercury orbit.
fleet/orbiter/bepicolombo.json.best_known_for: Joint ESA + JAXA twin-orbiter Mercury mission — MPO + Mio at Mercury, 2026 arrival

fleet/orbiter/cassini.json.name: Cassini-Huygens
fleet/orbiter/cassini.json.tagline: Saturn orbiter; Huygens landed on Titan
fleet/orbiter/cassini.json.description: The Saturn orbiter (2004–2017) that carried ESA’s Huygens lander to Titan — still the only landing on a moon of an outer planet. Discovered the active geyser plumes of Enceladus and the global ocean beneath its icy crust. Ended in a planned plunge into Saturn’s atmosphere.
fleet/orbiter/cassini.json.best_known_for: Saturn orbiter; Huygens landed on Titan

fleet/orbiter/chandrayaan1.json.tagline: India's first Moon mission. Discovered widespread surface water on the Moon (M3 + MIP, 2009). Lost contact 2009-08-29 after only 312 days
fleet/orbiter/chandrayaan1.json.description: India's first mission beyond Earth orbit and its first to the Moon. Launched 2008-10-22 from Satish Dhawan Space Centre on a PSLV-XL, Chandrayaan-1 entered a 100-km polar lunar orbit on 2008-11-12. Carried 11 instruments from 6 countries (India, USA, UK, Germany, Sweden, Bulgaria) — most consequentially NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3) which detected the absorption-band signature of OH/H₂O across vast swathes of the lunar surface, particularly at high latitudes (Pieters et al., 2009, Science 326). Its 35-kg Moon Impact Probe (MIP) was released 2008-11-14 and impacted near the rim of Shackleton Crater at the lunar south pole (Jawahar Sthal, ~89.5°S), becoming the first Indian artefact on the Moon and recording lunar atmospheric water vapour during descent. Spacecraft contact was lost 2009-08-29 after ~10 months / 3400 orbits — half of its planned 2-year mission, but the science return was already game-changing. Remains in lunar orbit, re-acquired by NASA Goldstone radar in 2017.
fleet/orbiter/chandrayaan1.json.best_known_for: India's first Moon mission. Discovered widespread surface water on the Moon (M3 + MIP, 2009). Lost contact 2009-08-29 after only 312 days

fleet/orbiter/change-2.json.name: Chang'e 2
fleet/orbiter/change-2.json.tagline: Second Chinese lunar orbiter; first to visit asteroid 4179 Toutatis
fleet/orbiter/change-2.json.description: China's second lunar orbiter, launched 2010-10-01. Chang'e 2 orbited the Moon from 2010 to 2011, then departed lunar orbit in June 2011 for an extended deep-space mission. It proceeded to the Sun-Earth L2 point (arriving August 2011), then departed L2 in April 2012 for a historic flyby of asteroid 4179 Toutatis, executing a close approach on 2012-12-13 at ~770 m distance — the first spacecraft to visit the asteroid. After the Toutatis encounter, Chang'e 2 continued into deep space on a heliocentric trajectory, becoming a drifting interplanetary object.
fleet/orbiter/change-2.json.best_known_for: Second Chinese lunar orbiter; first spacecraft flyby of asteroid 4179 Toutatis (Dec 13, 2012, ~770 m closest approach)

fleet/orbiter/change1.json.tagline: China's first lunar mission. 200-m global topo map; deliberate Mare Fecunditatis impact 2009-03-01 — first Chinese object on the Moon
fleet/orbiter/change1.json.description: The first phase of China's Lunar Exploration Program (CLEP), and CNSA's first mission beyond Earth. Launched 2007-10-24 from Xichang Satellite Launch Center on a Long March 3A, Chang'e 1 (named after the Moon goddess of Chinese folklore) entered a 200-km circular polar lunar orbit on 2007-11-07. Carried 8 instruments including a CCD stereo camera, laser altimeter, imaging spectrometer, gamma-ray and X-ray spectrometers, microwave radiometer, solar wind detector, and high-energy particle detector. Produced China's first full lunar global topographic map at 120-200 m resolution and elemental abundance maps of Th, K, U, O, Si, Mg, Al, Ca, Ti, Fe. Mission deliberately ended 2009-03-01 with a controlled impact at 1.50° S, 52.36° E in Mare Fecunditatis — China's first object on the lunar surface, paving the way for Chang'e 3 (2013 surface landing) and Chang'e 5 (2020 sample return). Operated 16 months — 4 months past nominal.
fleet/orbiter/change1.json.best_known_for: China's first lunar mission. 200-m global topo map; deliberate Mare Fecunditatis impact 2009-03-01 — first Chinese object on the Moon

fleet/orbiter/clementine.json.tagline: Joint BMDO + NASA lunar orbiter — first global multispectral map and first bistatic-radar evidence for polar water ice
fleet/orbiter/clementine.json.description: Officially the Deep Space Program Science Experiment (DSPSE). Conceived by the Ballistic Missile Defense Organization to qualify lightweight sensors in deep-space conditions, with NASA collaborating on lunar + asteroid science. Launched 1994-01-25 on a Titan IIG, entered lunar polar orbit 1994-02-19 for 71 days of mapping. Imaged every square kilometre of the Moon at 100-300 m resolution across 11 wavelengths — the first complete global lunar map. The bistatic radar experiment using Clementine's transmitter and DSN ground antennas found enhanced echoes at south-polar Shackleton crater consistent with water ice, predating LCROSS by 15 years. A failed thruster firing aborted the planned Geographos asteroid flyby and ended the mission.
fleet/orbiter/clementine.json.best_known_for: First complete global lunar multispectral map and first hint of polar water ice — 1994

fleet/orbiter/dart.json.name: DART
fleet/orbiter/dart.json.description: The first planetary defense impactor. Deliberately collided with the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos in September 2022, shortening its orbital period around its parent Didymos by 33 minutes — proving that kinetic deflection is a viable planet-protection technique.

fleet/orbiter/dawn.json.tagline: Only spacecraft to orbit two extraterrestrial worlds — Vesta then Ceres via ion propulsion
fleet/orbiter/dawn.json.description: NASA Discovery-class mission powered by three NSTAR xenon ion thrusters that produced the 11 km/s of total delta-v needed to enter orbit around Vesta, escape, cruise three years, and enter orbit around Ceres. Mapped both bodies in unprecedented detail — Vesta's southern Rheasilvia basin, Ceres' bright Cerealia Facula spots, ammoniated phyllosilicates, and cryovolcanism at Ahuna Mons. Mission ended 2018 when reaction-control hydrazine was exhausted; the spacecraft remains in a stable orbit around Ceres.
fleet/orbiter/dawn.json.best_known_for: Only spacecraft to orbit two extraterrestrial worlds — Vesta (2011-2012), Ceres (2015-2018)

fleet/orbiter/europa-clipper.json.name: Europa Clipper
fleet/orbiter/europa-clipper.json.tagline: First mission dedicated to characterising Europa's habitability
fleet/orbiter/europa-clipper.json.description: NASA's mission to study the habitability of Jupiter's icy moon Europa — believed to harbour a global liquid-water ocean beneath a 15-25 km ice shell, possibly the most accessible potentially-habitable environment in the solar system. Largest planetary mission spacecraft ever launched (~6000 kg). ~102-m² solar arrays generate enough power at Jupiter's distance to drive nine instruments through 49 close Europa flybys, designed to map the entire moon while limiting the spacecraft's dose in Jupiter's brutal radiation belts.
fleet/orbiter/europa-clipper.json.best_known_for: First mission dedicated to Europa habitability

fleet/orbiter/exomars-tgo.json.name: ExoMars TGO
fleet/orbiter/exomars-tgo.json.description: ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter, in orbit at Mars since 2016. Sniffs the atmosphere for methane and water vapor that could hint at biology or geology, and relays data for Mars surface missions via its UHF relay.
fleet/orbiter/exomars-tgo.json.best_known_for: Trace gas analysis at Mars; relay for ESA and NASA surface missions

fleet/orbiter/galileo.json.name: Galileo
fleet/orbiter/galileo.json.tagline: First Jupiter orbiter; 8 years of measurements
fleet/orbiter/galileo.json.description: The first Jupiter orbiter (1995–2003), and the only mission to drop a probe into Jupiter’s atmosphere. Also discovered evidence for a subsurface ocean on Europa — making it one of the most consequential planetary missions ever flown.
fleet/orbiter/galileo.json.best_known_for: First Jupiter orbiter; 8 years of measurements

fleet/orbiter/giotto.json.tagline: First close-up images of a cometary nucleus — flew 596 km past Halley's Comet at 68 km/s in 1986
fleet/orbiter/giotto.json.description: ESA's first deep-space probe. Spin-stabilised drum-shaped bus protected by a Whipple-shield dust bumper, built around the Halley Multicolour Camera plus 9 other instruments contributed by 11 European countries, NASA, and Japan. Closest approach to comet 1P/Halley on 1986-03-14 at 596 km — the bumper survived, though a 100 mg dust strike 14 seconds before closest approach offset the spin axis and broke camera contact. Reactivated in 1990 for a 200 km flyby of comet Grigg-Skjellerup in 1992, the first time a spacecraft returned to a different cometary target.
fleet/orbiter/giotto.json.best_known_for: First close-up images of a cometary nucleus — 596 km past Halley's Comet, 1986-03-14

fleet/orbiter/hayabusa-2.json.name: Hayabusa2
fleet/orbiter/hayabusa-2.json.description: Hayabusa2 is a deep-space orbiter built by NEC in Japan. Successfully returned ~5.4 grams of samples from asteroid 162173 Ryugu on December 6, 2020. After sample delivery, the spacecraft continued on an extended SHARP (Small Hazardous Asteroid Reconnaissance Probe) mission to other asteroids. It flew past asteroid Torifune on July 5, 2026, and is planned to rendezvous with asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031.
fleet/orbiter/hayabusa-2.json.best_known_for: First asteroid sample return to Earth from Ryugu (Dec 2020); continuing extended mission to Torifune and 1998 KY26

fleet/orbiter/hayabusa.json.name: Hayabusa
fleet/orbiter/hayabusa.json.tagline: First asteroid sample ever returned to Earth
fleet/orbiter/hayabusa.json.description: JAXA's pioneering asteroid sample-return mission. Launched 2003-05-09 to Itokawa carrying four μ10 microwave-discharge ion thrusters. Survived a hydrazine leak, three of four reaction wheels failing, an ion engine failure, and seven weeks of lost communications before engineers nursed it back to Earth with one working engine assembled from the surviving halves of two damaged ones. Sample capsule recovered at Woomera AUS 2010-06-13 with 1500 μg of Itokawa material — the first asteroid sample ever returned to Earth.

fleet/orbiter/hope.json.name: Hope (EMM)
fleet/orbiter/hope.json.description: The UAE's Hope orbiter — Emirates Mars Mission, known in Arabic as Al-Amal. Reached Mars in 2021 and provided the first holistic global view of the Martian atmosphere through a complete Martian year. Built in partnership with the University of Colorado LASP.
fleet/orbiter/hope.json.best_known_for: First Arab interplanetary mission; first holistic global view of the Martian atmosphere through a Mars year

fleet/orbiter/juice.json.tagline: ESA flagship to Jupiter — first orbiter ever to settle around a Galilean moon (Ganymede, 2034)
fleet/orbiter/juice.json.description: Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer. Launched 2023-04-14 on an Ariane 5 ECA+ for an 8.5-year cruise via Earth-Venus-Earth-Earth gravity assists to Jupiter arrival in July 2031. Once in the Jovian system, JUICE flies ~35 times past Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto before entering Ganymede orbit in 2034 — the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than Earth's. Ten-instrument payload includes ice-penetrating radar (RIME), spectrometers, magnetometer, and a laser altimeter, optimised to characterise the three icy moons as potentially habitable subsurface-ocean worlds.
fleet/orbiter/juice.json.best_known_for: ESA Jupiter flagship — first orbiter ever around a Galilean moon (Ganymede), arrival 2031-2034

fleet/orbiter/juno.json.name: Juno
fleet/orbiter/juno.json.description: NASA’s polar Jupiter orbiter, in orbit since 2016. Solar-powered (a first at Jupiter’s distance), spinning to maintain stability, and orbiting close enough to Jupiter’s cloud-tops to risk severe radiation damage with each pass.

fleet/orbiter/lro.json.tagline: NASA's active lunar recon orbiter. LROC's 0.5 m/pixel imagery is the source of every Apollo + Luna + Chang'e landing-site photo here
fleet/orbiter/lro.json.description: NASA's active flagship lunar orbiter — operating continuously since 2009-06-23. Launched 2009-06-18 with LCROSS on an Atlas V from Cape Canaveral, LRO's payload of 7 instruments has remapped every aspect of the Moon at unprecedented resolution. The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) NAC (Narrow-Angle Camera, 0.5 m/pixel at 50 km altitude) has imaged every Apollo, Luna, Surveyor, Chang'e, Vikram, Beresheet and Hakuto landing site — every "tier-2 LROC" image in this app's /moon hotspots came from LROC NAC. LOLA (Laser Altimeter) gave the most detailed topography of any solar-system body. Diviner mapped surface temperature 10 K precision; LAMP detected widespread surface H₂O down to lunar dawn; LEND mapped neutron flux at <10 km resolution. As of 2026 still operational on extended mission, with no planned end-of-life — propellant supports operations through ~2030+.
fleet/orbiter/lro.json.best_known_for: NASA's active lunar recon orbiter. LROC's 0.5 m/pixel imagery is the source of every Apollo + Luna + Chang'e landing-site photo here

fleet/orbiter/lucy.json.name: Lucy
fleet/orbiter/lucy.json.tagline: First mission to the Jupiter Trojans
fleet/orbiter/lucy.json.description: NASA's 12-year multi-flyby mission to 6 Jupiter Trojan asteroid systems and 2 main-belt asteroids (11 total encounters including satellites). Three Earth gravity assists shape a single trajectory visiting both the L4 and L5 Trojan clouds. Carries 1003 kg of hydrazine — more propellant than dry mass. Named for the 1974 Australopithecus afarensis fossil, in turn named for the Beatles song — the implication being that Trojans preserve early-solar-system material the way the fossil preserves early-human history.
fleet/orbiter/lucy.json.best_known_for: First mission to the Jupiter Trojans

fleet/orbiter/luna10.json.tagline: First spacecraft to orbit the Moon (or any body other than Earth) — entered lunar orbit 1966-04-03, three years before Apollo 8
fleet/orbiter/luna10.json.description: First spacecraft to orbit the Moon — and the first artificial satellite of any body other than Earth. Launched 1966-03-31 from Baikonur on a Molniya rocket, Luna 10 entered lunar orbit 1966-04-03 with a 349 × 1015 km orbit at 71.9° inclination, three years before Apollo 8 reached the Moon with humans aboard. Measured the lunar magnetic field (~3 nT, essentially zero), micrometeoroid flux, gamma-ray emission, ionising radiation, and solar plasma — the gamma-ray data was the first compositional remote sensing of the Moon, suggesting basalt-like mare composition. Famously played the "Internationale" anthem during the 23rd Congress of the Soviet Communist Party (1966-04-04). Operated 56 days / 460 orbits before its NiCd batteries depleted. Remains in lunar orbit.
fleet/orbiter/luna10.json.best_known_for: First spacecraft to orbit the Moon (or any body other than Earth) — entered lunar orbit 1966-04-03, three years before Apollo 8

fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-1.json.tagline: First US lunar orbiter (1966-08-14); mapped Apollo landing sites and took the first photo of Earth from lunar orbit (1966).
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-1.json.description: The first US spacecraft to orbit the Moon, four months after Luna 10. Launched 1966-08-10 from Cape Canaveral on an Atlas-Agena D, Lunar Orbiter 1 entered an elliptical lunar orbit on 1966-08-14. Its primary mission was to photograph candidate Apollo landing sites at sub-metre resolution — a 70 mm + 610 mm dual-lens camera system that developed film in-orbit (Bimat process) and scanned it for radio transmission to Earth. Captured the first photograph of Earth from lunar orbit (1966-08-23 — over two years before Apollo 8's more famous Earthrise) as a wide-angle shot taken during the 16th orbit. Returned 207 high-resolution + 207 medium-resolution frames mapping 4.1 million km² of the lunar surface. Deliberately crashed into the lunar far side on 1966-10-29 to clear the radio band for Lunar Orbiter 2.
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-1.json.best_known_for: First US lunar orbiter (1966-08-14). Mapped potential Apollo landing sites; took the first photograph of Earth from lunar orbit — over two years before the famous Apollo 8 Earthrise

fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-2.json.tagline: Second US lunar orbiter (1966-11-10). Took the 'Picture of the Century' — oblique view of Copernicus crater at ~45 km altitude
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-2.json.description: Second of the five Lunar Orbiter spacecraft. Launched 1966-11-06 from Cape Canaveral, entered lunar orbit 1966-11-10. Mapped 13 sites in the equatorial Apollo zone. On 1966-11-24, Frame 162 captured an oblique view of the 93-km Copernicus crater from 45.8 km altitude looking north — a never-before-seen Earth-style mountain landscape on another world. Newspapers called it the 'Picture of the Century'. The photo's release became a turning point in public engagement with lunar exploration. Returned 422 frames total across 33 days of imaging. Deliberately impacted 1967-10-11 at 4° S, 98° E (lunar far side) to prevent radio-frequency interference with Lunar Orbiter 5.
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-2.json.best_known_for: Second US lunar orbiter (1966-11-10). Took the 'Picture of the Century' — oblique view of Copernicus crater at ~45 km altitude

fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-3.json.tagline: Third US lunar orbiter (1967-02-08). Photographed Surveyor 1 sitting on the lunar surface — first photo of a spacecraft on another world
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-3.json.description: Third of the five Lunar Orbiter spacecraft. Launched 1967-02-04 from Cape Canaveral, entered lunar orbit 1967-02-08. Continued the Apollo site-mapping campaign with 477 frames across 30 days, including a celebrated 1967-02-22 photograph that resolved the 3-metre Surveyor 1 lander sitting on the Oceanus Procellarum surface — the first photograph of one spacecraft taken by another at another world. Mid-mission failure of the camera's film-transport system curtailed the imaging campaign on 1967-03-04. Continued to operate as an Apollo-tracking beacon for navigation tests. Deliberately impacted 1967-10-09 at 14.6° N, 91.7° W.
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-3.json.best_known_for: Third US lunar orbiter (1967-02-08). Photographed Surveyor 1 sitting on the lunar surface — first photo of a spacecraft on another world

fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-4.json.tagline: Fourth US lunar orbiter (1967-05-08). First polar lunar orbit; mapped 99 % of the near side at 60 m/pixel + far-side regions
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-4.json.description: Fourth of the five Lunar Orbiter spacecraft, and the first to fly a high-inclination polar lunar orbit. Launched 1967-05-04 from Cape Canaveral, entered a 6111 × 2706 km polar orbit on 1967-05-08. Mission redirected from Apollo site-selection (the first three Orbiters had already done that job) to broad scientific mapping. Returned 419 frames covering 99 % of the lunar near side at 60 m/pixel resolution plus the first detailed imaging of significant far-side regions. The frames remain the highest-resolution coverage of the lunar near side at this scale until the modern LRO era. Impact in October 1967 at 22-30° W on the far side after the radio failed.
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-4.json.best_known_for: Fourth US lunar orbiter (1967-05-08). First polar lunar orbit; mapped 99 % of the near side at 60 m/pixel + far-side regions

fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-5.json.tagline: Final US lunar orbiter (1967-08-05). Completed far-side mapping at 60 m/pixel; impacted 1968-01-31 ahead of Apollo lunar operations
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-5.json.description: Fifth and final Lunar Orbiter spacecraft. Launched 1967-08-01 from Cape Canaveral, entered polar lunar orbit 1967-08-05. Returned 633 frames in 35 days — closing out the Lunar Orbiter programme's near-complete coverage of both lunar hemispheres at high resolution. Imaged 36 high-priority science targets selected from gaps in the earlier Orbiters' coverage and from Surveyor / Apollo landing-site needs. After the 1968-01 end-of-mission decision, deliberately crashed 1968-01-31 at 2.79° S, 83.04° W to clear lunar orbital space ahead of Apollo. The five Orbiters together photographed 99 % of the Moon at 60 m/pixel — until LRO began its 0.5 m/pixel LROC NAC programme in 2009, this was the highest-resolution global lunar map ever made.
fleet/orbiter/lunar-orbiter-5.json.best_known_for: Final US lunar orbiter (1967-08-05). Completed far-side mapping at 60 m/pixel; impacted 1968-01-31 ahead of Apollo lunar operations

fleet/orbiter/lunar-prospector.json.tagline: NASA Discovery polar orbiter — neutron-spectrometer hydrogen finding at both poles 1998; deliberate Shackleton impact ended mission 1999
fleet/orbiter/lunar-prospector.json.description: The third NASA Discovery-class mission (and the first competitively selected) and the first dedicated NASA science mission to the Moon since Explorer 49 (1973). Launched 1998-01-07 on an Athena II from Cape Canaveral, Lunar Prospector entered a 100-km circular polar orbit. Its neutron spectrometer detected sharp neutron-flux deficits over both lunar poles (Feldman et al., 1998 / 1999) — consistent with ~2 × 10⁹ tonnes of hydrogen-rich material (most plausibly water ice) in permanently shadowed polar craters. The gravimeter, magnetometer, gamma-ray and alpha-particle spectrometers also delivered global maps of crustal composition and remnant magnetism. End of mission 1999-07-31: deliberately impacted near Shackleton crater hoping to release a detectable water-vapour plume; none was seen (the lithium-7 fluorescence experiment that would have detected it was a long shot). The hydrogen finding stood until LCROSS (2009) and Chandrayaan-1 / M3 (2009) provided independent confirmation.
fleet/orbiter/lunar-prospector.json.best_known_for: NASA Discovery polar orbiter — neutron-spectrometer hydrogen finding at both poles 1998; deliberate Shackleton impact ended mission 1999

fleet/orbiter/magellan.json.name: Magellan
fleet/orbiter/magellan.json.description: Magellan is a deep-space orbiter built by Martin Marietta in USA. Radar-mapped 98% of Venus's surface. Mission ended in 1994.

fleet/orbiter/mangalyaan.json.name: Mangalyaan (MOM)
fleet/orbiter/mangalyaan.json.tagline: First Asian Mars mission; first successful try
fleet/orbiter/mangalyaan.json.description: India’s first interplanetary mission and the first successful Mars mission by an Asian space agency. Delivered an orbiter to Mars on its first attempt — a feat no other national space agency had managed (ESA, a multi-national organization, succeeded on its first Mars attempt with Mars Express in 2003). Operated for nearly eight years before contact was lost in 2022.
fleet/orbiter/mangalyaan.json.best_known_for: First Asian Mars mission; first successful try

fleet/orbiter/mariner-4.json.name: Mariner 4
fleet/orbiter/mariner-4.json.dispatch: Mariner 4 did what no machine had done: it photographed another planet. Small and spare, built to fly past Mars once and send home whatever it could in the hours it had, it carried a camera and a tape recorder across the solar system and in July 1965 returned the first close-up pictures ever taken of another world — 22 grainy frames of a cratered, moon-like surface. Those images ended a century of speculation about Martian canals and civilisations in a single afternoon, and proved a spacecraft could cross interplanetary space and bring back a planet’s face. Every camera humanity has since sent to another world descends from this one.
fleet/orbiter/mariner-4.json.description: The first successful Mars flyby — July 1965. The 22 grainy black-and-white photos returned ended over a century of speculation about Martian canals and life by showing a cratered, Moon-like surface.

fleet/orbiter/mariner-9.json.name: Mariner 9
fleet/orbiter/mariner-9.json.tagline: First spacecraft to orbit another planet
fleet/orbiter/mariner-9.json.dispatch: Mariner 9 was the first machine to stop at another planet instead of flying past. Where the earlier Mariners glimpsed Mars in a few hours, it carried enough fuel to brake into orbit and stay — and it arrived to find the whole planet buried under a global dust storm. So it waited. When the dust settled it mapped all of Mars, and the survey revealed a world the flybys had missed entirely: the largest volcano in the solar system, a canyon a continent wide, and the dry channels of ancient rivers. It proved that an orbiter patient enough to watch a planet over time sees what no flyby ever can.
fleet/orbiter/mariner-9.json.description: The first spacecraft to orbit another planet (Mars, November 1971). Mapped 100% of the Martian surface — including the global dust storm that hid everything for the first month and the first close-up of Olympus Mons.
fleet/orbiter/mariner-9.json.best_known_for: First spacecraft to orbit another planet

fleet/orbiter/mars-express.json.name: Mars Express
fleet/orbiter/mars-express.json.tagline: ESA's first Mars orbiter; Europe's first planetary mission
fleet/orbiter/mars-express.json.description: Mars Express is a deep-space orbiter built by EADS Astrium in Europe. ESA's first Mars orbiter; Europe's first planetary mission. In service since 2003.
fleet/orbiter/mars-express.json.best_known_for: ESA's first Mars orbiter; Europe's first planetary mission

fleet/orbiter/mars-odyssey.json.tagline: Longest-lived Mars asset ever — orbiting since 2001-10-24. Gamma-ray + neutron water-ice maps; UHF relay for the surface fleet
fleet/orbiter/mars-odyssey.json.description: The longest-lived spacecraft ever to operate at Mars — entered Mars orbit 2001-10-24 and is still active in 2026, surpassing every other Mars mission's lifetime. Launched 2001-04-07 on a Delta II from Cape Canaveral, named after Arthur C. Clarke's '2001: A Space Odyssey'. Carried THEMIS (Thermal Emission Imaging System, 100-m visible / 100-m infrared imaging that mapped global surface mineralogy) and the gamma-ray spectrometer suite GRS + HEND + NS — Boynton et al. (2002, Science 297) used HEND neutron spectroscopy to map global near-surface water ice, the discovery that drove every subsequent lander-mission target selection. Also serves as the primary UHF relay for Mars-surface assets (MERs, MSL, InSight, Perseverance) and a backup for Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Extended-mission fuel reserves expected to last to 2026-2027.
fleet/orbiter/mars-odyssey.json.best_known_for: Longest-lived Mars asset ever — orbiting since 2001-10-24. Gamma-ray + neutron water-ice maps; UHF relay for the surface fleet

fleet/orbiter/mars2-orbiter.json.tagline: Soviet companion orbiter to Mars 2 — second spacecraft ever in Mars orbit (after Mariner 9 by 13 days). Operated 1971-11-27 to 1972-08
fleet/orbiter/mars2-orbiter.json.description: The orbital half of the Soviet Mars 2 mission. Launched 1971-05-19 on a Proton-K from Baikonur, Mars 2 reached Mars 1971-11-27 — just 13 days after Mariner 9 became the first Mars orbiter. Its lander attempted descent on 1971-11-27 but its parachute failed to deploy and the lander crashed (the first man-made object on Mars, but no telemetry). The orbiter half was much more successful, returning ~60 image frames + extensive measurements of the upper atmosphere, magnetic field, and surface temperatures during the same global dust storm that compromised Mariner 9's early imaging. Carried infrared and ultraviolet spectrometers, photometers, a Lyman-alpha sensor, magnetometer, plasma analyser, and cosmic-ray detectors — the same instrument suite as Mars 3 Orbiter. End of mission 1972-08-22 after 362 orbits.
fleet/orbiter/mars2-orbiter.json.best_known_for: Soviet companion orbiter to Mars 2 — second spacecraft ever in Mars orbit (after Mariner 9 by 13 days). Operated 1971-11-27 to 1972-08

fleet/orbiter/mars3-orbiter.json.tagline: Soviet companion orbiter to Mars 3 — orbited Mars from 1971-12-02 through 1972-08; first measurements of Mars upper atmosphere temperature
fleet/orbiter/mars3-orbiter.json.description: The orbital half of the Soviet Mars 3 mission (its lander made the first soft landing on Mars 1971-12-02 but only transmitted for 14.5 seconds before signal loss in a global dust storm). The orbiter was much more successful — entered a highly elliptical 1500 × 211400 km Mars orbit on 1971-12-02, the third spacecraft ever to orbit Mars (after Mariner 9 on 1971-11-14 and Mars 2 Orbiter on 1971-11-27). Carried infrared and ultraviolet spectrometers, photometers, a Lyman-alpha sensor, magnetometer, plasma analyser, and cosmic-ray detectors. Returned the first measurements of the upper atmosphere temperature profile, mapped surface temperatures (peak +13 °C, lowest -93 °C), and confirmed atmospheric water vapour. Returned approximately 60 image-frames; image quality was compromised by Mars' global dust storm that was already in progress when the orbiter arrived. End of mission 1972-08-22.
fleet/orbiter/mars3-orbiter.json.best_known_for: Soviet companion orbiter to Mars 3 — orbited Mars from 1971-12-02 through 1972-08; first measurements of Mars upper atmosphere temperature

fleet/orbiter/maven.json.name: MAVEN
fleet/orbiter/maven.json.tagline: Mars atmospheric loss to solar wind
fleet/orbiter/maven.json.description: NASA's atmospheric orbiter at Mars — Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. In Mars orbit since 2014, studying how the planet lost its early thick atmosphere to solar wind erosion over billions of years.
fleet/orbiter/maven.json.best_known_for: Studying Mars atmospheric loss to solar wind; revealed Mars lost its atmosphere over billions of years

fleet/orbiter/messenger.json.tagline: First Mercury orbiter — 6 planetary gravity assists over 6.6 years to bleed energy before insertion in 2011
fleet/orbiter/messenger.json.description: NASA Discovery-class MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging mission. Launched 2004-08-03 on a Delta II 7925H-9.5. The 6.6-year cruise used 6 gravity assists (1 Earth, 2 Venus, 3 Mercury) to lose ~5 km/s of heliocentric energy — direct orbit insertion would have needed impossible delta-v. Mercury orbit insertion 2011-03-18; mapped the planet for 4 years. Discoveries: water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters, organic-rich dark material at the poles, exosphere composition, a magnetic field offset from the planet centre, abundant hollow-bottomed pits. Impacted Mercury 2015-04-30 after exhausting propellant — left a 16 m artificial crater near the north pole.
fleet/orbiter/messenger.json.best_known_for: First Mercury orbiter — 4 years mapping the planet, ended in controlled impact 2015-04-30

fleet/orbiter/mro.json.name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
fleet/orbiter/mro.json.description: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter is a deep-space orbiter built by Lockheed Martin in USA. Highest-resolution Mars imaging from orbit. In service since 2005.

fleet/orbiter/osiris-rex.json.name: OSIRIS-REx
fleet/orbiter/osiris-rex.json.tagline: Sample-returned Bennu (2023); now en route to Apophis
fleet/orbiter/osiris-rex.json.description: NASA’s asteroid sample-return mission. Approached asteroid Bennu in 2018, captured a sample with its TAGSAM arm in 2020, and returned the sample capsule to Utah in September 2023. Now redesignated OSIRIS-APEX, en route to asteroid Apophis for its 2029 close Earth flyby.
fleet/orbiter/osiris-rex.json.best_known_for: Sample-returned Bennu (2023); now en route to Apophis

fleet/orbiter/parker-solar-probe.json.name: Parker Solar Probe
fleet/orbiter/parker-solar-probe.json.tagline: Closest spacecraft to the Sun ever flown
fleet/orbiter/parker-solar-probe.json.description: NASA's Sun-grazing mission. Launched 2018-08-12 on a Delta IV Heavy + Star 48BV stack at the highest C3 ever achieved for a science payload (154 km²/s²). Seven Venus gravity assists over six years walked perihelion in from 0.16 AU (P1) to 0.046 AU (P22, 2024-12-24) — 9.86 solar radii, 6.1 million km from the Sun's surface. At P8 (2021-04-28) Parker dipped below the Alfvén critical surface — the first spacecraft to enter the Sun's corona. Peak speed at perihelion: 192.22 km/s, the fastest human-made object ever.
fleet/orbiter/parker-solar-probe.json.best_known_for: Closest spacecraft to the Sun ever flown (9.86 R☉)

fleet/orbiter/phobos-2.json.name: Phobos 2
fleet/orbiter/phobos-2.json.tagline: Last Soviet planetary mission; lost at Phobos approach
fleet/orbiter/phobos-2.json.description: The last Soviet planetary mission. Reached Mars orbit in January 1989 but lost contact with Earth on March 27, 1989, just before its planned encounter with the moon Phobos. Phobos 2 returned 37 images of Phobos before contact was lost. The loss was attributed to an on-board computer failure causing loss of attitude control and power, though the complete sequence was never fully reconstructed.
fleet/orbiter/phobos-2.json.best_known_for: Last Soviet planetary mission; lost at Phobos approach

fleet/orbiter/pioneer-10.json.name: Pioneer 10
fleet/orbiter/pioneer-10.json.tagline: First spacecraft to traverse the asteroid belt
fleet/orbiter/pioneer-10.json.description: The first spacecraft to traverse the asteroid belt and the first to fly past Jupiter (December 1973). Carried the Pioneer plaque — the etched gold-anodized aluminium drawing of human figures + solar system that Carl Sagan and Frank Drake designed in three weeks.
fleet/orbiter/pioneer-10.json.best_known_for: First spacecraft to traverse the asteroid belt

fleet/orbiter/pioneer-11.json.tagline: First spacecraft to encounter Saturn — Jupiter flyby in 1974 then gravity-assist to Saturn in 1979
fleet/orbiter/pioneer-11.json.description: Spin-stabilised RTG-powered probe (~259 kg), sibling of Pioneer 10 with the same bus and Pioneer Plaque message-to-the-stars. Launched 1973-04-06 on an Atlas SLV-3D Centaur D-1A + Star-37E from Cape Canaveral. Jupiter flyby 1974-12-03 at 43 000 km — the closest of any Pioneer encounter, returned the first polar-region images and the gravity assist needed to reach Saturn. Saturn encounter 1979-09-01 at 21 000 km from the cloud tops — first detailed images of the ring system, discovery of a new ring (F-ring) and a new moon, confirmation of Saturn's nearly-aligned magnetic field. Continued outbound observations until last contact 1995-11-24. Now ~93 AU from the Sun, headed toward Aquila.
fleet/orbiter/pioneer-11.json.best_known_for: First spacecraft to encounter Saturn — 1979-09-01 flyby, sibling to Pioneer 10

fleet/orbiter/psyche-spacecraft.json.name: Psyche
fleet/orbiter/psyche-spacecraft.json.tagline: First mission to a metal-rich M-class asteroid
fleet/orbiter/psyche-spacecraft.json.description: NASA's mission to a ~230-km M-type asteroid believed to be the exposed metal core of a differentiated proto-planet. Launched 2023-10-13 on a Falcon Heavy from Kennedy LC-39A; uses four SPT-140 Hall-effect ion thrusters as the primary cruise propulsion and a 2026 Mars gravity assist en route to a 2029 Psyche rendezvous. Carries a magnetometer, multispectral imager, and gamma-ray + neutron spectrometer.
fleet/orbiter/psyche-spacecraft.json.best_known_for: First mission to a metal-rich M-class asteroid

fleet/orbiter/rosetta.json.name: Rosetta
fleet/orbiter/rosetta.json.tagline: First spacecraft to orbit a comet (67P)
fleet/orbiter/rosetta.json.description: ESA’s comet rendezvous mission. Caught up to Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko in August 2014, deployed the Philae lander (which bounced and fell into a crevasse), and accompanied the comet through its 2015 perihelion before crash-landing on the surface itself in September 2016.
fleet/orbiter/rosetta.json.best_known_for: First spacecraft to orbit a comet (67P)

fleet/orbiter/smart-1.json.tagline: First European Moon mission — solar-electric ion drive. Spiralled to the Moon over 13 months; deliberate impact 2006-09-03
fleet/orbiter/smart-1.json.description: ESA's first lunar mission and the first European spacecraft to reach the Moon. SMART = Small Missions for Advanced Research in Technology — and the technology that mattered was a Hall-effect solar-electric ion thruster (PPS-1350, the largest such thruster flown at the time). Launched 2003-09-27 as a shared payload on an Ariane 5 from Kourou, the 367-kg spacecraft used its 1.2-kW xenon ion drive over 13 months to slowly raise its Earth orbit, eventually captured by lunar gravity 2004-11-15. Operated for 16 months in a polar lunar orbit, returning high-resolution AMIE camera imagery, the first X-ray fluorescence elemental maps of the Moon (D-CIXS), and infrared mineral spectroscopy (SIR). Deliberately impacted Lacus Excellentiae (34.4° S, 46.2° W) on 2006-09-03 02:42 UTC — the impact flash was observed from the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope.
fleet/orbiter/smart-1.json.best_known_for: First European Moon mission — solar-electric ion drive. Spiralled to the Moon over 13 months; deliberate impact 2006-09-03

fleet/orbiter/solar-orbiter.json.name: Solar Orbiter
fleet/orbiter/solar-orbiter.json.tagline: First detailed imaging of the Sun's polar regions
fleet/orbiter/solar-orbiter.json.description: ESA-led Solar Orbiter is the first spacecraft designed to image the Sun's polar regions in close detail — using repeated Venus gravity assists over a decade to climb out of the ecliptic toward ~33° heliographic inclination. Carries ten instruments combining remote sensing (PHI magnetograph, EUI extreme-UV imager, SPICE spectrometer, STIX X-ray imager, METIS coronagraph, SoloHI heliospheric imager) with in-situ measurement (magnetometer, energetic particles, solar-wind plasma, radio + plasma waves). Launched 2020-02-10 from Cape Canaveral on a NASA Atlas V 411. First perihelion 2020-06-15 at 0.51 AU. Working perihelion 0.28 AU (~62 R☉), inside Mercury's perihelion distance.

fleet/orbiter/tianwen-1.json.name: Tianwen-1
fleet/orbiter/tianwen-1.json.tagline: First Chinese Mars mission; delivered Zhurong
fleet/orbiter/tianwen-1.json.description: CNSA's first Mars mission — an orbiter that carried the Zhurong rover to the Martian surface in May 2021. After releasing Zhurong, the orbiter continued solo science operations including high-resolution imaging and surface mapping.
fleet/orbiter/tianwen-1.json.best_known_for: First Chinese Mars mission; orbiter delivered the Zhurong rover in May 2021

fleet/orbiter/ulysses.json.tagline: First spacecraft to observe the Sun's poles from above + below the ecliptic — Jupiter gravity assist 1992
fleet/orbiter/ulysses.json.description: Joint ESA + NASA solar / heliospheric mission, built by Dornier with US scientific contribution. Launched 1990-10-06 from STS-41 Discovery on a high-energy trajectory direct to Jupiter — the only way to fling a spacecraft out of the ecliptic plane without prohibitive delta-v. Jupiter flyby 1992-02-08 deflected the spacecraft into an 80°-inclination heliocentric orbit (1.3 × 5.4 AU, 6.2-year period) — the first and still only spacecraft to fly over the Sun's poles. Three complete polar orbits gave us the heliospheric current sheet 3D structure, the faster polar / slower equatorial solar wind, and the only multi-decade record of polar coronal hole behaviour over a complete solar cycle. Mission ended 2009.
fleet/orbiter/ulysses.json.best_known_for: Only spacecraft to fly over the Sun's poles — joint ESA / NASA, 1990-2009

fleet/orbiter/vega-1.json.tagline: Soviet Venus + Halley's Comet double mission — Venera lander, first interplanetary balloon, then Halley flyby
fleet/orbiter/vega-1.json.description: First spacecraft of the international Halley armada. Launched 1984-12-15 on a Proton-K / D-1. The 4920 kg flyby bus carried a ~1500 kg descent module that separated for Venus arrival 1985-06-11 — the lander touched down at 7.5°N, 177.8°E for 56 minutes of surface science, while a first-of-kind helium-filled balloon aerostat floated in the cloud deck at 54 km altitude for 46 hours tracking wind speeds and atmospheric structure. The flyby bus continued on its 9-month cruise and encountered comet 1P/Halley 1986-03-06 at 8889 km — the first Halley encounter of the armada, providing the targeting data ESA's Giotto used 8 days later for its much closer 596 km approach.
fleet/orbiter/vega-1.json.best_known_for: Soviet Venus + Halley double mission — first interplanetary balloon, first Halley flyby

fleet/orbiter/vega-2.json.tagline: Sibling of Vega 1 — second Soviet Venus + Halley double mission, lander + balloon then Halley flyby
fleet/orbiter/vega-2.json.description: Identical twin of Vega 1, launched 1984-12-21 (6 days after Vega 1). 4920 kg flyby bus + ~1500 kg descent module with second Venera-style lander + helium aerostat. Venus arrival 1985-06-15: lander touched down at 8.5°S, 164.5°E (Aphrodite Terra), returned 57 minutes of surface science; balloon floated in the cloud deck for 46 hours alongside Vega 1's. The flyby bus continued and encountered comet 1P/Halley 1986-03-09 at 8030 km — the second Halley encounter of the armada, 3 days after Vega 1 and 5 days before Giotto. Vega 1 + Vega 2 tracking refined the Halley nucleus position to within 50 km for Giotto's much closer approach.
fleet/orbiter/vega-2.json.best_known_for: Sibling of Vega 1 — second Soviet Venus + Halley double mission, 1986-03-09 Halley flyby

fleet/orbiter/viking1-orbiter.json.tagline: Companion orbiter to Viking-1 lander — relay + 50000 surface images at 150-300 m/pixel, the first global Mars map. Operated 1976-1980
fleet/orbiter/viking1-orbiter.json.description: The orbital half of NASA's Viking 1 mission — the first US Mars orbiter and one of two near-identical Viking orbiters that returned ~50,000 surface images at 150-300 m/pixel between 1976 and 1980. Launched 1975-08-20 from Cape Canaveral on a Titan IIIE-Centaur, Viking 1 entered Mars orbit 1976-06-19; the orbiter spent a month surveying candidate landing sites before releasing the Viking 1 lander 1976-07-20 to the first successful US Mars landing at Chryse Planitia. The orbiter then continued as a science platform for nearly four more years, building the first global topographic + thermal map of Mars, surveying Phobos + Deimos, and acting as a UHF relay for the lander. Out of attitude-control gas 1980-08-07. Deliberately raised to a 357 × 33614 km park orbit that's expected to remain stable through ~2024 (decayed ~2025 per Aerospace Corp re-entry forecast).
fleet/orbiter/viking1-orbiter.json.best_known_for: Companion orbiter to Viking-1 lander — relay + 50000 surface images at 150-300 m/pixel, the first global Mars map. Operated 1976-1980

fleet/orbiter/voyager-1.json.name: Voyager 1
fleet/orbiter/voyager-1.json.description: The most distant human-made object — over 25 billion kilometers from the Sun and growing. Crossed the heliopause into interstellar space on August 25, 2012. Carries the Golden Record. Still transmitting on its 470 W RTG.

fleet/orbiter/voyager-2.json.name: Voyager 2
fleet/orbiter/voyager-2.json.tagline: Only spacecraft to visit all four giant planets
fleet/orbiter/voyager-2.json.description: The only spacecraft to visit all four giant planets — Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1981), Uranus (1986), Neptune (1989). Followed its twin Voyager 1 into interstellar space in November 2018. Carries an identical Golden Record.
fleet/orbiter/voyager-2.json.best_known_for: Only spacecraft to visit all four giant planets

fleet/rover/curiosity.json.name: Curiosity (MSL)
fleet/rover/curiosity.json.description: NASA’s nuclear-powered Mars Science Laboratory rover, on Mars since August 2012. Discovered organic molecules, ancient stream-bed environments, and evidence that Mars’ Gale Crater was habitable in the past. Still operational over a decade later.

fleet/rover/exomars-rosalind-franklin.js.tagline: ESA's 2028 Mars rover — 2-m drill to search for biosignatures at Oxia Planum. Paused by Roscosmos pull-out 2022, retargeted to NASA launch
fleet/rover/exomars-rosalind-franklin.js.description: ESA's first Mars rover, named after the DNA pioneer Rosalind Franklin. Designed to land at Oxia Planum (an ancient clay-bearing Mars region selected for high biosignature-preservation potential) and use a 2-metre subsurface drill — deeper than any prior Mars mission — to acquire samples from depths protected from the cosmic-ray and UV radiation that destroys surface organics. The Analytical Laboratory Drawer holds three life-detection instruments: MOMA (Mars Organic Molecule Analyser, a gas chromatograph + dual-source mass spectrometer), MicrOmega (infrared imaging spectroscopy), and the Raman Laser Spectrometer. Originally targeted for 2022 launch on a Russian Proton with a Russian-built landing platform (Kazachok); after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, ESA suspended cooperation, and Rosalind Franklin's launch was deferred. Currently scheduled for 2028 on a NASA-provided launch vehicle with an ESA / Airbus-rebuilt landing platform.
fleet/rover/exomars-rosalind-franklin.js.best_known_for: ESA's 2028 Mars rover — 2-m drill to search for biosignatures at Oxia Planum. Paused by Roscosmos pull-out 2022, retargeted to NASA launch

fleet/rover/lrv-apollo.json.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle
fleet/rover/lrv-apollo.json.dispatch: The Lunar Rover was the first car on another world, and its entire reason to exist was reach. On foot, an astronaut can't stray far from the lander — walk too far out and you can't walk back if the suit starts to fail. Wheels rewrote that math: Apollo 15 through 17 ranged kilometres from home, turning a single landing spot into a proper field area and letting geologists actually choose where to look. Building it was its own puzzle — it had to fold flat into a wedge on the side of the Lunar Module, unfold on the surface, then drive through abrasive dust and hundreds of degrees of temperature swing on wire-mesh wheels and battery power. It never went fast. It went far, and that was the whole point.
fleet/rover/lrv-apollo.json.description: The Lunar Roving Vehicle — the first crewed rover. Three Apollos (15, 16, 17) used it to extend their surface exploration, covering up to 35.9 km per mission (Apollo 17 record). Built by Boeing and Delco; folded into the LM’s descent stage.

fleet/rover/lunokhod-1.json.name: Lunokhod 1
fleet/rover/lunokhod-1.json.tagline: First wheeled vehicle to roam another world
fleet/rover/lunokhod-1.json.description: The first wheeled vehicle to roam another world. Operated for ten months on the Moon’s Mare Imbrium between November 1970 and September 1971, driven via radio link by a five-person team in Crimea. A pressurised "tub" warmed by a polonium heater overnight.
fleet/rover/lunokhod-1.json.best_known_for: First wheeled vehicle to roam another world

fleet/rover/lunokhod-2.json.name: Lunokhod 2
fleet/rover/lunokhod-2.json.tagline: Roamed 39 km on the Moon — record till 2014
fleet/rover/lunokhod-2.json.description: Lunokhod 2 is a planetary rover built by NPO Lavochkin in USSR. Roamed 39 km on the Moon — record till 2014. Mission ended in 1973.
fleet/rover/lunokhod-2.json.best_known_for: Roamed 39 km on the Moon — record till 2014

fleet/rover/opportunity.json.name: Opportunity (MER-B)
fleet/rover/opportunity.json.description: Opportunity (MER-B) is a planetary rover built by NASA JPL in USA. Twin to Spirit; operated for nearly 15 years on Mars. Set the off-world driving record at 45.16 km and discovered hematite 'blueberries' indicating past water. Retired 2019.
fleet/rover/opportunity.json.best_known_for: Twin to Spirit; ~15-year, 45 km Mars operation

fleet/rover/perseverance.json.name: Perseverance (Mars 2020)
fleet/rover/perseverance.json.description: NASA’s sample-caching rover, on Mars since February 2021. Carried Ingenuity, the first off-Earth helicopter; has collected 33 of 43 sample tubes for eventual return to Earth. Looking for biosignatures in Jezero Crater’s ancient delta.

fleet/rover/pragyan.json.name: Pragyan
fleet/rover/pragyan.json.description: Pragyan is a planetary rover built by ISRO in India. First lunar south-pole rover; Chandrayaan-3. Dormant since 2023.

fleet/rover/sojourner.json.name: Sojourner
fleet/rover/sojourner.json.description: Sojourner is a planetary rover built by NASA JPL in USA. First Mars rover; Pathfinder mission. Mission ended in 1997.

fleet/rover/spirit.json.name: Spirit (MER-A)
fleet/rover/spirit.json.description: Spirit (MER-A) is a planetary rover built by NASA JPL in USA. Mars Exploration Rover; 6-year operation. Last contact in 2010.

fleet/rover/yutu-2.json.name: Yutu-2
fleet/rover/yutu-2.json.tagline: First rover on the lunar far side; Chang'e-4
fleet/rover/yutu-2.json.description: China’s Chang’e-4 rover, the first rover to operate on the lunar far side. Landed in Von Kármán crater in January 2019 and operated for over six years, far exceeding its three-month design lifetime; largely stationary since early 2024.
fleet/rover/yutu-2.json.best_known_for: First rover on the lunar far side; Chang'e-4

fleet/rover/yutu.json.name: Yutu
fleet/rover/yutu.json.description: Yutu is a planetary rover built by CAST in China. First Chinese lunar rover; Chang'e-3. Mission ended in 2016.

fleet/rover/zhurong.json.name: Zhurong
fleet/rover/zhurong.json.description: Zhurong is a planetary rover built by CAST in China. First Chinese Mars rover; Tianwen-1. Dormant since 2022.

fleet/space-suit/a7l.json.name: Apollo A7L
fleet/space-suit/a7l.json.tagline: The first operational lunar surface suit — Apollo 11 through 14
fleet/space-suit/a7l.json.dispatch: A pressure suit on the Moon is really a spacecraft you wear — the smallest crewed vehicle Apollo built, sized for one. The A7L had to do everything a capsule does — hold pressure, supply oxygen, carry away heat and exhaled carbon dioxide, shield against a temperature swing of hundreds of degrees between sunlight and shadow — while still letting a person kneel, walk, and pick up a rock. Those two demands fight each other, because anything holding pressure wants to go stiff as a balloon. Its answer was twenty-one layers built around a rubber-coated bladder, with the backpack making the whole thing self-contained for hours. It was the first suit rated to walk on another world, and for its missions it was the only thing between a human being and vacuum.
fleet/space-suit/a7l.json.description: First operational lunar surface suit. Hard upper torso, soft-fabric arms and legs, integrated lunar overboots, PLSS backpack with sublimator cooling and LiOH CO₂ scrubber, OPS emergency O₂ cylinder above the PLSS. Operating pressure 3.7 psi pure O₂ — lowest of any flown suit, to maximise mobility for walking in 1/6 g. Flew on Apollo 11 (the first Moonwalk), Apollo 12, and Apollo 13–14. Worn by Buzz Aldrin in the iconic gold-visor lunar surface photo.
fleet/space-suit/a7l.json.best_known_for: The suit worn on Apollo 11–14 — the first to support EVA on another world

fleet/space-suit/a7lb.json.name: Apollo A7LB
fleet/space-suit/a7lb.json.tagline: The J-mission suit — added a waist joint so astronauts could sit in the Lunar Rover
fleet/space-suit/a7lb.json.dispatch: Sometimes a whole era of exploration turns on one joint. The A7LB was the A7L with a flexible convolution added at the waist — a small-sounding change that let an astronaut bend at the middle and sit down. That is the difference between walking a couple of kilometres from the lander and driving a rover across tens of them; between a two-hour moonwalk and a three-day field campaign. The last three Apollo landings — the long-stay science missions with the rover and, finally, a trained geologist — were only possible because the suit at last let people sit, reach, and work for hours at a stretch. The engineering headline is a waist joint; the result was the most productive science of the entire program.
fleet/space-suit/a7lb.json.description: A7L derivative for the extended J-class lunar missions. The signature change was a waist-joint convolution that allowed astronauts to bend forward and sit in the Lunar Roving Vehicle — without it, the J-mission EVAs of Apollo 15, 16, and 17 would not have been possible. Same PLSS, OPS, and 3.7 psi pressure as A7L; same gold visor. Also used on Skylab 2, 3, and 4 (1973–1974) in a modified configuration, with final EVA on February 3, 1974.
fleet/space-suit/a7lb.json.best_known_for: The J-mission suit (Apollo 15, 16, 17) — added a waist convolution that let astronauts sit in the Lunar Roving Vehicle

fleet/space-suit/aces.json.name: ACES
fleet/space-suit/aces.json.tagline: The orange Shuttle pressure suit worn after Challenger made shirtsleeve ascent unacceptable
fleet/space-suit/aces.json.description: Full-pressure launch-entry suit developed by David Clark Company. Replaced the earlier Launch Entry Suit (LES) starting in 1994. Detachable gloves, parachute harness integrated, distinctive international-orange colour for water-recovery visibility. Worn on every Space Shuttle ascent and re-entry through STS-135 in 2011.
fleet/space-suit/aces.json.best_known_for: The orange "pumpkin" suit worn for every Space Shuttle launch and re-entry after Challenger

fleet/space-suit/axemu.json.name: AxEMU
fleet/space-suit/axemu.json.tagline: Next-gen US EVA suit, to be tested on Artemis III
fleet/space-suit/axemu.json.description: Axiom Space's contracted EVA suit for NASA's Artemis lunar return. Heritage from the EMU but with mobility joints comparable to Apollo's A7LB, a regenerable amine CO₂ scrubber, HD video in the helmet, and dust-resistant joints for lunar surface use. Outer-layer styling by Prada. In qualification testing; to be tested in Earth orbit on Artemis III (2027) and worn on the Moon from Artemis IV.
fleet/space-suit/axemu.json.best_known_for: Next-generation US EVA suit, to be worn on the first Artemis landing (Artemis IV)

fleet/space-suit/crew-dragon-iva.json.name: SpaceX IVA Suit
fleet/space-suit/crew-dragon-iva.json.tagline: The white slim-fit Crew Dragon IVA suit, flown since Demo-2
fleet/space-suit/crew-dragon-iva.json.description: SpaceX-designed launch-entry pressure suit. Single-piece front-entry, touchscreen-capable gloves to operate Crew Dragon's tablet console, custom-3D-printed helmets fitted to each crew member. Worn for ascent and re-entry on Crew Dragon. Distinctive minimalist white-and-black aesthetic.
fleet/space-suit/crew-dragon-iva.json.best_known_for: The white slim-fit IVA suit worn on every NASA ISS Crew Dragon flight since Demo-2

fleet/space-suit/emu.json.name: EMU
fleet/space-suit/emu.json.tagline: The white US spacewalk suit — every American EVA from the Shuttle to the ISS
fleet/space-suit/emu.json.description: Extravehicular Mobility Unit — modular EVA suit with a hard upper torso, soft fabric arms and legs, and a Primary Life Support System backpack. Operates at 4.3 psi pure O₂. First EVA flown on STS-6 (April 1983) and still in service on the ISS more than 40 years later. SAFER mini-thruster pack added in 1994 for tether-loss rescue (1.4 kg N₂, ~3 m/s Δv).
fleet/space-suit/emu.json.best_known_for: The white US spacewalk suit that has flown every American EVA from the Shuttle through the ISS

fleet/space-suit/feitian.json.name: Feitian
fleet/space-suit/feitian.json.tagline: China's EVA suit — derived from the Orlan, first flown on Shenzhou 7 in 2008
fleet/space-suit/feitian.json.description: Chinese rear-entry EVA suit with architectural similarities to the Soviet Orlan design. First flown on Shenzhou 7 in 2008 when Zhai Zhigang became the first Chinese taikonaut to spacewalk. Now in operational use on the Tiangong space station's Wentian airlock. The name means "flying heaven" — a reference to the celestial flying spirits (feitian) from Buddhist cave art at Dunhuang, depicted on the suit's arm badge.
fleet/space-suit/feitian.json.best_known_for: China's EVA suit — used by Zhai Zhigang on the country's first spacewalk during Shenzhou 7

fleet/space-suit/krechet-94.json.name: Krechet-94
fleet/space-suit/krechet-94.json.tagline: The Soviet lunar suit that never flew — its DNA lives in every Orlan and Feitian
fleet/space-suit/krechet-94.json.description: Soviet lunar surface suit developed for the cancelled N1/L3 crewed lunar program. Single-piece rear-entry design with the PLSS built into the back hatch — the architectural pattern shared with the Orlan (both developed concurrently in 1967–1969) and later adopted by the Feitian. Krechet hardware survived the program's cancellation and lives in museum collections (notably the Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics, Moscow). Name means "gyrfalcon" — the largest of the Falcon birds.
fleet/space-suit/krechet-94.json.best_known_for: The Soviet lunar suit that never reached the Moon — its rear-entry architecture became the DNA of every Russian and Chinese EVA suit since

fleet/space-suit/orlan-mks.json.name: Orlan-MKS
fleet/space-suit/orlan-mks.json.tagline: The latest of a 50-year line of Russian rear-entry EVA suits
fleet/space-suit/orlan-mks.json.description: Latest variant of the Orlan family — Russian rear-entry EVA suit that has flown continuously since Salyut 6 in 1977. The cosmonaut steps in through a backpack-mounted hatch that locks shut in one motion, eliminating the airlock pre-breathe required by lower-pressure US suits. Operating pressure 5.8 psi (400 hPa) pure O₂. Used on the ISS Russian segment. Earlier Orlan variants served on Salyut and Mir stations.
fleet/space-suit/orlan-mks.json.best_known_for: The latest variant of the Orlan family — Russian rear-entry EVA suit, in service since the 1977 Salyut program

fleet/space-suit/shenzhou-iva.json.name: Shenzhou IVA Suit
fleet/space-suit/shenzhou-iva.json.tagline: China's launch-entry suit, worn on every Shenzhou flight since 2003
fleet/space-suit/shenzhou-iva.json.description: Chinese launch-entry pressure suit derived from the Soviet Sokol family. Used on Shenzhou 5 in 2003 when Yang Liwei became China's first taikonaut, and on every subsequent Shenzhou mission. Back-entry seam, fixed helmet, umbilical-fed; the architectural similarity to Sokol reflects China's early space-program technology transfer from Russia.
fleet/space-suit/shenzhou-iva.json.best_known_for: Worn by every Chinese taikonaut on every Shenzhou flight since 2003

fleet/space-suit/sokol-kv-2.json.name: Sokol KV-2
fleet/space-suit/sokol-kv-2.json.tagline: The Soyuz launch-entry suit, mandatory since the 1971 Soyuz 11 decompression deaths
fleet/space-suit/sokol-kv-2.json.description: Soft pressure suit worn inside the Soyuz descent module on every launch and re-entry since Soyuz T-2 in 1980, replacing the original Sokol-K. Back-entry seam (laced shut), fixed helmet with flip-up visor, umbilical for O₂ + comms + cooling water. Not designed for spacewalking — it is the backup that keeps the crew alive long enough to land if cabin pressure fails.
fleet/space-suit/sokol-kv-2.json.best_known_for: The only suit worn on Soyuz — created after the Soyuz 11 decompression deaths in 1971

fleet/space-suit/sokol-m.json.name: Sokol-M
fleet/space-suit/sokol-m.json.description: Replacement for Sokol KV-2 — incorporates lessons learned over 50 years of Soyuz launch-entry operations. Slated for Russia's PTK / Orel crewed spacecraft. Same general architecture (back-entry, umbilical-fed) with modernised materials and ergonomics.

fleet/space-suit/starliner-suit.json.name: Boeing Blue (Starliner IVA)
fleet/space-suit/starliner-suit.json.description: Lightweight launch-entry pressure suit built by David Clark Company for Boeing's CST-100 Starliner commercial-crew vehicle. Touch-screen-compatible gloves, integrated communications cap, vented helmet. Debuted on the Crew Flight Test mission (June 2024) flown by Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams, who returned via Crew-9 in February 2025 after Starliner returned uncrewed.
fleet/space-suit/starliner-suit.json.best_known_for: Boeing's blue IVA suit for the CST-100 Starliner, debuted on the Crew Flight Test 2024

fleet/station/iss.json.name: International Space Station
fleet/station/iss.json.dispatch: The International Space Station is the largest structure humanity has ever built in space and the place every thread of the space age converges. Its Russian core descends directly from Salyut and Mir; its American segment from Skylab; it was assembled by the Space Shuttle, is crewed by Soyuz, resupplied by the descendants of the Progress freighter, and carries laboratories built by Europe and Japan — nearly every earlier program present in it as heritage. Assembled from 1998 and continuously crewed since November 2000, it is the longest unbroken human presence off Earth in history, and the clearest proof of a single idea: that the greatest things in space are built not by winning a race but by former rivals choosing, decade after decade, to build them together.
fleet/station/iss.json.description: The International Space Station — humanity’s longest continuously crewed habitat, occupied since November 2000. Assembled across more than 40 launches by NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, and CSA. Currently scheduled for deorbit around 2031.

fleet/station/mir.json.name: Mir
fleet/station/mir.json.dispatch: Mir was the first modular space station — and the bridge between two eras of spaceflight. Where every station before it was launched whole, Mir was assembled in orbit over a decade, module by module, growing into a sprawling complex that stayed aloft for fifteen years. It set the endurance record that still stands (Valeri Polyakov's 437 unbroken days, proof a crew could survive a Mars-length flight), outlived the Soviet Union that built it by a decade, and survived a fire and a depressurising collision in 1997 that its crew fought off by hand. In its final years American Shuttles docked with it and US astronauts lived aboard — the rehearsal, in hardware and in trust, for the International Space Station that inherited nearly everything Mir worked out.
fleet/station/mir.json.description: The first modular space station, assembled in orbit between 1986 and 1996 and continuously occupied for almost 10 years (1989–1999), with a final crew visit in April–June 2000. Hosted American astronauts during the Shuttle-Mir program (1995–1998) — the partnership that made ISS possible.

fleet/station/salyut-1.json.name: Salyut 1
fleet/station/salyut-1.json.dispatch: Salyut 1 was the first space station in history — launched in April 1971, two years ahead of America's Skylab, and the moment the Soviet Union turned its lead in endurance into a permanent presence in orbit. Its triumph was also its tragedy: the first crew to live aboard it, Soyuz 11, died during their return when a valve vented their cabin to vacuum, and the station was never occupied again. It proved a station could be built and reached — and, at the highest cost, taught the lesson that reshaped every crewed spacecraft after it.
fleet/station/salyut-1.json.description: The world’s first space station — launched 1971, occupied for 23 days by the Soyuz 11 crew (Dobrovolski, Volkov, Patsayev), all of whom died on return when their capsule depressurised. Salyut 1 was deorbited later that year.

fleet/station/salyut-2.json.tagline: First Almaz military station — depressurised on orbit before any crew arrived; reentered 1973-05-28 after 54 days
fleet/station/salyut-2.json.dispatch: Salyut 2 was not really a Salyut at all — it was the first Almaz, a secret military reconnaissance station flown under the civilian name to hide its purpose. It never carried a crew. Days after reaching orbit it lost pressure and began to tumble, its systems failing, and it re-entered without ever being occupied. A rough, hidden start to the military half of the programme, and a reminder of how unforgiving the early station-building years were.
fleet/station/salyut-2.json.description: The first of the three Soviet military Almaz space stations — publicly called Salyut 2 to disguise its real purpose (DoD-style reconnaissance, with a 6.4-m focal-length panoramic camera and a film-return capsule). Launched 1973-04-03 on a Proton-K from Baikonur, Salyut 2 reached orbit successfully but debris from the Proton's spent third stage — which exploded three days after launch — struck the station ~10 days later, tearing off both solar panels and puncturing the hull. The resulting power loss caused depressurisation on the 13th day (1973-04-14), rendering the station unusable before any crew could be sent. The planned crew (Pavel Popovich + Yury Artyukhin) instead flew on Salyut 3 the following year. Salyut 2 reentered the atmosphere 1973-05-28 — the shortest-lived station program in history at that point. Its existence as a military station was only declassified after the Soviet Union's collapse.
fleet/station/salyut-2.json.best_known_for: First Almaz military station — depressurised on orbit before any crew arrived; reentered 1973-05-28 after 54 days

fleet/station/salyut-3.json.tagline: Second Almaz military station — Soyuz 14 crew Jul 1974; Soyuz 15 failed automatic docking; reportedly tested an onboard cannon 1975-01-24
fleet/station/salyut-3.json.dispatch: Salyut 3 was Almaz — a crewed military reconnaissance station, its true purpose buried under the civilian name. Its single crew, Soyuz 14, spent about two weeks aboard operating long-focus cameras to photograph targets below, in the era before automated spy satellites made human eyes unnecessary. Most famously, before it was deorbited, Salyut 3 test-fired a rapid-fire cannon in orbit — the only known instance of a weapon being fired from a crewed spacecraft.
fleet/station/salyut-3.json.description: The second Soviet military Almaz station — again publicly called Salyut 3 to mask its surveillance role. Launched 1974-06-25 on a Proton-K, Salyut 3 hosted one short crew mission (Soyuz 14, Popovich + Artyukhin, 15 days, 1974-07-03 to 1974-07-19) which exercised the station's 6.4-m Agat camera + film-return capsule. A second crew attempt (Soyuz 15, Sarafanov + Demin, 1974-08-26) failed the automatic Igla rendezvous and returned the same day. Just before deorbit on 1975-01-24, Salyut 3 reportedly test-fired its onboard Nudelman cannon (sources cite either 23-mm or 30-mm calibre) — the only known instance of a weapon firing in space (recoil was absorbed by the station's attitude-control thrusters; the round disintegrated in the atmosphere). Reentered the atmosphere 1975-01-24.
fleet/station/salyut-3.json.best_known_for: Second Almaz military station — Soyuz 14 crew Jul 1974; Soyuz 15 failed automatic docking; reportedly tested an onboard cannon 1975-01-24

fleet/station/salyut-4.json.tagline: Civilian DOS-4 station — hosted Soyuz 17 (29 days) + Soyuz 18 (63 days, then-longest spaceflight) crews; deorbited 1977-02-03
fleet/station/salyut-4.json.dispatch: Salyut 4 was where the civilian station line finally found its feet. A DOS science station, it worked reliably where earlier stations had failed — hosting two crews, one for 29 days and one for 63, and carrying a solar telescope and a full science program. After the deadly start of Salyut 1 and the on-orbit failures that followed, Salyut 4 was the quiet proof that the Soviet Union could now keep a station and its crews healthy and productive for weeks at a time.
fleet/station/salyut-4.json.description: The fourth civilian Salyut (DOS-4), built by the Korolev bureau and operated by the Soviet civilian space programme rather than the military Almaz line. Launched 1974-12-26 on a Proton-K, Salyut 4 carried a 25-cm OST-1 solar telescope, an X-ray telescope, and a complement of life-sciences experiments. Hosted two long-duration crews: Soyuz 17 (Gubarev + Grechko, 29 days, 1975-01-11 to 1975-02-09) and Soyuz 18 (Klimuk + Sevastyanov, 63 days, 1975-05-24 to 1975-07-26, then the longest crewed spaceflight in history). A third attempt — Soyuz 18a (Lazarev + Makarov, 1975-04-05) — suffered a 21-g booster failure during launch, returning the crew safely after the highest-ever landing g-load survived by humans. Salyut 4 hosted Soyuz 20, an automated dog/biological-experiment 3-month visit, before re-entering on 1977-02-03 after 26 months.
fleet/station/salyut-4.json.best_known_for: Civilian DOS-4 station — hosted Soyuz 17 (29 days) + Soyuz 18 (63 days, then-longest spaceflight) crews; deorbited 1977-02-03

fleet/station/salyut-5.json.tagline: Last Almaz military station — Soyuz 21 + Soyuz 24 crews; Soyuz 23 failed approach; reentered 1977-08-08 after 412 days
fleet/station/salyut-5.json.dispatch: Salyut 5 was the last of the Almaz military stations, flown in 1976 under the usual civilian disguise. Two crews were sent: the first, Soyuz 21, was evacuated early amid reports of a foul odour and a stressed crew; the second, Soyuz 24, completed a normal stay. Soon after, automated reconnaissance satellites had improved to the point that cosmonauts with cameras were no longer worth the risk, and the military Almaz line was quietly retired — leaving the future to the civilian stations.
fleet/station/salyut-5.json.description: The third and last Soviet military Almaz station. Launched 1976-06-22 on a Proton-K, Salyut 5 hosted two crews: Soyuz 21 (Volynov + Zholobov, 49 days, 1976-07-06 to 1976-08-24 — cut short by acrid odours the crew traced to a corroded film-return capsule seal) and Soyuz 24 (Gorbatko + Glazkov, 17 days, 1977-02-07 to 1977-02-25 — first cosmonauts to swap a station's atmosphere through vent + recharge). Soyuz 23 (Zudov + Rozhdestvensky, 1976-10-14) failed to dock after the Igla rendezvous system malfunctioned; the crew survived a high-water splashdown in Lake Tengiz, the only Soviet water landing. Salyut 5 was the last Almaz mission flown — the program was cancelled after the station deorbited on 1977-08-08.
fleet/station/salyut-5.json.best_known_for: Last Almaz military station — Soyuz 21 + Soyuz 24 crews; Soyuz 23 failed approach; reentered 1977-08-08 after 412 days

fleet/station/salyut-6.json.name: Salyut 6
fleet/station/salyut-6.json.dispatch: Salyut 6 was the breakthrough — the station where the Soviet programme cracked permanence. Its second docking port meant an uncrewed Progress freighter could dock and pump in propellant, air, water, and supplies while a crewed Soyuz stayed attached at the other end, so the station no longer had an expiry date. It hosted crew after crew in continuous relay, set endurance records past half a year, and welcomed the first Interkosmos guests — the first people in space who were neither American nor Soviet. Every operational pattern of Mir and the ISS was rehearsed here.
fleet/station/salyut-6.json.description: The first multi-port Salyut, capable of receiving Progress resupply ships and rotating long-duration crews. Continuously occupied (with breaks) for nearly five years between 1977 and 1982 — the model for every modular station that followed.

fleet/station/salyut-7.json.name: Salyut 7
fleet/station/salyut-7.json.dispatch: Salyut 7 was the last Salyut and the bridge to Mir — and the setting for the hardest repair job ever attempted in orbit. In 1985, after the abandoned station fell silent, frozen, and slowly tumbling, two cosmonauts flew up, manually docked with the dead and unpowered hulk, and brought it back to life by hand, thawing it out and restarting its systems one by one. Salyut 7 carried the two-port, Progress-resupplied architecture to full maturity and handed it, essentially complete, to the modular station that would replace it.
fleet/station/salyut-7.json.description: The last Salyut, in service 1982–1991. Famously revived by Vladimir Dzhanibekov and Viktor Savinykh in 1985 after losing power and tumbling — the first orbital salvage mission. Reentered uncontrolled in 1991 over Argentina.

fleet/station/skylab.json.name: Skylab
fleet/station/skylab.json.dispatch: Skylab was America's first space station, and one of history's great acts of improvisation — an entire orbital workshop built inside the empty hydrogen tank of a spent Saturn V upper stage. Rather than design a station from scratch, NASA converted the hardware the cancelled Moon landings had left over into a house-sized laboratory with crew quarters, a shower, and a crewed solar observatory. Nearly destroyed at launch when its sun shield tore away, it was saved by the first crew's improvised repairs and went on to prove the thing every later station assumed: that people can live and work in orbit for months, and fix their spacecraft when it breaks.
fleet/station/skylab.json.description: America’s first space station, built from a Saturn V S-IVB upper stage. Three crews of three each lived aboard between 1973 and 1974, conducting solar observations and zero-g experiments. Reentered uncontrolled over Australia in 1979.

fleet/station/tiangong-1.json.name: Tiangong-1
fleet/station/tiangong-1.json.tagline: First Chinese space station; single-module testbed
fleet/station/tiangong-1.json.description: Tiangong-1 is a space station built by CAST in China. First Chinese space station; single-module testbed. Launched in 2011, hosted two crewed visits (Shenzhou 9 in 2012 and Shenzhou 10 in 2013); contact lost March 2016 and reentered uncontrolled April 2, 2018.
fleet/station/tiangong-1.json.best_known_for: First Chinese space station; single-module testbed

fleet/station/tiangong-2.json.name: Tiangong-2
fleet/station/tiangong-2.json.description: Tiangong-2 is a space station built by CAST in China. Second Chinese station testbed. Launched in September 2016, hosted Shenzhou 11 (30-day mission, October–November 2016, China's longest crewed mission at the time) and Tianzhou-1 cargo ship (2017); deorbited July 19, 2019.

fleet/station/tiangong.json.name: Tiangong
fleet/station/tiangong.json.description: China’s modular space station — Tianhe core plus Wentian and Mengtian science labs, fully assembled in October 2022 and continuously crewed since June 2022. With a mass of ~66 t and pressurised volume of ~110 m³, Tiangong is smaller than Mir (130 t) but represents China’s permanent station capability; the only currently-operational space station outside ISS.
